articles.title: 100,000 Britons bought into SpaceX – our growth companies should be next
articles.summary:
If we want people to be able to share in the growth of the companies like SpaceX that they use every day then access before they list on the public markets matters as much as gaining access after an IPO, says Andy Field

There was a lot of coverage globally when Space X floated in June this year. Over 100,000 UK investors applied for shares (almost $1bn of orders) in what was the largest IPO in history. At the same time – others across the globe, including Germany, France, Japan, Australia and Canada were also investing. None of these countries had to re-write its rules to enable this as each of them used a gateway which was already established and set up. In the UK, this was the ‘Public Offer Platform Regime’ which the FCA brought into play this January. This effectively lets companies raising over £5m sell shares widely without a stock market listing.

SpaceX was offering retail investors the opportunity to invest on the same terms as the big banks and institutions “pre-IPO”.  In many respects, the risk of the business mirror those of many private companies looking to scale up in the UK, just on a global scale. The time has come for a grown-up discussion about the benefits of investing in these types of companies as part of a diversified portfolio.

Most of the growth of a company now happens before most of us get the opportunity to ‘buy in’. By the time everyday investors get their chance, much of the value has already gone to the funds and wealthy investors who were able to get in early. I think that if we want people to be able to share in the growth of the companies that they use every day then access before they list on the public markets matters as much as gaining access after an IPO.

Of course, regulated crowdfunding (the UK being one of its pioneers) has been working to achieve this for more than a decade now yet the gateways that worked for Space X don’t work for (for example) a small fast-growing company in Manchester seeking investors from outside the UK. In the EU, there is one licence (ECSPR) which covers the whole single market yet even then only eight per cent of the money raised through EU crowdfunding platforms in 2024 came from investors outside of the platform’s own country.

Mutual recognition

What seems to be holding things back is a lack understanding and mutual recognition. Firms have strict limits on how much they can raise, compliance costs for platforms are huge, disclosures can’t easily be compared between countries and settlements are slow (and manual) for smaller issuers. But importantly each jurisdiction writes its rules in isolation treating the world outside the national boundary as almost irrelevant.

Research from the Global Equity Crowdfunding Alliance (GECA) suggests that the fixes to these should be achievable by the policymakers, regulators and platforms that are in place now. Examples include recognising where national rules already achieve the same outcome across territories, secondary markets (allowing for an exit strategy) should be built at the same time as fundraising, a common baseline for what information investors are given could be agreed and new settlement technologies could be properly tested with findings both good and bad being published and shared.

GECA has just released a position paper as a result of a global discussion about the Space X raise and its possible implications for the crowdfunding industry. The problems and suggested fixes that I mention above are included in the recommendations of that paper.

I think that the UK is one of the territories that is in prime position to become the global hub for private market fundraising. Here in the UK, we have a regulator that has shown it can open new routes to market, a well-established and experienced crowdfunding industry and, when considering the Space X raise, we also have proof that British retail investors will turn up in their tens of thousands when they’re given a way in. I guess at the minute what is missing is the ambition to have it all joined up across borders. But that’s where GECA steps in.

Andy Field is executive steering committee lead at the Global Equity Crowdfunding Alliance (GECA) and a director of the UK Crowdfunding Association.

articles.title: Lord Agnew: AI has made the need for better numeracy more urgent
articles.summary:
Bringing more everyday maths into the classroom is a good start – now the government should go further, writes Lord Agnew

When I was a Treasury minister, I was struck by how crucial just three concepts are to the maths that every adult in the UK must understand: inflation, compound interest and spreading risk. These core principles underpin the vast majority of the big financial decisions adults will make in their lives, from taking out a mortgage, deciding which credit card offers the best value or investing in an ISA. And most immediate of all, the huge commitment to student debt – a 40-year obligation where the interest will compound relentlessly if they do not become high earners.

It is therefore encouraging that the government has announced every child will be taught the ‘big three’, chiming with the Numeracy for Life Committee’s new report, Making it Count. In it, we identified these concepts as a benchmark for financial capability, and ministers deserve credit for putting them at the heart of what children will learn.

I would now encourage them to go further and build on the momentum that’s already been generated. The report shows how much further as a society we need to go to put numeracy on an equal footing with literacy. Can you imagine the reaction if it was revealed 8m adults had the literacy skills of a nine-year-old? It would rightly generate immediate action; yet the fact the same number share the numeracy skills of a year four pupil does not. 

Numeracy and the workforce

Over recent months, my Committee heard from employers ranging from Santander and Barclays to National Grid, EDF and BT. Many said numeracy was a problem that needed attention, and many are running their own catch-up training programmes to get their employees up to speed. 

But the industries of tomorrow will make us even more reliant on having a workforce that’s confident in its numbers. Employers told us that artificial intelligence in particular is increasing the need for better numeracy. 

Central to this is a shift from calculation to judgement. That is, knowing whether the answer a chatbot produces actually makes sense. From financial services to energy and the digital economy, the sectors that will power Britain’s growth will depend on the workforce of tomorrow having the right judgement.

So ministers should treat this announcement as a first step. Two more would make a real difference.

What else is needed

First, the teachers delivering these lessons are often not maths specialists. They need proper training in the concepts themselves, not just a new set of lesson plans. We all know the positive impact an engaging teacher can have. 

Second, the red tape that makes it harder for employers to get into classrooms should be cut. The businesses we heard from are eager to show pupils why numbers matter, and we should let them. Too often pupils can’t see how the maths they learn in the classroom connects to the world of work. Seeing it applied would be transformational.

The government is clearly listening and I commend them for it. However, if we are to tackle the systemic societal issues caused by poor numeracy it must now go further. I will be the first to praise them if they do. 

Lord Agnew is a former Treasury minister and chair of the Numeracy for Life Committee in the House of Lords

articles.title: Our next Mayor must give London’s built environment back its mojo
articles.summary:
London’s next Mayor must champion architecture, the built environment, and bold city-making to drive an urban renaissance and restore the city’s civic ambition, says Jay Morton

The race to be the next Mayor of London has started and it’s the Conservatives who have been first out of the blocks

Being Mayor of London is like being Spiderman: with great power comes great responsibility – but also opportunity. Whoever wins truly has the chance to shape one of the greatest cities in the world. 

Not just theoretically or politically but physically. The Mayor has powers to reshape the city, from transport infrastructure and building homes to ensuring the multiple villages that make up London thrive. As an architect, I always feel that London does best when its Mayors take a passion and interest in architecture and the built environment. 

London’s architecture is the jewel in its crown. I moved to London in the Blair era, eager to study architecture at the Bartlett. I arrived just weeks after the 7/7 bombings, and London’s resilience made me proud. “We are Londoners” was everywhere, a shared determination to keep going. Alongside it was a tangible ambition to build. London had won the Olympic bid and it felt like anything was possible. London’s skyline was transformed. There was ambition about what London could become. Ken Livingstone appointed Richard Rogers as his chief adviser on architecture and urbanism, and the architecture and urbanism unit brought design into the heart of City Hall. Architecture wasn’t simply something that happened as a consequence of development. It was part of a wider vision for the capital.

Boris Johnson also took an interest. Like or loathe the Garden Bridge, the proposed Thames Estuary airport or the ArcelorMittal Orbit, they were big ideas. They showed an appetite for thinking about London at a city-wide scale.

Look north too. As Mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham put place at the centre of his politics. He used Mayoral Development Corporations to drive regeneration from Stockport to Old Trafford.

Sadiq Khan’s approach has been quieter on architecture, although his mayoralty has faced huge challenges. On air quality, particularly through the expansion of ULEZ, he has demonstrated the scale of change that mayors can pursue.

However national politics and international events shape cities too. In the last decade we’ve had Brexit, Covid leading to a seemingly endless drive to do everything for less, even at the expense of civic ambition. The ambition to merely survive not thrive.

The relocation of City Hall from central London to the Crystal in the Royal Docks feels like the epitome of this. A decision driven by the desire to save rather than a vision of what London’s civic heart should look like. And in any case, as Lord John of Southwark, former council leader, argued on my Architects for Change podcast, even those savings warrant scrutiny.

Somewhere along the way, we seem to have lost the confidence to think big about our city. Now, London needs that confidence back.

Urban renaissance

We need an urban renaissance and we need to build. London’s built environment is worth £111bn a year, 19 per cent of the city’s economy, and supports more than 620,000 jobs. But the construction sector currently feels worse than 2008. London’s housebuilding is collapsing and the money is leaving.

London’s success has always depended on its ability to attract talent, investment and ideas. But increasingly, the very people who make London such a creative, vibrant and exciting place cannot afford to live here. That includes the young architects, designers and builders who will actually shape the city.

London is currently home to some of the world’s most celebrated architecture practices, alongside hundreds of smaller studios. London’s chartered practices alone turn over £2.8bn a year. They create the buildings, streets and neighbourhoods that act as attractive adverts for a London people want to visit, work and live in.

So we need to think seriously about what a resilient city looks like in 2030 and beyond. How do we adapt to rising temperatures, flooding and extreme weather? How do we create neighbourhoods where children can play, older people can thrive and everyone can move around safely?

How do we make London greener, healthier, more affordable and more beautiful?

The answer lies not just in architecture and creative urbanism but political leadership.

The next Mayor, whoever it is, whatever their rosette needs to champion the built environment, not simply as an economic driver, but as one of the most powerful tools we have to tackle inequality, respond to climate change and improve people’s lives.

And frankly I want some fabulousness too. Some sparkle. Buildings and public spaces that inspire us and that Londoners can feel proud of. Why not appoint a City Architect to drive that collective longer term ambition? 

Of course, London’s finances are challenging. The housing delivery model is under severe strain, and the next Mayor will inherit difficult decisions. But that makes ambition more important, not less. We need action to get London building again, not just for today’s Londoners who desperately need homes, but for Londoners of the future too.

I want to see the next Mayor be passionate about the built environment and give London its mojo back. I’m calling for nothing short of an urban renaissance.

articles.title: Wave of policy change is ‘overwhelming’ pension providers, says top Schroders executive
articles.summary:
A relentless wave of regulatory reform in the pensions sector is “overwhelming” providers and placing them under operational strain, a senior Schroders executive has said.

Rachel Harris, head of UK Institutional at the FTSE 100 funds group, said the stream of consultations, legislative changes and regulatory frameworks brought forward by government and regulators has triggered a “seismic change” across Britain’s retirement savings industry.

Pension providers, typically workplace schemes and master trusts, have seen an overhaul ranging from the Pension Schemes Act, the incoming Value for Money framework, and a fresh consultation from the Financial Conduct Authority into the pension charge cap.

In an interview with City AM, Harris said: “Some of this stuff needs to be done. But I do think it has led to pretty seismic changes in terms of how we think about pensions in the UK.

“Every week there’s another piece of news out there on pension schemes you don’t necessarily expect.”

She noted that while asset managers like Schroders are able to manage the wave of change through public policy teams, for the actual providers it can be hard to manage the workload, particularly as both the government and City watchdog are introducing various policies and consultations.

“Trying to keep up with all the different policy frameworks that are being issued by all the various different regulators…not necessarily so much for us sitting in asset management, but if you think about the actual providers and how overwhelming it is for them, I think it can be really difficult,” she said.

Large managers and master trusts boast sizable internal policy teams to manage the workload coming off the back of policy shakeups, but smaller single-employer trusts face a more difficult challenge in managing changes, Harris warned.

In particular, the Value for Money framework, which is set to be implemented from 2028, has faced backlash for placing a greater burden on smaller schemes. 

Master trusts spread fixed governance and reporting costs across thousands of members, but smaller schemes must compile the same annual datasets across a much smaller base, driving up costs and pushing more towards consolidation.

Plans for guided retirement

Pensions minister Torsten Bell also recently unveiled plans for an overhaul of how private workers could draw their pensions in a bid to close the retirement gap between the public and private sector.

Joint proposals from the Department for Work and Pensions, the FCA and the Pensions Regulator outlined that providers will be required to offer workers an annual income as standard in retirement. 

The plans, dubbed ‘Guided Retirement’, will “resurrect” the option of having an inflation protected pension that provides a secure income for private sector retirees and prevents them from having to make complex financial decisions. 

Harris, who was appointed head of UK Institutional in March of this year, noted that private sector providers “haven’t had to do [this] up until now”, but the growing number of defined contribution savers and retirees has forced the issue onto the government agenda.

She also added the UK is ahead of Australia when it comes to helping savers turn their pots into steady retirement income, despite the country often being held as the gold standard for workplace pensions.

“They’ve had super funds going forever… we’re actually ahead of them on retirement income thinking, which I find slightly peculiar,” she said.

While critics have warned that pooling savers into collective schemes risks stripping away personal choice and flexibility, Harris stressed that proposals, known as collective defined contribution (CDC) schemes, are designed as an optional safety net rather than a one-size-fits-all mandate.

“CDC is an option. It’s not the only option. For some people it will work and it will make things better, which is the whole point of us trying to fix the retirement problem,” she said.

She added that appetite for collective schemes is primarily concentrated among “paternalistic” employers and family-run businesses “where it is…a more palatable option”.

Mansion House blues

The heavy regulatory backdrop comes as policymakers lean on DC schemes to channel billions into the UK economy through the Mansion House Accord.

Under the agreement, 17 of the top providers, including Aviva and Aegon UK, agreed to allocate at least 10 per cent of default assets to private markets by 2030. Five per cent of this total is earmarked for the UK.

But the agreement has come under scrutiny. Despite 3.3 per cent of assets being allocated to private markets, according to the latest update from the Association of British Insurers, the allocation is heavily skewed away from equities.

The vast majority of capital – around 70 per cent – has been invested into property, equalling £8bn. In contrast, just £500m was invested into private equity.

However, Harris warned that political pressure and wider industry ambitions cannot override a provider’s legal obligation to secure the “best possible” returns for savers—or the need for providers to build up expertise before rushing into higher-risk assets like venture capital.

“You can set up a pension fund, but you’re going to have a board of trustees, and the trustees have a fiduciary duty,” Harris said. “The fiduciary duty… is to provide them with the best possible risk-adjusted returns.”

While acknowledging frustrations from venture capital managers that pension funds are moving “too slow”, Harris noted that trustees must balance domestic ambitions against diversification.

articles.title: Private capital rejects claim that lack of new projects is holding back investment
articles.summary:
The UK’s private capital sector has rejected pension bosses’ claims that planning bottlenecks are slowing domestic investment as funds continue to flood into property.

Venture capital and private equity figures have pushed back against arguments that a lack of “shovel-ready” projects is preventing the deployment of capital into the UK economy, following comments from industry leaders.

Speaking at the Pension Insurance Corporation investment conference, Todd Solash, chief executive of pension group Athora, said: “There is no shortage of capital, the sector is ready today… looking for long-term, stable, predictable returns.”

“It comes down to being funded and predictable, knowing when it will be in the ground, when it will be completed. The biggest opportunity… is simplifying the planning and approval process to get projects in the ground faster.”

Insurers expect up to £1tn in defined benefit pension transfers over the next decade, arguing that money could help fund Britain’s £750bn infrastructure shortfall if planning rules are eased.

Parminder Kohli, chief executive of the government’s Office for Investment, echoed Solash, arguing that providers are waiting on a clearer pipeline.

“There is a huge investor appetite for the UK,” he said, “The key question is having investable projects with local support and a high degree of certainty over their lifetime. 

“There is no shortage of capital willing to come to us, it is just about creating the right opportunities.”

Investing in high-growth projects

But UK Private Capital rejected the suggestion that the UK suffers from a shortage of investable deals, noting that a number of overseas retirement funds are backing growth companies at a higher rate than domestic schemes, urging schemes to look beyond property in order to generate returns.

Michael Moore, chief executive of UK Private Capital, said: “There is no lack of investible opportunities in private capital. Pension funds have the second biggest private capital hub in the world on their doorstep.”

On average, 16 times more pension investment from around the world enters private funds than UK pension capital, which Moore said “demonstrates both the breadth of investable opportunities” in Britain.

“We must continue the focus on getting pension funds invested into high-growth businesses. Otherwise, savers risk missing out on the next generation of British success stories,” he added.

Mansion House frustration

The pushback comes amid growing frustration from the venture capital sector over providers failing to invest in high-growth assets, particularly those who signed the Mansion House Accord.

Under the accord, 17 of the country’s major workplace pension providers pledged to allocate 10 per cent of default contribution assets to private markets by 2030, five per cent of which would enter the UK.

But the latest figures show that schemes overwhelmingly favour bricks and mortar.

Of the £10.7bn committed to UK private markets under the Accord, £8bn has flowed into property and real estate. Just £500m has been allocated to UK private equity and venture capital.

But officials have acknowledged that UK schemes have been slow to build the internal expertise required to back private assets compared with international peers such as Canada and Australia.

Kohli pointed to Associated British Ports, which was taken private in 2006, in a £2.8bn deal backed by Canadian pension giant OMERS, before fellow fund CPP Investments also took  a stake in 2015.

Last month, the pension funds agreed to sell their stake to IFM Investors, an infrastructure manager owned primarily by Australian pension funds and UK workplace scheme Nest, in a deal valuing ABP at roughly £10bn. 

“We haven’t built that muscle,” said Kohli, “Collectively, we have failed to get that capital into our domestic markets… We are only taking baby steps towards it.”

articles.title: Tottenham star acquires stake in British midlife supplements brand Muto
articles.summary:
Tottenham Hotspur and Wales footballer Ben Davies has acquired a stake in British supplements brand Muto as it targets expansion in elite sport.

Muto is the brainchild of Harley Street nutritionist and cellular biologist Dr Richie Barclay and specialises in supplements for those approaching or in middle age.

“My wife tried Muto and loved the results,” said Davies, 33, who obtained a degree in economics and business while playing for Spurs. 

“From that point on, we believed in the product, loved the brand and when we reached out and met Richie, we could see his passion and vision for the brand and wanted to be on board.”

Barclay only launched Muto in February last year and has previously raised more than £600,000.

The brand’s flagship product, NAD+ Cellular Complex, was recently certified by Informed, a global quality assurance programme for the sports and supplement industry.

That seal of approval means it is free from 285 substances banned in elite sport and is designed to help it gain traction among athletes.

Davies to help Muto become trusted health brand

Joining Davies in acquiring a stake in Muto is media and tech executive Shaun Gregory, who has also become an advisor to the company.

“Longevity and wellness are topics close to my heart and something I take seriously,” said Gregory, executive chairman of Bridgepoint-backed marketing firm MVF.

“Muto got my attention because it’s backed by years of scientific evidence and underpinned by real experts in the field. 

“When I started to appreciate the difference between short-term stimulants and what Muto provides, it was a no-brainer for me to get involved.”

Barclay said: “Ben and Shaun joining our cap table brings far more than capital. Ben operates at the very top of elite sport, and Shaun brings an extensive career in advertising and media. 

“Both will be invaluable as we execute our evidence-led strategy and work towards our mission of becoming the most trusted longevity and health brand in Europe.

“Trust is built in many ways: through the clinical research we conduct, the scientific advisors who guide us and the quality of the products we create. 

“The shareholders we choose to partner with play a key role in reinforcing that mission too.”

articles.title: Fifa hack branded wake-up call for sport after cyberattack spree
articles.summary:
Sports organisations have been warned they are a growing target for cybercrime after Fifa admitted it had been hacked.

Files relating to personal and business details were among those accessed, downloaded and offered on the dark web in the Fifa cyber attack.

It followed the hacking of Spanish football league LaLiga and the paralysing of the International Ice Hockey Federation’s website in recent days.

“While the incidents aren’t linked, together they show that bad actors are growing bolder and that sport is now a major target,” said Chris Dimitriadis, chief global strategy officer at IT governance experts ISACA.

“These organisations hold huge, centralised stores of data, from customer details to financial information, about millions of fans who trust them. That makes them particularly attractive to criminals, and the damage doesn’t stop at the breach. 

“The stolen data gives attackers what they need to pose convincingly as a club or governing body, which puts fans, members and partners directly in the firing line for phishing.

“This must be a wake-up call for sport. Sporting bodies need to extend cybersecurity governance to shared platforms and third-party providers, set up coordinated incident response and warn fans now about what to look out for.”

Fifa, LaLiga and IIHF hacked within days

The previously unknown Handsome Boy Hacking Club claimed credit for the hack on Fifa, which condemned “the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data”.

It follows the cyber attack on LaLiga, which led to access to customers’ personal data being accessed last week.

The International Ice Hockey Federation’s website has been down for more than a week in a cyberattack that appears to be linked to its ban on Russia.

The landing page was initially replaced with an image of Russian players celebrating and the messages “Scared to face Russia?” and “You banned the only team you can’t beat”. 

It came days after a row erupted over Russia’s eligibility for upcoming IIHF World Championships.

articles.title: City firms Lloyd’s Register and M&G backed divisive ‘glass box’ demolition
articles.summary:
Square Mile firms M&G and Lloyd’s Register backed the controversial demolition of an Edwardian building at the heart of the City, to be replaced with a “glass box”.

The City of London Corporation has approved divisive plans to demolish a 116-year-old building at 68 Fenchurch Street next to the historic East India Arms pub on the east of the Square Mile.

The removal of the building, to be replaced by a modern, glass-walled structure, has been slammed by heritage associations and London mayoral hopeful James Cleverly. 

But a number of heavyweight City firms which neighbour the site had signalled their support for the demolition ahead of its approval by the local authority, planning documents show.

M&G Real Estate, the property arm of the FTSE 100-listed insurer and which has offices nearby, wrote to the City of London Corporation to register its “strong support for the application and the design proposals”. 

“In our view, the proposals represent an appropriate and positive response to the opportunities and constraints presented by this important City location,” the firm wrote.

“The new building and proposed use would, in our view, enhance this part of the City and contribute positively to the character, vitality and long-term success of the surrounding area.”

Lloyd’s Register, a marine classification firm which occupies the building behind 68 Fenchurch, said the proposed development, which would replace an art-nouveau facade with an exposed metal staircase, is “thoughtful, well-resolved and appropriate”.

“We feel that the new building will make a positive and complementary contribution to the setting of our own building,” they added.

Objectors said the plans would “destroy the townscape” (RSHP City of London Design and Access Report)

Shepherd Neame, which owns the neighbouring East India Arms, told the City Corporation that the plans would make a “positive and complementary contribution to the setting of Fenchurch Street”. 

Aldgate Connect business improvement district, which covers the area of the development, and advisors to New College Oxford, which owns the freehold to a neighbouring site, also registered their support for the proposals.

Despite the support of neighbouring firms, heritage societies have fiercely opposed the proposals, claiming the new structure would rid Fenchurch Street of one of its most treasured buildings.

‘No benefits’ to demolition

Morgan Ellis Leah, a conservation adviser at the Victorian Society, told the City Corporation the plans would cause “high-level, irreversible” harm to the surrounding area and “destroy the carefully maintained townscape”.

The existing building is “a well-preserved example of the Free Style, with distinctive oriel windows, stepped gables, and restrained Art Nouveau motifs in Portland stone”.

Historic England said in planning documents that it does not support the development, claiming that the new building would not bring “any benefits to the historic environment”.

James Cleverly, the Conservative candidate to be Mayor of London, told City AM he opposes the development and pledged to slash planning regulation if elected.

The mayoral hopeful said: “I want London to be a beautiful place, and for it’s planners, builders, and architects to put beauty at the heart of their work. 

“It does not serve anyone for a building to be redeveloped to be both less beautiful, and less functional. We should not shy away from building in a manner we know works, and we know contributes to our public realm.

“As Mayor I will look at every unnecessary and overburdensome regulation and structure that stops us building beautiful. I will build a London we can all be proud of.”

Supporters of the proposals point out that the existing building is not listed, and that the new development would be free to use by community groups on four days of the week.

A spokesperson for the City of London Corporation said: “The City of London has existed for nearly 2,000 years, and protecting our heritage is a key consideration in the planning process.

“In the case of 68 Fenchurch Street, redevelopment was approved because the existing building could not meet modern regulatory standards, including fire safety and accessibility requirements. Without the approval, the building would have remained unviable and stood empty.”

articles.title: US maker of Malboro mulls bid for FTSE 100 giant Imperial Brands
articles.summary:
The US firm that makes Malboro cigarettes is mulling a bid for FTSE 100 giant Imperial Brands in a move that could add to the exodus of London Stock Exchange heavyweights.

Altria Group, whose companies also include Philip Morris USA, told markets on Thursday it is in early talks regarding a takeover of Imperial Brands but no agreement has yet been reached.

Under UK takeover rules, Altria will has until 5pm on December 24 to announce a firm intention to make an offer or walk away. The London market will close at lunchtime on Christmas Eve.

Imperial Brand shares were up 16 per cent on the news to 3,472p. The firm, whose brands include Golden Virginia and JPS, commands a £26bn market valuation.

Bloomberg previously reported that Japan Tobacco was evaluating a potential acquisition ⁠of Imperial Brands.

Threat of FTSE 100 exodus continues

The group’s departure from the City would ramp up pressure on the stock market after foreign buyers and private equity buyers swooped on London-listed companies throughout 2026.

US property giant Prologis tabled a £14bn takeover for FTSE 100 real estate firm Segro earlier this year, while Easyjet was taken private by Apollo for £5.7bn.

The takeover talks follow Imperial Brands confirming it will cut between 2,100 and 2,500 further jobs across its international operations before 2030. This follows the firm already reducing its headcount by 2,100 in the last financial year.

“Throughout this transformation, we are committed to following appropriate consultation processes and supporting our people,” the firm told shareholders. 

The Bristol-based firm saw its revenue fall by 1.5 per cent to £31.7bn in the year to September. Its operating profit dipped by 10 per cent to £3.1bn, which the group blamed in part on its cost-savings programme.

Lukas Paravicini, chief executive officer of the firm, said: “While continuing to invest in and build future consumer capabilities, underpinned by new technologies, we are confident of achieving at least £320 million of annual savings by 2030.”

articles.title: Nvidia rally runs out of steam as Wall Street battles AI jitters
articles.summary:
Global stock markets rallied on Thursday after a bruising session on Wall Street, as investors continued to grapple with mounting concerns over Nvidia’s corporate governance and AI spending.

The FTSE 100 climbed 1.5 per cent in morning trading, while Germany’s Dax gained two per cent and France’s Cac 40 rose 1.8 per cent.

The recovery followed a volatile session on Wall Street on Wednesday, which saw the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite plunge as much as 4.6 per cent before recovering to close 0.62 per cent lower.

The S&P 500 closed 0.25 per cent lower, while the Dow Jones reversed a 1,100-point decline to finish 0.33 per cent higher.

Nvidia shares fell 3.9 per cent, extending losses for a second consecutive session after Monday’s spectacular 31.5 per cent rally following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as chief executive.

The Nasdaq remains down 7.28 per cent this month, while the Nasdaq 100 briefly entered bear market territory on Wednesday, having fallen 20 per cent from its October peak.

“The damage, in other words, has been trimmed rather than repaired,” said Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG.

US markets are closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving and will reopen for a shortened trading session on Friday.

Nvidia faces ongoing pressures

Pressure on Nvidia intensified on Wednesday after S&P Global Ratings placed the chipmaker’s AA credit rating on watch for a potential downgrade, citing concerns over board oversight and corporate governance.

Meanwhile, Nvidia has instructed manufacturing partners to suspend shipments of servers containing its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to the Financial Times.

The move follows fresh US export controls introduced last week, designed to prevent Chinese companies from accessing advanced American chips through overseas data centres.

Uncertainty also persists over the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s reinstatement.

Reuters reported that senior US intelligence officials remain divided over whether Alice Huang, the former technology executive with whom the Nvidia boss reportedly had an affair, had links to Chinese intelligence.

The FBI has reportedly assessed that available intelligence does not establish that she was an officer or asset of Chinese intelligence, while the CIA has left open the possibility that further evidence could emerge.

Huang is due to face questioning from three congressional committees next week, as scrutiny mounts over President Donald Trump’s intervention in securing his return.

Bond markets flash warning over AI spend

Beyond Nvidia, investors are growing increasingly nervous over the cost of financing the AI infrastructure boom.

The cost of insuring against debt defaults at Oracle, Alphabet, SpaceX and Coreweave has reached record highs, according to IG, while yields on Coreweave’s bonds have climbed to nearly 18 per cent.

“Bondholders are taking a considerably less cheerful view of the AI spending boom than equity buyers did at the start of the week,” Beauchamp said.

The sell-off has been compounded by hotter-than-expected US inflation figures, with core personal consumption expenditure inflation rising to 3.3 per cent in October.

Markets are now pricing in a near-certainty that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates by 25 basis points in December, threatening to push up borrowing costs for technology companies financing multibillion-dollar infrastructure projects.

Fresh US tariff proposals targeting 14 economies have added to the uncertainty.

Jonathan Unwin, UK head of portfolio management at Mirabaud, said the firm had used Monday’s relief rally to further reduce its equity exposure.

“We think the AI trade is peaking, more Federal Reserve rate hikes are on the agenda…and strong corporate earnings might have peaked,” he said.

Anthropic, which made its blockbuster stock market debut last week, recovered from an almost 10 per cent intraday decline to close 1.1 per cent higher on Wednesday, although it remained below its $83 listing price.

Asian technology stocks recovered some ground on Thursday, with Japan’s Softbank climbing 7.3 per cent and memory chipmaker Kioxia surging 12.6 per cent.

South Korea’s Kospi edged 0.3 per cent higher following Wednesday’s 6.2 per cent slump.

articles.title: Lobbyist told Mandelson to be ‘warmer’ to China in speech
articles.summary:
A lobbyist told Lord Peter Mandelson to include “warmer language” towards China in a speech on diplomacy when he was ambassador to the US. 

Newly-released files show that Mandelson was urged to be more sympathetic to the country, which has had a difficult relationship with the UK amid a series of espionage cases despite trading flows. 

An email from an unnamed director at Global Counsel, the lobbying firm founded by Mandelson, suggested that Mandelson should borrow “sentences from His Majesty’s Government’s script of warmer language towards China”. 

The speech in mid-2025 was set to argue that the US and China would compete to “dominate the world”. Mandelson hoped to argue that the US needed allies in order to win the economic and geopolitical battle. 

The lobbyist responded: “The speech’s main argument – as I read it – is that we need to work with Trump’s US or China will dominate the world and that would be a very bad thing (and that the US needs allies if it’s to win that contest). That is a powerful argument but it’s pure hostility towards China does not obviously align with what looks like HMG’s considerable effort to achieve a rapprochement with China [sic]. 

“I think you need a couple of sentences from HMG’s script of warmer language towards China, both to explain the balance of HMG’s policy and to minimise problems with our China relationship and goals.”

The Global Counsel figure also made suggestions on “toning down some parts of your apologia of the Trump administration” given there was public “scepticism” of the president’s administration, such that it would be “unpersuasive if [Mandelson] came across as having drunk the Kool Aid”. 

China relations with the UK called into question

The Labour government has held that it should expand economic ties with China even as intelligence services have warned of its security threats. 

Its official line, taken from the party’s manifesto, states that the UK should “co-operate where we can, compete where we need to, and challenge where we must”. 

MI5 recently issued an espionage alert to universities warning that a Chinese conglomerate which had funded academics in return for access to research had boosted China’s intelligence service.

Mandelson, whose appointment as US ambassador in late 2024 came back to bite former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer due to warnings about his previous links to Russia and the paedophile Jeffrey Epstein, is facing a Metropolitan Police investigation into alleged misconduct in public office related to his historical dealings. Mandelson has always maintained his innocence.

New emails surrounding Mandelson’s appointment were released after the police granted the Cabinet Office the right to proceed with a ‘humble address motion’ brought by the Tories, which has sought to provide transparency on his role as US ambassador. 

Files released in the US appeared to show that Mandelson, who was formerly the business secretary and a Labour grandee, shared confidential information with Epstein around the time of the Great Financial Crisis. 

Mandelson was promised ‘light touch’ vetting

In the UK, various rounds of publications around Mandelson’s appointment and time as US ambassador raised questions about Starmer’s judgment and contributed to the pressure leading to his resignation as Prime Minister in the summer. 

The latest tranche also showed that Mandelson asked details of a particular meeting with a former colleague to be kept “under the radar”. One former government official, Sir Olly Robbins, who was sacked by Starmer, also promised that his vetting process would be “light touch”.

Andy Burnham pledged “political reform” so that “vested interests aren’t running large within the system”.

articles.title: ‘Today should have been a celebration’: Inside the battle to save Poundland
articles.summary:
Making their way to work on Thursday morning, Poundland’s thousands of staff couldn’t help but wonder how many more commutes they had left. In the discount retailer’s near-600 stores across the country, shop workers were briefed via conference call by Barry Williams, Poundland’s managing director, and Alix Partners, who will oversee the company’s administration. 

Williams told staff “today should have been a day of celebration given the unique turnaround of the business on the high street,” one Poundland employee said. In conversations at the retailer’s stores and in its Walsall headquarters, staff have expressed their “thanks” to its management and “concern” over the decisions made by Gordon Brothers, its owner, another said.

“While [it was] difficult news to share, there was support from colleagues for Barry’s efforts over recent weeks and it finished with a round of applause for him. He’s much loved by the colleagues,” another person with knowledge of the briefing said.

‘We turned Poundland around’

Poundland’s management and its owners have been split over whether the retailer is showing signs of improvement. Williams told staff on Wednesday they had worked “tirelessly” to return the company to growth, amid reports that Poundland is on track for an £18m profit.

But Gordon Brothers have insisted that the retailer remains “vulnerable to inflationary pressures or any downturn in sales and margin” and had not completed its recovery.

Poundland’s staff are overwhelmingly supportive of Williams and have been disappointed by the investment firm’s messaging, one employee said. “We’ve all worked our absolute damnedest to turn the business round, and we’ve done it.”

A virtual ‘thank-you’ card addressed to Barry Williams is circulating among Poundland’s workers and the volume of messages has stretched the document to more than 160 pages, sources said.

Another employee said they don’t know when stores will begin to close, though the company considers its staff to be “at risk.” They added: “It’s certainly been a difficult and uncertain period for employees, particularly with the concerns about job security and the future of the business.”

Meanwhile, Poundland’s administrators are being flooded with emails. Alix Partners has already received dozens of ‘kite-flying’ inquiries into the retailer, feigning interest at buying either the whole company or some of its stores, sources said.

The administrators’ first task will be to wade through their packed inboxes and determine which of these approaches are genuine, and which are opportunistic. Top of Alix Partners’ list will be Xyra Group Holdings, Martin Property Group, Premier Quality Foods and Zachert Private Equity, who had all been vying to buy the retailer solvently in the hours before its collapse.

Gordon Brothers decided none of these bids could be completed before a court order stalling Poundland’s creditors was due to lapse. Though each of these bidders had been hoping to buy the retailer as a going concern, Xyra and Premier have already expressed their interest in buying the company out of consideration.

These proposals will be prioritised by administrators, sources said, because they have already completed much of the work towards a deal, including due diligence and lining up their funding. 

Administrators face huge task

In a statement provided to Sky News, Premier owner Idris Mohammed claimed he had not been able to stump up “enough funding to address the historic liabilities while still leaving sufficient cash in the business to pay staff and suppliers, replenish stock and keep the shelves full”.

One industry observer described this as an “extraordinary” admission. The government has faced calls to partially fund a takeover of Poundland’s in order to protect jobs. Liam Byrne MP, chair of Parliament’s business select committee, has urged ministers to “help bridge finance” for a sale, though people close to the process have said this would be unlikely.

Beyond the immediate future facing Poundland and its 11,000 workers, the retailer’s collapse will send shockwaves through the UK’s high streets. The administration makes it more likely that the company will be broken up between a host of retail buyers.

Poundland’s stores will continue trading for now and no job losses will occur immediately, people close to the matter said, though administrators have not yet worked out how much longer the business can continue to run.

An industry source said they expect Alix Partners to go “back out to the market” and review existing and new bids for the retailer “from scratch”. The process to find a buyer was being run by City advisory firm Alvarez & Marsal before Poundland’s administration but this responsibility switched to Alix Partners as soon as the retailer collapsed. 

Staff at the New-York based consultancy will now be racing to get to grips with the reams of performance data, takeover proposals and funding documents involved in the attempted sale, though they had been drawing up contingency plans for a number of weeks.

A spokesperson for the administrators said on Wednesday that they welcome approaches from “anybody interested in acquiring the business in part or as a whole, as well as UK retail operators with open employment opportunities”.

Many of the retailers interested in buying just parts of Poundland have already committed to taking on all the employees at the stores they would acquire, though staff at sites which are not bought could lose their jobs. 

High street shake-up

If Poundland is split apart by administrators, this process would see high street stalwarts like Tesco, Lidl, Iceland, B&M and The Range tussle to pick up the best-quality space in the UK’s towns and cities. The retailers which get their choice of stores will be given a significant leg-up in the intense battle to woo Britain’s increasingly cash-strapped shoppers.

Since its foundation in 1991, Poundland has become a staple of high streets across the UK, building up to a footprint of about 600 stores. Should the retailer’s brand cease to exist as part of this administration, discount rivals like B&M and Home Bargains will hope to gain more shoppers looking for cheap groceries and discounted homeware.

But Poundland’s struggles will give pause to its competitors. In theory, the retailer’s huge footprint and cheap products would have positioned it well to capitalise on the cost-of-living crisis, though it ultimately failed to stay afloat.

Poundland’s collapse has already provoked questions over the role of private equity in the UK’s high streets. Gordon Brothers has been bruised by its attempted sale of the retailer, during which time it has been dubbed an asset-stripper and a “high street raider”.

Parliament’s business select committee, which subjected the US investment firm to a two-hour grilling earlier this month, has demanded that it stays away from Poundland in future, by not taking up the potentially lucrative role of liquidating its stock. 

Andy Street, a former Tory regional mayor and boss of John Lewis, has urged the government to use insolvency rules to “go after” Gordon Brothers “with the full force of the law”. He said earlier this month: “I do not yet believe the government has gone as far as it should in protecting these jobs.”

articles.title: Paul Sherwin: The worst business faux pas? A wet handshake – dry your hands properly!
articles.summary:
Each week, we dig into the memory bank of the City’s great and good. Today, Paul Sherwin, managing director at workplace design firm Oktra, takes us through his career

CV

Name: Paul Sherwin

Job title: Managing director at Oktra

Previous roles: MD at Maris Interiors; senior designer at Morgan Lovell

Age: 51

Born: Surrey, England

Lives: Bromley, Kent

Studied: BA (Hons) Design at Leeds Metropolitan University

Talents: Spotting potential in people and helping them grow into it. I love mentoring and pushing people to develop professionally.

Motto: Maximum joy, minimum fuss!

Biggest perk of the job: Turning a client’s ideas for their office into reality, then seeing those spaces come to life across the City and the London skyline.

Coffee order: Latte with whole milk

Cocktail order: Negroni

Favourite book: 1984 by George Orwell

Comfort movie: The Shawshank Redemption

What was your first job?

Working at my dad’s local rugby club at age 10. I’m not sure that would be legal nowadays! It was great training in customer service and mental maths. The pay wasn’t too bad either: a bottle of Coke and a Mars bar for an afternoon’s work.

What was your first role in the big city?

I started out in London as a designer at a large design and construction business, a couple of years after graduating in Design from Leeds Metropolitan University. It was a very junior role, but I was hungry for growth and professional development, and I’m grateful for where it took me.

When did you know you wanted to build a career in the City?

I have always loved London. It’s where the best companies and talent connect to the global market, and as someone who consults with big companies, there’s no better place to work. This is where the best work, buildings and projects are happening.

What’s one thing you love about the City of London?

I love the variety. So many areas of London have their own distinct identity – from the corporate grit of the City, to the classic elegance of Mayfair and the hustle and bustle of Soho.

And one thing you would change?

Fewer traffic jams.

What’s been your most memorable business lunch?

Meetings in the private dining room at Berry Bros. & Rudd are always memorable. It’s Britain’s oldest wine and spirit merchant, and the building itself is steeped in history, with the original timber floors and underground vaults. The chefs prepare a delicious lunch while an expert sommelier talks you through the wine pairings. Clients love it, and it’s helped us secure more than one new partnership.

And any business faux pas?

A wet handshake! Lesson learned: dry your hands properly after washing them, before any client handshake. First impressions are everything, and no one likes a damp hand.

What’s been your proudest moment?

Consulting with world-class companies like Deliveroo, Adidas and Lindt to shape their property decisions. It all helps to build happier teams, stronger performance and profitability, and above all, provide great spaces for people to work.

And who do you look up to?

My partner is the headteacher at a London comprehensive, and she’s responsible for 900 kids and 150 staff. So when I think I’ve had a bad day, I look at her and she brings me back to earth. Watching her give every child a shot at a brighter future is incredibly humbling.

What’s the best career advice you’ve ever been given?

Success is more about attitude than academic excellence. Some people are born into opportunity, but most of us have to earn it through graft and results. It tastes a lot sweeter when you’ve had to earn it.

And the worst?

That you’ve gone as far as you can go in your career. Be brave – if you know in your heart that you’ve got more to offer, ask for it, and if it doesn’t come, move on. Don’t waste precious time waiting for someone to give you a chance.

Are you optimistic for the year ahead?

It’s exciting and daunting in equal measure. AI is developing so rapidly, and it will radically reshape every business we work with and how we operate – including why people
come into the office and what that space needs to offer them in the long term. This is both an opportunity and a challenge.

We’re going for lunch, and you’re picking. Where are we going?

Farmer J, every time, for a salad or a high-protein hot lunch. The concept of quality food served fast has really taken off in London, and they do it better than most. If you’re hungry, Blacklock for a steak or Brigadiers for a curry are my top recommendations.

And if we’re grabbing a drink after work?

Somewhere you can actually talk, particularly with a small group. City Arts Bar on Ironmonger Lane is a dark, cosy room with velvet armchairs and quiet corners, and it’s the kind of place where the more sensitive conversations happen.

Where’s home during the week?

Bromley. I’m there most weekends too, but I’ll head into London for a culture fix at the iconic galleries or the ballet. Other times, it’s just to enjoy a great English pub and a pint of Guinness.

And where might we find you at the weekend?

I’m a huge live music fan, so you’ll find me at gigs at Brixton Academy or the Hammersmith Apollo. On a quieter night, I love to stroll round Soho and enjoy counter dining at Pulpo or Kiln.

You’ve got a well-deserved two weeks off. Where are you going and who with?

Somewhere hot with my partner and our kids. When the kids were younger, it was all about places that kept them busy in the day, and now they’re older, we’re looking further afield. Texas, Tokyo and Abu Dhabi are all on our bucket list.

articles.title: Football clubs face criminal charges over child abuse. Are they ready?
articles.summary:
Changes to the law mean companies – including football clubs – can now be held liable for offences such as child abuse by their senior management and owners, write lawyers Helen Harvey and Charlotte Moss.

Earlier this month, the Football Association launched Voices of Truth, a digital platform paying tribute to survivors of child sexual abuse in football.

It marked 10 years since revelations by former footballers led the FA to commission an independent inquiry into historic abuse, which culminated in the Sheldon Review in 2021. But the anniversary is not just a moment to remember; it brings renewed attention on where accountability for misconduct in football should lie today.

A recent change in the law raises an important question: could clubs themselves be prosecuted for alleged abuse by individuals? Since June, under the Crime and Policing Act 2026, companies can be held criminally liable for offences committed by senior managers while acting in the course of their role.  

A senior manager is someone who plays a significant role in making decisions about, or managing, the whole or a substantial part of a company’s activities. But determining who counts as a senior manager is not straightforward.

Prosecutors will look beyond an individual’s job title, employment status or pay to consider their influence over how the business is run. Government guidance makes clear that directors and senior officers, such as CFOs and COOs, would normally fall within the definition. Club owners may too, depending on how involved they are in its running. 

However, senior management is not limited to board members or those performing executive roles, and could include those with significant responsibility for functions such as HR.

For football clubs, this could extend to individuals not traditionally considered senior management. For example, coaches or those responsible for player selection, managing player contracts or overseeing a club’s grassroots programme could be caught, depending on their responsibilities. 

Clubs may need to review safeguarding measures

Crucially, the offence must have been committed while the senior manager was acting within the “actual or apparent scope of their authority”. This does not mean that the criminal conduct was authorised in some way – it just means it happened when the person was doing their job. 

For instance, a coach who sexually assaults a player while demonstrating a technique during a training drill may be considered to be acting within the scope of their authority as the conduct occurred in the course of their coaching duties. The same could apply to a club CEO who uses a meeting about a player’s contract or future at the club to commit a sexual offence. 

However, with no case law to consider, it is not yet clear who will qualify as a senior manager and when their conduct will fall within the scope of their authority. 

The Act also makes it a criminal offence to deliberately prevent or discourage someone from reporting suspected child sexual abuse where they are legally required to do so. Although this “obstruction offence” has not yet come into force, once implemented, it could give rise to corporate liability if committed by a senior manager acting within the scope of their authority.

Where allegations of criminal misconduct arise, football clubs must now consider their own potential corporate exposure, rather than dealing with the matter solely through internal disciplinary proceedings and individual accountability.

Clubs may therefore want to revisit their training and safeguarding procedures to ensure they are robust and that the responsibilities of those in senior positions, including coaching staff, are clearly understood. 

A decade on from survivors’ bravery in disclosing their experiences, the onus is now well and truly on clubs to do everything in their power to stamp out abuse.

Helen Harvey is a Senior Associate and Charlotte Moss an Associate in the Corporate Crime and Investigations team at Michelman & Robinson UK LLP.

articles.title: Taliban reportedly strips women of their names in Afghan province, now being called 'goat' or 'grandmother'
articles.summary:
The Taliban have reportedly banned the use of women's names in official documents in a northern Afghan province, with some women being referred to by degrading animal names, according to a report by Spanish newspaper El País.

The latest assault on women's rights under Taliban rule reportedly extends to medical records and prescriptions in Afghanistan's Balkh province, raising fears that the restrictions could spread nationwide.

Healthcare workers and other public employees have been instructed to address women as "Bibi," meaning grandmother or old woman, according to reporting by Afghan news outlet Zan Times and The Guardian cited by El País.

MOSCOW, TALIBAN FORGE MILITARY ALLIANCE IN POWER GRAB AFTER US AFGHANISTAN EXIT: REPORTS

Afghan women's rights activist Lalah Osmany, who is based in Germany, told El País that testimony from women, doctors and civil rights activists indicates some women are also being referred to in degrading terms such as "goat" or "cow."

"This is a systematic process of dehumanization," Osmany told the newspaper.

An Afghan activist speaking under a pseudonym confirmed the reported order to El País, although she said it had so far been ignored.

Zubaida Akbar, who directs the Afghanistan program at women's rights organization Femena, warned that the Taliban could eventually impose the ban nationwide, citing previous instances in which local restrictions were expanded across the country.

IRAN FLOGS FEMALE SINGER 74 TIMES FOR PERFORMING WITHOUT HIJAB IN VIRAL YOUTUBE CONCERT

Femena has counted more than 144 decrees restricting Afghan women's rights, according to El País.

Girls have been barred from studying beyond age 12, while women have been shut out of most professions and subjected to restrictions on speaking in public, the newspaper reported.

Some Afghan women have resorted to running underground businesses and secret schools in defiance of Taliban restrictions, according to Associated Press reporting published Nov. 17.

IRAN TO EXECUTE FIRST FEMALE PROTESTER TIED TO ANTI-REGIME UNREST

One Kabul beauty salon owner, whose identity was concealed for her safety, reopened her business after authorities raided her previous salon and confiscated her equipment.

"But now, they won’t even allow that; for women in Afghanistan, working has become a crime," she told the AP.

An assistant teacher at a secret school in Kabul described living in constant fear of arrest.

"We are absolutely terrified of that possibility," she told the AP.

Mohammad Aslam, a spokesman for the Taliban's Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, defended the broader restrictions in comments to the AP, saying women could conduct business and social affairs provided they adhered to Islamic Sharia law and existing laws.

Osmany also warned that the reported naming ban could endanger female patients by increasing the risk of medical errors if prescriptions and medical records are filed under identical names.

Afghan women already face severe barriers to medical care under Taliban rule, including restrictions on male doctors treating female patients and bans on women pursuing medical training, according to El País.

In 2017, Osmany launched a campaign to have Afghan women's names included on official documents, including their children's birth certificates.

ARMY VET LAWMAKER MARKS ABBEY GATE ANNIVERSARY WITH BLISTERING MESSAGE FOR BIDEN-HARRIS: 'ABJECT FAILURE'

Despite receiving death threats from extremists, her campaign helped secure a change in 2020 allowing mothers' names to be voluntarily included on such documents. That progress was short-lived.

The Taliban swept back into power in August 2021 as the U.S.-backed Afghan government collapsed amid then-President Joe Biden's chaotic military withdrawal, leaving the country once again under the control of Islamist extremists.

The withdrawal drew widespread condemnation after 13 American service members, mostly Marines, were killed in an ISIS-K terrorist attack during the evacuation from Kabul.

Biden faced further backlash from Gold Star families after checking his watch during the dignified transfer of fallen American troops at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware.

Five years later, Afghan women and girls have seen hard-won freedoms stripped away under Taliban rule. Now, activists warn, even their very identities are under threat.

"Calling a woman by her real name in Afghanistan is an act of resistance," Osmany told El País.

articles.title: Low levels of common vitamin could be stealing nearly 30 minutes of your sleep
articles.summary:
Middle-aged and older adults with low levels of vitamin D slept about 23 minutes less per night than people with normal levels, according to a new study that tracked sleep with wearable sensors.

The study, led by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and the National Institute on Aging, used data collected from 2012 to 2019 as part of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging.

The researchers looked at blood tests and sleep data from 460 adults ages 40 and older, averaging 71 years of age.

ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES

After dividing the participants into three groups by vitamin D level, they found that the highest group slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night than the group with the lowest levels.

People with lower levels also stayed awake longer after waking up at night — a pattern that held regardless of age, gender or race.

The connection between vitamin D and sleep was strongest among Black participants, who made up about 22% of the group.

"Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to White adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels," lead author Diefei Chen, a doctoral candidate in epidemiology at the Bloomberg School, said in a press release.

CAN WEARABLES DETECT HEART PROBLEMS EARLY? DOCTOR BREAKS DOWN REAL DATA

Most earlier studies on vitamin D and sleep relied on people reporting how well they thought they slept. In this study, researchers used blood draws and actigraphs, which are watch-like motion sensors that measure sleep and wake times.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The team also checked vitamin B12, which previous studies linked to sleep. While higher levels correlated with less nighttime wakefulness in women and more in men, the authors noted the results were statistically inconclusive.

The findings were published on Oct. 14 in The Journal of Gerontology: Medical Sciences.

Poor sleep and vitamin D deficiency are both widespread among older adults, with previous research linking sleep disturbances to higher risks of dementia, heart disease and diabetes.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The study had several limitations. Because the researchers looked at snapshots of data rather than testing a treatment in a clinical trial, they could only establish a link between vitamin D and sleep.

The findings did not prove that low levels cause poor sleep or that taking supplements will fix it.

Because blood tests can't distinguish between vitamin D from sunlight, food or supplements, the study could not determine whether the source matters.

In addition, the researchers did not track whether changing a person's vitamin D levels over several years leads to changes in their sleep.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Because everyone in the study was 40 or older and had no cognitive impairment, the results may not apply to younger people or adults with memory and thinking problems.

"These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health," senior author Adam Spira, a mental health professor at the Bloomberg School, said in the news release.

articles.title: Tiny English village battles government over migrant housing plan amid crime fears for women
articles.summary:
A rural Oxfordshire village of just over 350 people is taking on the British government, finding itself at the center of a national debate over immigration and public safety.

Residents of Piddington, a small community about 10 miles from the famous Oxford University and known more for its rural setting and centuries-old parish church than political activism, voted overwhelmingly in September to secede from the United Kingdom in a symbolic referendum. The 285-26 vote came after residents learned Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government planned to house more than 1,200 male asylum seekers at a former Ministry of Defence base in Bicester — less than a mile from the village.

What began as a local planning dispute has since become one of Britain's most closely watched immigration battles. The controversy intensified earlier this month when the government approved plans for the asylum accommodation center despite objections from local officials, residents and the Thames Valley Police and Crime Commissioner.

WHO IS ANDY BURNHAM? BRITAIN'S NEW PRIME MINISTER AND LONGTIME TRUMP CRITIC

"The Piddington situation reflects a political choice by the Burnham government to start locating asylum seekers across the whole country, to share the burden equally," Alan Mendoza, executive director of the Henry Jackson Society, told Fox News Digital. He added that most locations selected to house migrants "do not vote Labour usually," adding that some residents view the policy "as a form of political punishment."

On Nov. 12, Housing and Communities Secretary Angela Rayner approved planning permission for the project, despite opposition from local residents and officials. The government argued the facility is needed as part of its broader effort to reform the UK's asylum system and expand the use of alternative accommodation sites.

200,000 SMALL BOAT ARRIVALS LOOM AMID UK RAISING THREAT LEVEL TO ‘SEVERE’ FOLLOWING RECENT TERROR ATTACK

"I think it's fair to say we were shocked by the news," Michael Nixon, a member of the Piddington Parish Council, told Reuters at the time of the decision, "because we are a very small village. We have a total of 350 residents, including 46 children. We don't have too much else in the village. There's no shop. There's no pub. You know, we are just a small rural community, and to have the thought of 1,250 lone men on our doorstep, without any consultation, without any thought about how that could be absorbed into our village, really shocked us."

A Home Office spokesperson said the government is "working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country" and moving away from the use of asylum hotels. The spokesperson added that former military sites, such as MoD Bicester, are designed to be "self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to minimize the impact on the local community."

Not everyone is convinced the government's assurances will be enough.

In an Oct. 16 letter to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, Thames Valley Police and Crime Commissioner Matthew Barber warned that local residents had "genuine concerns" about the project’s impact on "their safety and security." He added that "given the open nature of the site we know that there will be an increased risk to the public."

Barber went further, writing: "We must expect an increase in crime as a result of the Government's proposals… it is naïve to consider that such a large population of single men will not bring with it a greater risk of violent and sexual offenses."

EU ADMITS IT ‘DIDN’T HAVE CONTROL’ ON MIGRATION AS BLOC RUSHES CRACKDOWN AHEAD OF NEW RULES

In an interview on GB News last month, Piddington resident Christina Gower said villagers had been advised by rural policing personnel that officers could take up to 45 minutes to respond to an emergency call and that the best thing residents could do in the meantime was to "run and hide." Thames Valley Police has not publicly confirmed that guidance.

Mendoza said, "It is understandable [residents] feel abandoned when they lack the enforcement mechanisms to deal with potential criminal outbreaks in what are usually very peaceful areas."

Government planning documents show officials considered concerns about community safety, policing demand and the safety of women and girls before approving the project. The documents state that security measures would help mitigate those concerns, but acknowledge they "cannot eliminate all risk."

The Home Office said that while planning permission has been granted, a final decision on whether the MoD Bicester site will ultimately be used for asylum accommodation has not yet been made.

In the meantime, residents of what parish chairman Tim McNally declared the "Principality of Piddington" remain defiant, saying they have no intention of backing down. What began as a local dispute over a former military base has evolved into a national test case in Britain's ongoing battle over immigration, public safety and who bears the burden of accommodating asylum seekers.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.
