articles.title: Libyans pledge to retaliate after Ukraine strikes Russian warship near Benghazi, killing 2 soldiers
articles.summary:
The Libyan National Army (LNA) has vowed to retaliate after a Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian warship moored at a Benghazi port killed two Libyan soldiers.

"With deep sadness and sorrow, and with hearts believing in the decree and destiny of Allah, the General Command of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces mourns two of its heroic sons belonging to the Naval Forces General Staff," the LNA wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday.

Calling the Ukrainian attack "sinful aggression," the LNA also quoted the Quran, writing, "And those who have wronged are going to know to what [kind of] return they will be returned."

RUSSIA WARNS OF 'PREVENTIVE NUCLEAR ATTACK' AS MEDVEDEV CLAIMS UKRAINE, NATO CROSSED LINE

The LNA said the soldiers, identified as Al-Taher Abdullah al-Sadiq and Lieutenant Ali Mohammed al-Said, died Tuesday from injuries sustained during the Sunday attack.

Libya's eastern government, the Government of National Stability, was joined by the country's U.N.-recognized western government, the Government of National Unity, based in the capital, Tripoli, in criticizing the attack.

US CALLS TURKEY-LIBYA MARITIME DEAL 'UNHELPFUL AND PROVOCATIVE' AMID REGIONAL BACKLASH

"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of the Government of National Unity has expressed its condemnation and denunciation of statements made by the Ukrainian President regarding the execution of military operations targeting Russian naval vessels in the vicinity of the city of Benghazi," the Ministry wrote in a statement.

The Tripoli-based government also denied accusations that the Ukrainian attack was launched from Libyan territorial waters.

FRENCH TROOPS SECRETLY DEPLOYED INSIDE UKRAINE AS EX-NATO CHIEF PRAISES MACRON'S 'GUTS'

"The Ministry categorically rejects the conduct of any foreign military operations within Libyan territory or its territorial waters," it added.

Despite the denial, Libya's eastern government requested an investigation into the possibility that the drone strike was launched from Western Libya, citing information that Ukrainian military could be present in "areas around Misrata, Zawiya and other potential locations," according to news outlet Al Arabiya.

NATO FIGHTER JET CLEARED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN MISSILE OVER POLAND AS WARSAW PUSHES FOR US TROOPS

Western Libya's government criticized the Benghazi-based eastern government for hosting Russian ships in the first place.

"Hosting illicit foreign forces and granting them access to national facilities invites the spillover of external conflicts into the country," Tripoli said, according to Al Arabiya.

The Benghazi-based LNA is the military arm of Libya's eastern government, one half of the ruling party in the North African nation. Following the fall of former Libyan dictator Muammar Qadaffi, rivaling power factions made claims on ruling the nation.

The United Nations-backed western government counts the U.S. and European Union among its supporters. The eastern government is broadly aligned with Russia and is not formally recognized by the U.N.

Russia supported Libya's vow for revenge.

"Well, certainly, no state will leave an attempt on the lives of its servicemen unpunished," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in a video.

Ukraine, while confirming the strike, claimed it was self-defense.

"Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasize that Ukraine's actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended to harm Libya or its people," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a message posted to Telegram.

Sybiha also said that the ships it attacked — Russian naval vessels and cargo ships transporting military equipment — were valid military targets as defined by the United Nations Charter's Article 51.

"Ukraine is not 'dragging' anyone into the war or 'transferring' the war anywhere," Sybiha added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also confirmed a separate drone strike on a Russian ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday.

Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Christians increasingly targeted across Europe as watchdog warns of rising hostility
articles.summary:
Attacks targeting Christians across Europe rose 44% last year, according to a new report from the Vienna-based Observatory on Intolerance and Discrimination Against Christians in Europe (OIDAC).

Their research documented 2,465 anti-Christian hate crimes and incidents in 2025, with France, England and Wales, Germany and Austria recording the highest totals.

"Our primary concern with the new data is that anti-Christian attacks that target persons, individuals themselves, have risen," OIDAC executive director Anja Tang told Fox News Digital. "Clergy and people responsible for places of worship were those who were most attacked and also where numbers increased most strongly."

CHRISTIAN WOMAN PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO NEW 'ORWELLIAN' CHARGES FOR STANDING AND SILENT PRAYER

She added, "These would be people who were present, were visible, recognizable as Christians and kind of associated with a church." Tang noted that while OIDAC’s numbers are "quite conservative," saying "aggression against individuals is highly underreported" across Europe.

The group said French authorities recorded a 70% increase in attacks on individuals, the highest in Europe, although Tang notes the French government has not yet published a detailed explanation of the increase. OIDAC argues the increase in attacks against individuals warrants separate attention from incidents involving vandalism, theft and arson targeting religious property.

The findings come as the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe's (OSCE) Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) has increased its focus on anti-Christian hate crimes, publishing a dedicated guide on the issue in 2025. ODIHR said the guide was developed in response to continuing reports of assaults, threats, vandalism, arson and desecration targeting Christian communities, and noted that such incidents can undermine the ability of Christians to practice their faith freely.

ODIHR also told Fox News Digital that underreporting remains "a significant challenge" in addressing anti-Christian hate crimes and stressed that attacks motivated by anti-Christian prejudice should be investigated with the same diligence as attacks motivated by antisemitism, anti-Muslim hatred or other forms of bias.

WORLD-FAMOUS CATHOLIC SHRINE TORCHED, 'DEVIL IN A SKIRT' SCRAWLED ON VIRGIN MARY STATUE

The findings have also drawn concern from Alessandro Calcagno, deputy general secretary of the Commission of the Bishops’ Conferences of the EU (COMECE) and advisor on fundamental rights and freedom of religion within the EU. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Calcagno says "the vital and courageous work constantly carried out by" OIDAC "underscores the importance of EU mechanisms to counter a phenomenon that does exist in Europe and that therefore cannot be ignored at the institutional and policy level."

Lorenzo Vidino, director of the Program on Extremism at George Washington University, says anti-Christian incidents appear to stem from a mix of sources, including anti-religious activists, some individuals from Muslim backgrounds and ordinary vandalism.

Vidino said anti-Christian attacks often receive less public attention than similar incidents involving other faith groups. "There's no question there's been acts of violence against Muslims, against Jews and that's despicable. And when it happens, it is prosecuted," he tells Fox News Digital. "When the same act happens against churches or Christian sites, it doesn't happen in the same way."

STATE DEPARTMENT PRESSES EGYPT TO RESPECT RELIGIOUS FREEDOM AS CHRISTIAN CONVERT FACES POSSIBLE EXECUTION

"While the law might be neutral, the common perception of things is not neutral, and so those incidents are not prioritized," he said.

"Political considerations, public perceptions or prevailing narratives should never determine whether an incident is taken seriously," ODIHR stressed. Adding, "The guiding principle must be equality before the law and equal protection for everyone."

Calcagno says protecting places of worship "cannot be reduced to acts of terrorism, but should also cover other types of attacks against them," including vandalism, violence, profanation, disruptions of religious services, arson and harassment.

Tang said OIDAC is also concerned about migrant communities, including Christians fleeing persecution in the Middle East and asylum seekers "who have left Islam behind and are really facing quite severe aggression because of their choice of religion." She notes these groups "really need protection," and that most incidents involving these groups go unreported "out of fear of stigmatization."

Tang said she was surprised by the number of attacks "connected to pro-life convictions" and carried out by "left-wing extremist groups" that OIDAC categorized as anti-Christian incidents in German-speaking Europe, noting "the level of this violence was just significantly more than what I have seen in my time observing these trends."

CARRYING A BIBLE IN NORTHERN IRELAND HOSPITALS COULD BE A CRIME UNDER ABORTION BUFFER ZONE LAWS

She pointed to a café run by a Leipzig, Germany, church that was forced to close its doors after being vandalized over 26 times because of "their Christian worldview," and an Austrian church that was forced to evacuate in the middle of holy Mass due to "a fake bomb being placed there by left-wing groups… because it was a prayer connected to a pro-life event."

She said,"I find it shocking the level of violence that's often shown by groups who disagree, who plead for tolerance, but then themselves behave the most intolerant."

Calcagno backs OIDAC's call for a dedicated EU coordinator on combating anti-Christian hatred, a position COMECE has repeatedly requested and one it "hopes that the European Commission will take up in the near future." He stressed that such a role would complement existing EU coordinators addressing antisemitism and anti-Muslim hatred, positions that he said "rightly exist at the EU level."

In their statement, ODIHR emphasized that "addressing anti-Christian hate crimes is about ensuring that everyone, without distinction, can exercise their right to freedom of religion or belief without fear of intimidation, discrimination or violence... Ultimately, no community should have to compete for recognition or protection. The same standards of dignity, security and equal treatment must apply to everyone."

OIDAC is urging European governments to adopt recommendations contained in the OSCE's recent practical guide on anti-Christian hate crimes, including improving the recording of incidents, strengthening prevention efforts and expanding support for victims. The group also renewed its call for the EU to appoint a coordinator dedicated to combating anti-Christian hatred.

articles.title: Yemeni military official brands Iran Houthis’ ‘godfather,’ says Tehran is directing war
articles.summary:
Yemen’s military is vowing to defeat the Iran-backed Houthis and retake one of the world’s most strategic maritime choke points, warning that Tehran is directly involved in the planning and execution of a war with implications far beyond Yemen’s borders.

In an on-the-record briefing Tuesday attended by Fox News Digital, Col. Majed Abdullah Al-Nuzaily, the official spokesperson for the Yemeni Armed Forces, acknowledged recent military setbacks but insisted that government forces were prepared to counter the Houthi offensive.

"This is not a conventional battle against an isolated local armed group," Al-Nuzaily said. "What we have seen on the battlefield proves that we are not facing the Houthis alone. This is an Iranian battle: Iranian in its weapons, in its planning and command, and in its direction and timing."

RUBIO ACCUSES IRAN OF FLYING IRGC PERSONNEL INTO YEMEN AS HOUTHI THREAT ESCALATES

The colonel said external supply networks had provided the Houthis with ballistic and cruise missiles, sophisticated drones and advanced electronic warfare capabilities, enabling the group to threaten neighboring countries and international shipping. "Iran is the Houthis' patron, their godfather," he said.

Al-Nuzaily said Yemen’s Interior Ministry had identified 21 foreign experts working with the Houthis, including 14 from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and seven from Hezbollah, allegedly assisting with missile and drone operations, naval attacks and the selection of commercial ships to target. "And we have the evidence to prove it," he said.

The briefing comes as Yemeni government forces face mounting pressure from the Houthis, who, according to Al-Nuzaily, now control the coastline along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Mayyun Island, which sits in the middle of the strategic waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

HOUTHIS ENTER US 'KILL BOX' AFTER SEIZING RED SEA 'CORK,' FORMER PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS

"Bab el-Mandeb remains a priority. We retook it once in a matter of days. We will retake it again, and next time we will hold the mountains as well as the shore," he said.

Al-Nuzaily warned that Tehran views the waterway as a source of leverage against Washington.

"Control of Bab el-Mandeb is at the heart of Iran's strategy. Together with the Strait of Hormuz, it gives Tehran another card to play in its confrontation with the United States, and a way to improve its terms at the negotiating table."

But Yemeni officials warned that the Houthis are increasingly developing their own transnational terrorist network, including cooperation with Somalia-based al-Shabab, meaning a potential agreement between Washington and Tehran would not necessarily eliminate the threat.

NEW RISK FOR US CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT

"When ISIS paraded a single missile, the world trembled – and took action. Today, the Houthis have thousands of ballistic and cruise missiles," Al-Nuzaily said.

Ambassador Marwan Ali Al Noman, political adviser to Yemen’s minister of foreign affairs, expressed gratitude for the Trump administration’s support and the U.S. designation of the Houthis as a terrorist organization, while calling for greater international assistance.

"We are not asking anyone to fight this war for us," Al Noman said. "We are asking for partners."

SAUDI ARABIA TELLS TRUMP NOW IS THE TIME FOR MILITARY ACTION AS IRAN-BACKED HOUTHIS ADVANCE

He said Yemen was seeking military equipment, training, coast guard assistance and expanded sanctions against networks supplying the Houthis with weapons and financing.

Yemen launched Operation Dawn of Yemen on Oct. 4 with the stated objectives of restoring state institutions, retaking the capital, Sanaa, and ending Houthi rule.

Government forces have since faced setbacks, including a withdrawal from the Bab el-Mandeb earlier this month. Al-Nuzaily acknowledged that Houthi forces were approximately 37 miles from Aden, the seat of Yemen’s government, but insisted the city was secure and that military forces now operate under a unified command.

"Some say this war cannot be won," Al-Nuzaily said. "I say to them: you do not know the Yemeni people."

"For 12 years, they have been told to accept the Houthis. For 12 years, they have refused. They have buried their sons and kept fighting. They have lost their homes and kept fighting. They will not kneel to men who rule by fear, who send children to die and who answer to Tehran rather than to Yemen."

"Dawn has come to Yemen. It will not be turned back."

articles.title: Christian filmmaker's discovery of Jewish roots sparks mission to uncover centuries-old secret
articles.summary:
A leading evangelical Christian leader has embarked on a journey to trace the descendants of Jews forcibly converted to Catholicism in Spain and Portugal during the Inquisition around 500 years ago, hoping to help those of Hispanic and Latino descent, known as Anussim or crypto-Jews, rediscover their Jewish roots.

Through her film, "The Lost Jews of the Inquisition," Laurie Cardoza-Moore told Fox News Digital that she hopes to help people like herself uncover a history they may not even know their families carry. 

She says the Israeli government believes there could be millions of "Anussim," or hidden Jews. "Some know their family history, while others don’t," she said.

CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM

Emmy Award-winning documentary filmmaker and host of the television show "Focus on Israel," Cardoza-Moore also serves as president of Proclaiming Justice to the Nations (PJTN). She is also a member of the Tennessee Textbook and Instructional Materials Quality Commission.

For Cardoza-Moore, the journey began in 2002, in the aftermath of 9/11, when she decided to introduce a resolution in the Tennessee state legislature expressing support for Israel in its war on terror.

The following year, she was invited by the Jewish Federation of Nashville on a mission to Israel. During a visit to the Diaspora Museum at Tel Aviv University, now known as the ANU Museum of the Jewish People, Cardoza-Moore discovered that the surnames on both her mother’s and father’s sides of the family were of Jewish origin.

One Sabbath, the group was hosted by a family from Nashville that had immigrated to Israel. As the family recited the blessing over the challah, in keeping with Jewish tradition, Cardoza-Moore recalled her grandfather making the same bread. She remembered eating it on Friday nights as a child, when she called it "sweet bread."

Cardoza-Moore said memories suddenly began flooding back, including a conversation she had with her grandmother when she was four or five years old. She recalled admiring an anniversary ring her grandfather had bought her grandmother.

EVANGELICAL LEADER SLAMS PALESTINIAN OFFICIAL’S BIBLE CLAIMS AS ‘CONTEMPTIBLE’

"I remember saying, ‘Nana, that ring looks fit for a princess,’ and she said, ‘Well, you know we have a Jewish princess in our family,’" she told Fox News Digital.

After gathering evidence during the 2003 trip, Cardoza-Moore asked her father to contact her great-aunt to confirm the family's Jewish roots. She learned that her ancestors were Portuguese Jews who had been forced to convert to Christianity hundreds of years earlier.

"It was a tradition to conceal the identity of our family’s ancestors, and it was the responsibility of the patriarch or matriarch, whichever lived the longest, to reveal it to the next generation on their deathbed," she told Fox News Digital.

"As a student of the Bible, I knew that one day Israel would be restored, that Hashem would bring all 12 tribes back to the land to inhabit the land of their forefathers. I knew this prophetic history would unfold, but discovering that my family was part of this group of people transformed my life," she said.

Through her documentary, Cardoza-Moore said she hopes to spread this message beyond Spain and Portugal to the farthest reaches of the world where the Anussim fled, including Brazil, Argentina and Mexico.

She continues to travel across Southern Europe and South America to film interviews for the documentary, which is scheduled to premiere in Israel by fall 2027.

Cardoza-Moore said the return of the Anussim is particularly significant amid a sharp rise in antisemitism. Yet, 500 years after the Inquisition, some still fear revealing their Jewish ancestry, she said.

"This is a disturbing trend. There are groups within Israel working to bridge the gap and help the Anussim return to the land of Israel. That is the purpose of this documentary: to reach those who don’t know their ancestry, as well as those who know but keep it hidden, and help them understand that it is safe to come back and that Israel is waiting for them," she said.

Cardoza-Moore recalled speaking at a convention with a woman who approached her with her family and young children. After introducing herself and learning the woman's last name, Cardoza-Moore asked if she was Jewish.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

"She said they were Catholic, and I told her that her last name was Sephardic. Her face lit up. She was excited by the possibility that she might be descended from the Anussim and said she planned to look into her family history," Cardoza-Moore said.

Cardoza-Moore said certain surnames, including Nunez and Lopez, can offer clues to Sephardic Jewish ancestry. She explained that in Spain, the "Z" in some surnames was originally an "S," but that Jews who fled to Portugal changed it to a "Z" as a sign of their Jewish identity, allowing them to recognize one another.

"There are so many Hispanic and Latino surnames. In fact, one of the people I’m investigating is a country’s leader. I believe he may also be a descendant of the Anussim," she said.

"This is a very exciting journey, one that I get to share with others as they begin to realize that this is their family’s story, too. They start recalling things like, ‘I remember when family members would die, we would cover mirrors during the mourning period,’" she said.

Another reason Cardoza-Moore decided to produce the documentary was to educate Christians about the Inquisition and the Catholic Church’s treatment of Jews during that period.

DOMINICAN REPUBLIC JOINS GLOBAL FIGHT AGAINST ANTISEMITISM WITH LANDMARK MOVE

"There are many Christians, particularly evangelical Christians, who would be equally appalled by what was done to the Jewish people in the name of their God. As they learn what was done to the Jews in the name of Jesus, they will wake up and realize that this is unacceptable," she said.

Cardoza-Moore said she sees a growing movement among Christians turning away from Israel and the Jewish people, which she attributes to a lack of biblical education.

"We at PJTN have to change that. That is why we use the Bible and the Scriptures and refer to the prophets to remind Christians of their teachings, because Christians believe the prophets spoke the truth," she said.

As an evangelical leader, Cardoza-Moore said she had considered keeping her Jewish roots private but ultimately decided that fulfilling her calling was more important.

"If my ancestors were persecuted and forced into silence because of who they were, that is unacceptable. I will go to my grave fighting insidious hatred and holding the church and Christians accountable, because we are seeing antisemitism rise again and hearing the same blood libels from Christians that were spread in the past," she told Fox News Digital.

"We can’t be silent. We have to speak up and alert the church, because judgment will come. Genesis 12:3 says, ‘I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you, I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you,’" she added.

articles.title: How skipping breakfast to save room for dinner shocks your blood sugar and metabolism
articles.summary:
Fasting all morning to save room for a big holiday feast might seem like a smart strategy, but experts say it can have unwanted health effects, and that there are better ways to prepare.

When people go hours without food, blood sugar levels drop, triggering headaches, nausea and irritability, according to Gabrielle Kishner, a registered dietitian nutritionist and founder in New York City.

"Once we get those uncomfortable symptoms of hunger, we're going to eat really fast when we get into Thanksgiving, because we're starving," Kishner told Fox News Digital. "We're also going to crave more carbs and sugar to get that blood sugar back up."

DOCTORS SETTLE DEBATE OVER DRINKING COFFEE ON AN EMPTY STOMACH AND POTENTIAL HEALTH RISKS

Previous research has found that skipping daytime meals leads to significantly higher post-meal blood glucose spikes at dinner compared with eating regular meals.

Regular breakfast omission has also been linked to disrupted circadian rhythms, impaired insulin sensitivity and a sluggish metabolism, as well as compensatory eating later in the day.

To avoid coming to the dinner table starving, Kishner recommends eating a balanced breakfast within two hours of waking up and avoiding gaps of longer than four to six hours without food.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Combining carbohydrates, protein, fiber and healthy fats like Greek yogurt with berries and chia seeds, or avocado toast topped with hard-boiled eggs, helps stabilize energy and blood sugar, so diners arrive "comfortably hungry," she said.

If the main meal takes place early in the afternoon, a balanced midmorning snack containing two nutrient groups, like vegetables and hummus, can help bridge the gap.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

How diners build that first plate also affects digestion and energy.

Kishner recommends filling half the plate with fiber-rich fruits and vegetables, eating those first to slow digestion and help stabilize fullness.

The second half of the plate should be split evenly between protein, like turkey, and carbohydrates, such as stuffing or mashed potatoes.

Once the meal begins, pacing plays a major role in preventing gastrointestinal distress, Kishner said. Eating quickly makes it harder for the stomach to break down poorly chewed food, leading to bloating and discomfort.

It takes roughly 20 to 30 minutes for the stomach to send satiety signals to the brain, meaning fast eaters often consume far more food than they need before realizing they are full, according to Cleveland Clinic.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Kishner recommends pausing midway through the meal to assess hunger levels, and waiting 10 to 20 minutes after finishing a plate before going back for seconds.

Rich, creamy and sugary dishes take longer to digest, so sampling small portions from the dessert table helps to prevent stomachaches without making favorite foods off-limits.

For those who do end up overindulging, gentle movement afterward can ease the post-meal slump. Kishner suggests taking a 10- to 15-minute walk with family or friends after the meal to aid digestion and blood sugar regulation.

Blood sugar typically peaks 30 to 90 minutes after a meal, and even brief, light-intensity walking helps blunt glucose spikes and keep insulin levels steady. Drinking water throughout the day also helps to digest food, according to Kishner.

Above all, Kishner urges diners not to compensate the next morning by restricting food or skipping breakfast again, which only restarts the cycle of blood sugar crashes and overeating.

articles.title: Trump administration weighs targeting Iran's top regime leaders in bid to end war: report
articles.summary:
The Trump administration has renewed internal discussions about potentially targeting senior Iranian regime leaders in strikes that some officials believe could end the ongoing war, according to reports.

Citing a U. S. official and another source, NBC News reported Tuesday that some officials believe eliminating senior figures could pressure Tehran to end the conflict by showing that Washington can locate and strike the regime's leadership at any time.

Though the option has long been under consideration, it has "been under renewed discussion in recent weeks" as President Donald Trump deliberates over the next phase of the war, two sources told the outlet.

The deliberations come amid reports that Iran could be developing a radioactive "dirty bomb" and a report citing U. S. intelligence assessments of potential Iranian plots involving chemical weapons aimed at senior officials in Washington.

TRUMP WARNS IRAN ABOUT REPORTED PLOT AGAINST ADMIN OFFICIALS: 'WE TAKE IT VERY SERIOUSLY'

"We know a lot about what's happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We'll find out about it. We will not allow that," Trump had told reporters at the White House Nov. 20.

Iran's surviving leadership includes Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, after the elder Khamenei was killed in the opening strikes of the war Feb. 28.

Other senior figures in Iran's military and national security apparatus include Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Commander Ahmad Vahidi, armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Mohsen Rezaei, a former IRGC commander in chief reportedly appointed secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council in August 2026.

AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS

NBC News did not identify any of those officials as specific targets of the operations under discussion.

Administration officials opposed to the proposal have reportedly warned that targeting Iranian leaders could expose American officials to retaliatory attacks, stiffen the resolve of surviving regime figures and undermine future diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, now in its ninth month. 

The administration continues to weigh military options, enforce its naval blockade and assert control over the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.

The debate comes months after U. S. and Israeli strikes killed Iran's supreme leader and other senior military and intelligence officials, igniting a prolonged conflict centered on Tehran's nuclear program, ballistic missile capabilities and regional military activities.

Mojtaba Khamenei, who was reportedly injured in the strikes that killed his father, has not been seen publicly since assuming power, though he has warned Washington and Jerusalem against resuming major attacks on Iranian leadership.

MOJTABA KHAMENEI DEFIES ‘MALICIOUS’ ATTACKS AS US ARMY ZEROES IN ON IRAN’S 350,000 TROOPS

"If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for ending them," a statement attributed to Khamenei said.

The warning reportedly followed a meeting with senior Iranian military commanders, including Abdollahi, Hatami and Vahidi. On Oct. 31, Khamenei also directed Iran's armed forces to prepare an "immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response" to any future threats.

"The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing," a White House official told Fox News Digital Tuesday.

"The president has been clear that the greatest naval blockade in history, Operation Economic Outcast, and the new Task Force Iron Gate will continue with full effect. 

"President Trump has many options at his disposal and will make the best possible decision to ensure Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon. "

articles.title: Iran to execute 2 anti-regime protesters at dawn after 3 days in death row holding cells
articles.summary:
Two Iranian anti-regime protesters face execution within hours after spending three days in pre-execution holding cells at Ghezel Hesar Prison, according to a human rights organization warning that the men were sentenced to death following torture, forced confessions and unfair trials.

Milad Armoun, 27, and Navid Najaran, 34, are scheduled to be executed in the early hours of Wednesday, Nov. 25, according to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO).

The men were transferred to solitary confinement on Nov. 21 after Iran's Supreme Court upheld their death sentences.

IRANIAN BOXER ON DEATH ROW WINS HUMAN RIGHTS AWARD AS ATHLETES PUSH TO SAVE HIS LIFE

Both men were arrested during Iran's 2022 "Woman, Life, Freedom" uprising and are defendants in the high-profile "Ekbatan case," which stems from the killing of a member of Iran's Basij paramilitary force during nationwide anti-government demonstrations.

Exiled Iranian crown prince Reza Phahlavi said on X on Tuesday that the execution would take place at dawn.

IRANIAN REGIME CRITIC WARNS TRUMP DEAL COULD BE 'LIFELINE' FOR REGIME, CLAIMS PEOPLE ARE 'NERVOUS'

"Despite being acquitted of the murder charge, Milad Armon and Navid Najjaran have been sentenced to death by "hanging judge" Abolqasem Salavati.

"The execution orders for these two political prisoners have been sent to their lawyers, to be carried out at dawn on Wednesday, Azar 4."

"Milad and Navid were held in Ward 33 which houses those accused of murder before being transferred to solitary confinement in preparation for their executions today," a source told IHRNGO.

The men were sentenced to death in May by Branch 15 of Tehran's Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Abolqasem Salavati, on charges of efsad-fil-arz , or "corruption on earth," a capital offense under Iranian law.

Salavati has faced longstanding criticism from human rights organizations over his handling of political cases and the harsh sentences imposed on government opponents.

Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of Iran Human Rights, condemned the sentences and called for immediate international intervention.

"Milad Armoun and Navid Najaran were sentenced to death following torture, forced confessions and grossly unfair trials. Their executions would be an irreversible injustice and another example of the Islamic Republic’s use of the death penalty as a tool of political repression.

IRAN HANGS 2 PROTESTERS IN PUBLIC, CROWD CRIES 'DISHONORABLE' AS SECURITY FIRES TEAR GAS

"Strong international reactions may be the only way to save their lives. We urge the UN and all governments with diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic to intervene immediately to stop their executions," Amiry-Moghaddam said in a statement.

The Ekbatan case centers on the death of Arman Aliverdi, a member of the Basij, a volunteer paramilitary force affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Aliverdi was injured during unrest in Tehran's Ekbatan neighborhood in 2022, and died two days later. Iranian authorities accused several protesters of involvement in his death.

Armoun was arrested in Tehran in November 2022, while Najaran was detained the following month in Ahvaz.

Iran Human Rights alleged that both men were tortured and subjected to ill-treatment to obtain self-incriminating confessions subsequently broadcast by Iranian state media.

IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY

Defense attorneys also accused judicial authorities of barring lawyers from hearings, withholding case documents and obstructing appeals.

Earlier death sentences tied to murder charges were overturned, and Najaran was acquitted of involvement in the killing in a separate proceeding. However, the Revolutionary Court subsequently imposed death sentences under Iran's national security laws.

The death sentences of two other defendants, Mehdi Imani and Seyed Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, were overturned, and their cases referred for retrial, according to human rights organizations.

The "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement erupted in 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish Iranian woman detained by morality police over allegations that she improperly wore her hijab.

The demonstrations spread nationwide, becoming one of the most significant challenges to Iran's clerical leadership in decades.

articles.title: FDA approves first new breast cancer hormone therapy in over two decades
articles.summary:
A new early-stage breast cancer therapy has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration for the first time in more than two decades.

Wilserdly (giredestrant), an oral hormone therapy from San Francisco-based drugmaker Genentech, received the approval after positive trial results in treating adults with early-stage ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer.

This subtype is the most common form of the disease in which tumor growth is fueled by the hormone estrogen rather than excess levels of the HER2 protein.

NEW DRUG APPROACH OFFERS HOPE FOR PATIENTS WITH RECURRENT AGGRESSIVE CANCERS

The Phase 3 lidERA study showed that the drug reduced the risk of disease recurrence or death by 30% compared to standard endocrine therapy, including generic pharmaceuticals like tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors, according to a Genentech press release.

Patients were also less likely to quit treatment because of side effects like joint pain and hot flashes compared to standard options, the researchers noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The study found a reduction in cancer returning in distant parts of the body, like the bones, liver or lungs.

Aditya Bardia, M.D., global principal investigator of the lidERA breast cancer trial and professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, noted that this finding is "particularly significant" because once breast cancer spreads to distant organs, it is "generally no longer curable."

The foundational hormone therapies used for early-stage breast cancer have remained "largely unchanged" since the 2000s, Bardia told Fox News Digital.

"These medicines have saved countless lives, but there has been room for improvement, both in terms of effectiveness and tolerability," he said.

"Now, for the first time in more than two decades, we have a new foundational hormone treatment that has been shown to be more effective than our existing standard therapies in early-stage breast cancer."

Because most breast cancers are caught early and fall into the hormone receptor-positive subtype, the new therapy has the potential to help a large number of patients, Bardia added.

Earlier this year, the FDA also approved Wilserdly combined with everolimus, an oral cancer medication, for the treatment of adults with ER-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer whose disease had recurred during or after completing endocrine-based therapy.

This makes Wilserdly the "first and only" SERD (selective estrogen receptor degrader) that is FDA-approved to treat both early-stage and advanced ER-positive breast cancer.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Levi Garraway, M.D., chief medical officer and head of global product development, commented in a statement that the FDA approval is due to the drug showing "superior efficacy" against other therapies that have long been the standard of care.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Genentech, a member of the Roche Group, plans to continue investing in "broad development" of Wilserdly, exploring its potential across disease stages and in new treatment combinations, according to Roche Pharmaceuticals CEO Teresa Graham.

Bardia encouraged patients to speak with their oncologists about the new treatment option, particularly those whose recent diagnosis is "consistent with the regulatory label and approval of the drug. "

articles.title: Vatican releases Pope Francis' private diary detailing spiritual crisis, encounters with the devil
articles.summary:
Excerpts from the late Pope Francis' private diary published Tuesday reveal that the pontiff endured a two-year spiritual crisis beginning in 2021, writing that he felt tempted by the devil and struggled with the weight of wielding power over the Catholic Church.

The 160-page volume, "The Private Diary of Pope Francis," was compiled by Cardinal Victor Fernandez and spans entries from December 1992 through August 2024 — eight months before Francis died in April 2025 at age 88 — marking the first papal diary made public since the 1960s.

In a December 2022 entry, Francis described his crisis as "all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation," adding that he resisted becoming a leader "who uses others like puppets."

MYSTERIOUS BLOOD-SOAKED RELIC LINKED TO HISTORY'S MOST BELOVED SAINT, ST. FRANCIS OF ASSISI, GOES ON DISPLAY

Across the entries, Francis wrote that he believed he had seen the devil three times — including during a Vatican meeting — and recalled a June 2018 vision of hell.

"Last night I saw the entrance to Hell," he wrote in the 2018 entry. "I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me. I grabbed the Rosary as a weapon. I thank the Lord for this help."

Reacting Tuesday on "Varney & Co.," Fox News contributor and theologian Jonathan Morris said he was most struck not by the late pope's spiritual struggles, but by the Vatican's decision to publish them.

POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL

"I think the most surprising part is that this was actually published, not so much that it happened, " Morris said. "Spiritual warfare is a very basic Christian doctrine, and even the last things — death, judgment, heaven, hell. And apparently he saw the gates of hell. Those are the core beliefs of the church across all sorts of denominations within Christianity."

Morris added that Francis' successor, Pope Leo XIV — whom Francis praised in the diary as "a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man" — approved releasing the writings so they might help others facing similar trials.

Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: The End of Spain’s ‘Frankenstein’ Coalition? Presidential Plotting in Paris, Kushner & Kremlin Trap
articles.summary:
Catch up with the World This Week with Gavin Lee. In just 45 minutes, make sense of seven extraordinary days in global affairs, as Gavin and his handpicked panel of four leading international correspondents unpack the stories shaping the world — and the questions behind the headlines.

This week: Spain’s snap election; the presidential plotting unfolding over lunch at the Brasserie Concorde in Paris; Ukraine, Kushner and the ‘Kremlin Trap’; and the question hanging over Iran: whose side is time on?

Joining Gavin are New World Magazine columnist Emma-Kate Symonds; Constant Méheut, The New York Times correspondent in Ukraine; Venetia Rainer, Daily Telegraph Foreign Editor and host of Iran: The Latest; and Sarah Morris, France 24’s correspondent in Spain.

articles.title: The AI revolution: Will I lose my job?
articles.summary: Have you heard of FOBO? It stands for fear of being obsolete. So as AI spreads, is it going to impact women in the workforce more than men? And are we right to be fearful of becoming obsolete? The International Labour Organization has already found occupations dominated by women are nearly twice as likely to be exposed to job losses thanks to generative AI, compared to those dominated by men.

articles.title: Is Spain 'nostalgic' for Franco? Would traditional right PP consider an alliance with far-right Vox?
articles.summary: After eight years of socialist-led government, Spain is at a crossroads. Can Pedro Sánchez pull off another electoral comeback, or will the conservative Partido Popular make way for the far right into national government for the first time since the end of Franco's 40-year brutal reign? Just back from Madrid, Richard Werly, Europe correspondent for the Swiss daily Blick, joins Angela Diffley to examine the final days of campaigning and the generational divisions shaping Sunday’s snap elections. The youth are divided between the left and the far-right Vox party. Sánchez, nicknamed the “Teflon politician”, has campaigned heavily on housing and social issues. “We may see an outgoing prime minister performing better than expected,” says Werly.

articles.title: 'From bad to catastrophic: Iran's justice system was already unfair for many decades'
articles.summary: Amid war with the US and Israel, Iranian protesters continue to face death sentences following what Amnesty International describes as grossly unfair, torture-tainted trials. “The situation has changed from bad to catastrophic,” says Raha Bahreini, Iranian-Canadian human rights lawyer and Amnesty International's researcher on Iran. Bahreini discusses the aftermath of the January 2026 protests, the authorities' efforts to equate peaceful dissent with treason and espionage, and the extrajudicial killings of peaceful protesters. Amnesty International is calling for an international criminal justice mechanism, potentially a special tribunal. “There needs to be criminal accountability for these crimes against humanity.”

articles.summary: Climate-vulnerable countries fought for years to create a loss and damage fund. Four years on, demand far outstrips funding, pledges are scarce, and disaster-hit nations are still waiting for support.
