articles.title: AI solved the hardest problem in maths – is there anything it can’t do?
articles.summary:
Alzheimer’s disease, involving amyloid plaques in the brain, will be tough for AI to solve

JUAN GAERTNER/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY

The progress AI has made in mathematics this year is nothing short of extraordinary. In January, I was impressed to see relatively minor open problems tackled with the help of AI. Now, AI is being used to solve the hardest problems in maths. The obvious next question is, if AI can do this, is there anything it can’t do? That is the inference that the AI companies want us to make, but, in reality, the answer is much more nuanced.

Read more

Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis

We see this messaging in claims that AI can “solve X”, where X is any field of human endeavour you care to name. Biology is a big one. “Cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness – these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei while promoting the company’s recent initial public offering. “I think one day maybe we can cure all disease with the help of AI,” said Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, last year, adding that this could be “within the next decade or so”.

This phenomenon isn’t new: I call it “physicist brain”, after the propensity for physicists to wade into areas outside their expertise and declare simple solutions. More broadly, it is called Nobel disease, after the many Nobel prizewinners who have gone on to make, shall we say, less evidenced-backed claims. In general, there is a tendency to think that if an intelligent person is good at one thing, they are good at many other things that require intelligence. What is different now is that trillion-dollar companies and large swathes of the global economy now depend on this being true of artificial intelligence.

Advertisement

To be clear, I think we must now admit that AI is better at solving open mathematical problems than any human, and that this has happened faster than anyone ever expected. When I first saw the news in September that the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by OpenAI, I felt stunned. We had entered a new world. With the announcement of the Riemann hypothesis proof this week, I felt sick and had to go and have a lie-down. These were intellectual Everests I have marvelled at since my teenage years, conquered by a machine far sooner than anyone expected. You may have read my recent piece forecasting the future in 2096 – an early draft had a line, later removed, about three Millennium Prize Problems being solved by AI in the 2030s. We’ve had two this year alone.

But maths isn’t biology. Yes, we have seen advances like AlphaFold, Deepmind’s AI that can predict the structure of proteins, but this is biology at its most mathematical, a computational puzzle. True advances in biology and medicine require studying cells, animals and people, all of which can be frustratingly illogical and uncooperative. Amodei admitted as much in 2024, writing that “the main challenges with directly applying intelligence to biology are data, the speed of the physical world, and intrinsic complexity”. You can imagine mitigations here – AI-directed robotic labs, for example – but it doesn’t seem like we should expect massive speed leaps in capability comparable to those seen in mathematics. There isn’t an easy way to confirm that a biological discovery is correct, in the manner that the computer code Lean allows for mathematics.

Worse still are claims that AI will “solve climate change”. For Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, this came as a throwaway comment in a 2024 essay: “Although it will happen incrementally, astounding triumphs – fixing the climate, establishing a space colony, and the discovery of all of physics – will eventually become commonplace.”

But we already know the solution to climate change: reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net zero and the warming will stop. The blockers to doing so, as demonstrated by the recent failure of the COP31 climate summit, are political, not technological. Even if AI were to produce a blueprint for a perfectly functioning nuclear fusion reactor tomorrow, we would still have to build thousands of them across the globe in the next decade or so to avoid the most catastrophic warming effects. In the past decade, we have built 60 nuclear fission reactors, a technology we understand far better than an as-yet-mythical fusion power plant. Again, you can see how AI might offer some improvements, but not enough to counteract our fossil fuel use.

It is important for me to have some humility here, because one thing AI’s breakthroughs in mathematics this year has underlined for me is the need to change my mind when the evidence changes. I started that process with the early signs of AI progress in maths, but didn’t update my beliefs fast enough – though, to be fair to myself, neither did almost everyone else, including leading mathematicians such as Terence Tao, who, just weeks ago, said he didn’t expect the Riemann hypothesis to be solved by AI until 2050.

For that reason, I am on the lookout for early signs that AI success in biology is shifting. That could include an AI-designed drug proving useful in people – for example, Rentosertib, a leading candidate, is now undergoing a phase III trial as a treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a type of lung disease. The trial is expected to conclude in 2029, so we’re talking years of wait for any results. If the drug succeeds, that doesn’t necessarily provide a way for any other AI drug candidates to succeed, and the painfully slow process of molecule selection, animal testing and human trials is still hard to speed up.

If I’m forced to make a prediction, I can fairly confidently state that we will see yet more advances in AI maths in 2027. I also expect that we will see some completely unexpected results in other fields as well. But solving biology? Ending climate change? Defeating disease? These still feel, for now, like science fiction.

Read more

AI refutes 30-year-old mathematical assumption in computer science

Further AI reading

AI maths has become a spectator sport, thanks to a website dedicated to tracking agents attempting to solve the P vs NP problem, one of the remaining huge open problems in mathematics (see my explanation of it here). I don’t expect this approach to work – the models being used here are consumer ones, rather than the internal frontier models the AI firms have used for the big maths results so far.

As if to illustrate this, both OpenAI and Anthropic have released, with little fanfare, solutions to the VP vs VNP problem. This is a lesser version of the P vs NP problem, and doesn’t necessarily help us get any closer to solving its big brother.

And speaking of internal models, Axios reports that both Anthropic and OpenAI employees are concerned that their internal models are so powerful that they can’t safely be released. Take this with a big pinch of salt – Anthropic said the same about its Mythos model due to its cybersecurity abilities, then later released its Fable model, which is essentially just Mythos with some added guardrails. And don’t forget that, way back in the mists of 2019, OpenAI said that GPT-2 would be too dangerous to release. Today, you can run far more capable models on a smartphone, and no one finds that dangerous.

Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after a mere 11 days away following a scandal about his admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy. For a reminder of why Nvidia is so important to the AI industry, see my previous column.

A UN conference has failed to agree to a ban on autonomous weapons, as my colleague Matthew Sparkes predicted last week.

articles.title: The defence tech revolution is changing how we innovate
articles.summary:
Cpl Aaron J Stone/UK Ministry of Defence

Only five years ago, defence technology start-ups had little choice but to wait for government funding to build and test their inventions – often in complex, multi-year programmes. No longer, however: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has prompted such a fast, furious response that military innovation timescales have shrunk dramatically.

“Ukraine is becoming a real-world lab for military innovation, and it’s innovating at a pace greater than anything that we’ve seen previously,” says Ola Fashade, an air vice-marshal in the Royal Air Force and director of military digitalisation and the rapid AI delivery task force at the UK’s Ministry of Defence (MoD).

“Agility and tempo of adaptation is critical. In a contested battlespace, technology that works well on day one, by day eight has become a little muted – and by day twelve it’s probably no longer relevant. And if you don’t adapt over that period, what you have is a very expensive and ineffective bag of steel.”

Advertisement

That raises the question of how significant this accelerated innovation could become. In September 2026, New Scientist CoLab, sponsored by BAE Systems, brought together leading thinkers and investors from industry, the military and academia to discuss the factors driving this innovation and the lessons that can be transferred to other industries.

Staying alive

The investment for this step change is coming both from the technology incubators based within military prime contractors – like the Launchpad incubator at BAE Systems – and from a host of venture capital (VC) companies worldwide. “The idea behind Launchpad is to forge an ecosystem that gets technology from defence start-ups into the front line quicker, or into spinouts, before they run out of money and die,” says David Ewing, head of technology commercialisation at BAE Systems. In addition, VC funding is seeing a raft of new multibillion-dollar military tech players, dubbed neoprimes, that complement the work of the primes on bigger-ticket battlespace items.

The poster child for the neoprimes, says Samuel Burrell, a partner at the pan-European VC firm Expeditions Fund, is the nascent British air defence start-up Cambridge Aerospace, which reached a valuation of $3.4 billion with little but a convincing tech narrative: “They had no battlefield data, no product – just a compelling team and an idea on paper.” It wasn’t all talk: Cambridge Aerospace has begun delivering its Skyhammer air defence missile for taking out Shahed-type drones and cruise missiles. A solid-rocket-motor-powered ballistic missile interceptor, Starhammer, will ship in 2027.

In the maritime battlespace, meanwhile, fast-scaling neoprime Kraken Technology Group of Hampshire, UK, has raised $175 million from various VC firms, valuing it at $1 billion, to further develop its uncrewed surface vessel and drone technologies for users including the MoD, NATO and the US Special Operations Command. Key to it all succeeding, according to Amelia Gould, chief technology officer at Kraken, is a culture that actively nurtures iterative speed – to ensure battlefield systems stay ahead of emerging countermeasures: “Having really quick feedback loops from the warfightersin the field to r for high-consequence innovation,” Gould says.

Forging ecosystems

The shortening of feedback and iteration cycles, however, means tacticians must increasingly accept imperfect battlefield technologies. “We need to be much more open to minimum viable products, with relatively few safeguards, because, in conflict, staying alive is what matters,” says Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, CEO at Ploughshare, an MoD-owned specialist in turning technology into real-world applications, companies and growth. Ewing agrees: “We’ll definitely see a move away from having so many exquisite platforms, in programmes that take years to define, decades to deliver and decades to wind up, in favour of quicker cycles of technology validation, implementation and adoption.”

What kind of spinoffs could emerge from this new way of refining technology? Westwood hopes some powerful answers on clean energy (see box) may emerge. “If we get ourselves really motivated around the fact that we’re boiling the Earth, that could be a real technology driver here,” he says.

What makes Westwood so confident of a positive dividend outside the military? An example from history, he says: “We went into world war two with propeller-driven biplanes and came out six years later with jet fighter aircraft. And the subsequent innovation around the jet engine seeded the commercial air transport market that’s been such a huge influence on the way we all live now.”

Ukraine’s move has militaries around the world racing to emulate its iterative techniques, which are based on the low-cost technologies behind smartphones and consumer drones: artificial intelligence, mobile connectivity, satellite positioning, cloud storage, digital design systems and 3D printing. “It’s the ability to develop, deploy and iterate these technologies at scale that have been the driver for the drone technology that we see Ukraine using,” says Mark Westwood, director of defence and security at Cranfield University in the UK.

Read more about BAE Systems Launchpad at: baesystems.com/launchpad

The civilian dividend

One of the leading spinoffs from BAE Systems’ Launchpad incubator is start-up Nuclear Turbines of Manchester, UK, which has raised £15 million from four venture funds to begin developing a novel, passively safe 20-megawatt small modular nuclear reactor.

The reactor is designed to power data centres and industrial plant. Its novelty is a straightforward one, says CEO Jeremy Owston: instead of driving a vast steam turbine, like a regular reactor, its reactor heats and compresses air to much hotter temperatures to drive a small, commercial gas turbine – greatly simplifying and shrinking the overall power plant.

“We’re not building Hinkley Point. We’re targeting the early 2030s to get our reactor up and running and we don’t need tens of billions of pounds to do that. What we’re talking about will need a fraction of the price,” Owston says, adding that he is impressed by the willingness of the VC sector to back such ideas.

There are plenty more opportunities worth investing in, says Hetti Barkworth-Nanton at the MoD’s intellectual property spinoff unit, Ploughshare. “Of the billions spent every year in the UK on defence innovation, only a fraction results in IP being spun out. The track record of that innovation reaching civilian markets is weak.”

VCs are beginning to notice this opportunity. “There are so many of these funds and they just want to take a bet on something, and that’s great,” says Owston.

articles.title: Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location
articles.summary:
A northern gannet (Morus bassanus) tagged with biologging devices on its back and tail

Steve Votier

Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track.

Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage.

In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite “blind spots” also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

Advertisement

Read more

Most large fishing boats go untracked as ‘dark vessels’

Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are tracked only “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”.

The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets (Morus bassanus) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast.

Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters (Puffinus mauretanicus) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity.

Tammy Davies at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”.

Peter Ejbye-Ernst at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR) describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too.

A tagged northern gannet coming in to land in Wales

Steve Votier

“What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea.

In terms of its applications for cracking down on IUU, he says: “There’s a fine line between trying to understand something better and document it and then trying to control it and surveil it.”

There are caveats, as the study has a small sample size and records both false-negatives and false-positives. It also gives very little information on the type of activity vessels were carrying out. But, while the research isn’t a solution to the problem of IUU, it is “part of the toolbox” for understanding what is happening at sea, says Ejbye-Ernst.

The study didn’t differentiate between the size of vessels, but Rutter and his colleagues say this would be a good area for future research.

Powerful images show dark side of South-East Asia’s fishing industry

Photographer Nicole Tung captures the tough world facing South-East Asia’s fishers and their families in this series of images, which won her the Carmignac Photojournalism Award for fieldwork

“Animal-borne audio recorders could potentially be used to investigate other ecological interactions and human activities that are difficult to observe directly, particularly in the marine environment,” says team member Ana Bertoldi Carneiro, also at BirdLife International.

Hugo Tagholm at the charity Oceana says it is shocking that so many of the interactions were with unseen vessels, but he is concerned about attaching devices to seabirds on a broader scale to track this.

“Seabirds are already grappling with the harm caused by overfishing and climate breakdown, we don’t want to put them at even greater risk from vessel operators acting illegally,” he says.

“What we need is mandatory remote electronic monitoring across all fishing vessels, clear and effective laws and catch limits to protect and restore our seas, and truly deterrent sanctions for those breaking the law.”

Journal Reference:

Science Advances
DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh2224

articles.title: Exploring the cracks in the standard model of particle physics with Dr Harry Cliff
articles.summary:
The standard model of particle physics has been one of our most successful scientific theories, classifying the known elementary particles and describing three of the four fundamental forces. But it’s not perfect, and cracks are forming. Experimental particle physicist Dr Harry Cliff unpacks how the model works, where it is starting to fail and how we might find new physics in the gaps. He explains the true nature of the Higgs boson, the anomalies detected by particle accelerators and how we might finally detect dark matter.

Dr Cliff talks to New Scientist physics reporter Jacklin Kwan at the University of Cambridge.

Read more

At CERN’s Antimatter Factory, scientists probe the mysteries of matter

articles.title: AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it
articles.summary:
MARK SYKES/SPL/Alamy

There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. H. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”. Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof.

Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it. The consensus among mathematicians is that the proof, produced with the aid of AI, will hold, but that it will take much more work to make it comprehensible to humans.

However you feel about AI, this is a watershed moment, and one that demonstrates just how little we still understand about the capabilities of the technology. As recently as last month, leading mathematician Terence Tao speculated that AI would eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but that it may not happen before 2050. Now, some mathematicians are considering whether their hardest and most infamous remaining problems could be settled within months. In a year that has left mathematicians reeling, this may be the knock-out blow.

Advertisement

This is a watershed moment, and it shows just how little we understand about AI’s abilities

For non-mathematicians, the fall of the Riemann hypothesis is harder to interpret. In the past year, AI has seen incredible advances in both maths and coding, but it is perhaps no coincidence that in these arenas, with nothing more than computer code, answers can swiftly be checked and iterated upon, allowing for rapid improvement. When it comes to other human endeavours though, from art to zoology, such verification is far harder, involving either the messy physical world, or unknowable human taste – or both. Whether this verification gap can be closed may become the biggest question of our age. Answers on a postcard, please.

What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?

It has been called the hardest problem in mathematics, and now through a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, the Riemann hypothesis may have finally been solved

articles.title: Basic income trial in Peru aims to prove rainforest protection merits
articles.summary:
A basic income pilot scheme will pay communities in Peru to protect the rainforest there

Andrea Ramos/Cool Earth

A trial seeking to prove the environmental benefits of giving Indigenous populations living in rainforests unconditional cash payments will launch next year amid growing hopes that basic income payments could offer a fresh approach to rainforest protection.

The trial, which will last at least two years and potentially for four, will see almost 400 people living in the Peruvian Amazon receive cash payments equivalent to around £57 per person, per month. The hope is that by providing Indigenous people with income security, they will be less likely to sell or lease land to loggers, miners or agriculture industries that will deforest.

“We are trying to build autonomy into the communities,” says Caterina Cosmopolis at Cool Earth, a UK-based charity that will run the trial. “They can make their own decisions, they can find their own solutions.”

Advertisement

Read more

Ancient human settlements boosted biomass of today’s Amazon rainforest

The trial will build on a two-year pilot that Cool Earth launched in 2023 in which 211 people in three communities in Peru’s Junín province received cash transfers equivalent to £2 per day, to spend however they liked.

The cash payments were supplied alongside a programme of community-led training, covering financial education, climate change, environmental conservation and Indigenous rights.

In October, the University of Bath in the UK published the results of the pilot trial, reporting that the cash payments bolstered food security, improved community wellbeing and led to 90 per cent of participants adopting environmentally beneficial activities such as reforestation or reduced forest burning.

Free newsletter

Sign up to The Earth Edition

Sign up to newsletter

But the evidence for rainforest protection was limited by a lack of rigorous environmental monitoring or the use of control groups during the trial, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how effective the basic income was in preventing tropical forest degradation and deforestation.

The second trial is due to launch in March next year across three communities in Junín province, where tropical land is under pressure from the expansion of ginger plantations and illegal gold mining. Alongside the community that will receive the cash income – 1040 Peruvian soles, or roughly £228 per person, every four months – there will be two control communities that will receive no payments.

“We are trying to gather more evidence about what the results of cash transfer will be like in different communities,” says Cosmopolis. “If we have the same results, we might be able to say this works – that conservation basic income can work.”

Read more

How Bolivia’s gold rush is poisoning Indigenous communities

The new trial will provide the same additional training on conservation issues, and will more closely monitor the environmental effects of basic income support, says Cosmopolis. She says the first trial saw a steep reduction in Indigenous communities cutting new areas of forest and renting land to loggers, but admits that “we didn’t see if there was more or less deforestation in the area” over the course of the trial. The next trial will feature “a more rigorous impact evaluation”, she says.

Natalie York at the University of Manchester, UK, says the social results of the first pilot seemed positive, but warns that tying environmental performance to cash payments is a delicate task.

“When you start to ask the trial to prove particular environmental outcomes, if the receipt of the payments becomes conditional on that, then it becomes more like a payment-for-ecosystem-services system, which is a very different conservation model,” she says.

Indigenous groups threatened by gold exploration in remote Amazon

Gold mining in the municipality of São Gabriel da Cachoeira would drive deforestation and increase mercury pollution, say ecologists

Meanwhile, Johan Oldekop, also at the University of Manchester, warns that environmental gains aren’t guaranteed, pointing out that while some rainforest cash payment trials have reduced deforestation rates, results aren’t always wholly positive.

In Peru, a scheme already provides direct payments to Indigenous communities in the Amazon on the condition that their forest remains standing. Research indicates that the scheme has had “negligible” environmental benefits on land covered by the conservation scheme, in part because communities often volunteered to protect areas at low risk of deforestation.

Oldekop also says that Indigenous rainforest communities are often financially precarious. He warns that short-lived interventions like temporary cash trials can be destabilising unless they are well designed. “We need really, really strong evidence that you’re not leading to social and environmental harms when you do interventions like this,” he says.

articles.title: Hannah Fry: The bizarre reason humans are so vulnerable to choking
articles.summary:
Fran Pulido

One of the unexpectedly delightful things about becoming a well-known nerd is that other nerds, often with far more interesting jobs than mine, have started hunting me down in social settings to tell me the nerdiest things they know.

It almost always ends up being totally fascinating, and only occasionally mildly traumatising.

At a kid’s birthday party recently, I got chatting to one of the dads, who happens to be an ear, nose and throat consultant. I asked him if he used robotics for his surgeries. He said no, then proceeded to mime what he actually did instead. There followed a series of alarmingly enthusiastic slashing motions, like a scene from a horror movie, while in the background a group of 9-year-old girls sat quietly painting.

Advertisement

Free newsletter

Sign up to Professor Hannah Fry’s column

Sign up to newsletter

But the most bizarre thing about that conversation wasn’t the surgeon’s graphic re-enactment, it was what he went on to say about the totally ridiculous, illogical design of the human throat and what it tells us about the path of evolution.

The story starts by noticing that the human body (if you ignore all the unimportant bits hanging off the sides like limbs) is essentially just one giant tube.

Topologically, this makes perfect sense. Back in the earliest days of animal life, some organisms tried a flat design, like a pancake, with digestion done on one side. Others tried a little pocket, with the same opening serving as entrance and exit. But the one-way tube proved to be the most successful, because it allowed our ancestors to process their last meal while eating their next.

Those early creatures would travel through the world mouth first, which is why the sensory equipment evolved to be gathered around that end, with a brain nearby to make sense of everything.

Hannah Fry: I lost my dad to Alzheimer’s. New research into its origins is amazing

My lovely father died of Alzheimer's last year, and since then, I've been digging into the disease to try to understand what happened to him. I was astonished to discover that scientists think it may start in the nose, says New Scientist's new columnist, Professor Hannah Fry

Now, picture a human standing up, tilting their head back, to make them a nice straight tube, still without limbs (sorry, but this is what happens when you let a mathematician write a science column). The ears, eyes, nose and brain all sit together in a cluster, on what I’m going to call the north side of the digestive tube running through the middle.

So if you were deciding where the lungs should go, you’d surely put them on the same side of the tube as the nose, tucked in next to the spine. That way, you would have a neat tube for air and another for food, both running side by side, and even a first-year engineering student could draw a diagram of it for you.

Except that’s not where the lungs are. They ended up on the belly, or south, side of the body.

Which leaves us with this topological monstrosity, where air that comes in through your nose has to cut straight across the path of your food to get to your lungs. And everything you eat has to cut straight back across the path of your air to get to your stomach.

It would be like plumbing your gas main through the kitchen sink, fitting a little flap on top and trusting you to remember to shut it every time you do the washing up.

The reason for this mess is a fish. More than 420 million years ago, long before anything with a backbone had crawled onto land, a fish started gulping air at the surface. A little pouch on the belly side of its gut, just underneath the mouth, got better and better at soaking up oxygen, and that pouch became a lung. That fish became the ancestor of every mammal, bird, amphibian and reptile on Earth.

And because evolution is about being as lazy as you can possibly be without dying, the lungs stayed exactly where they were.

The extraordinary ways species control their own evolutionary fate

Natural selection isn't just something that happens to organisms, their activities also play a role, giving some species – including humans – a supercharged ability to evolve

So why didn’t the nose move instead? Swivel it round so it sits under the mouth on your chin and you have a much more mathematically pleasing face. Unfortunately, the smell cells are wired straight into the front of the brain, so move the nose and the brain has to come along with it.

There’s just no wiggle room. One end of your airway was anchored by your sense of smell, the other was fixed by an accident over 420 million years ago, and your throat is the bodge job evolution came up with to make it all work.

Snakes have a tube behind their tongue that they can use like a snorkel so that they can still breathe even when swallowing a whole deer in one go. Toothed whales have two completely separate tubes that twirl into position like waterslides. Most mammals, including dogs and cats, have a voice box that sits right up at the top of the throat, poking up into the back of the nose, and tubes for food that flow round either side of the wind pipe to the stomach.

Read more

Why honing your sense of smell could keep you sharp as you age

Human babies start off that way too, which is why they can suckle and breathe at the same time. But in the first six months of life, the human larynx drops down the neck, unplugging the airway from the back of the nose and leaving it wide open to whatever comes in from the mouth.

What’s left is a very human oddity. A single, shared chamber sitting low down at the back of your throat that is great for speaking, but does require your vocal folds to slam shut, the epiglottis to come down like a trapdoor and your airway to be sealed off every time you swallow.

As a result, humans have the questionable honour of being one of the few animals on Earth for whom every single mouthful is a potentially lethal exercise in anatomical coordination. Other animals can choke, sure, but our strange anatomy makes us the most vulnerable to choking of all mammals. Which is how roughly 162,000 people die globally each year.

But evolution, having left us in this mess, did at least make the trapdoor almost impossible to switch off. The surgeon – mid mime – told me that when he is in people’s throats performing surgery, the EEG monitor reading can be measuring almost no brain activity. Still, any little tickle in the throat and those folds will slam shut.

As you can imagine, I spent the rest of the party watching the children eat their cake very, very carefully. None of them choked, which, given the state of the plumbing, is frankly a miracle.

articles.title: Severe eczema healed by novel immune-calming pill in clinical trial
articles.summary:
Eczema causes itchy, inflamed rashes on the skin

Evgeniia Gordeeva/Getty Images

Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected.

“It definitely looks promising,” says Gayle Ross at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

Read more

Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it

Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13.

Advertisement

In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is effective, it has had limited uptake in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage.

Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab, but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema.

Free newsletter

Sign up to Health Check

Sign up to newsletter

In the clinical trial, 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks.

Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average 72 per cent reduction in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared with 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial.

“These results exceeded our expectations,” said Terence Rooney, the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a webcast on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end.

“It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross.

Read more

You can upgrade your immune system, but not in the way you think

The medication also appeared safe. A small proportion of participants developed conjunctivitis as a side effect, but it tended to be mild and didn’t cause anyone to discontinue treatment, said Rooney. In fact, since the trial, almost every participant has chosen to continue taking the daily pill as part of an ongoing study, he said.

People taking dupilumab can develop conjunctivitis, too, so “we’re pretty used to dealing with that”, says Ross.

Kymera Therapeutics is now planning a larger trial of KT-621 for treating eczema that is scheduled to begin in mid-2027. The company is also currently running a trial of KT-621 in people with asthma, since the condition is caused by the same overactive immune pathway operating in the lungs. It hasn’t yet said how much the drug will cost if it eventually receives regulatory approval.

articles.summary: Direct-to-cell technology could one day provide a lifeline for getting around authoritarian regimes’ internet shutdowns, but international law and technical limitations are holding the technology back for now

articles.title: The overlooked longevity nutrients that may add years to your life
articles.summary: An intriguing hypothesis proposes that certain nutrients in our food don’t just enable our survival, but have age-delaying functions, too – and efforts are under way to pin them down

articles.title: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
articles.summary:
A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November

AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy

A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels.

Read more

Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet?

The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency.

Advertisement

But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia.

Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates.

Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.”

Free newsletter

Sign up to The Earth Edition

Sign up to newsletter

The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change.

Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance commitments from richer countries.

Fossil fuel-dependent countries have long sought to delay, obstruct and divert climate talks from making a dent in the worldwide consumption of oil, gas and coal. It was oil-exporting countries that insisted all UN climate decisions should be made by consensus when the COP process was established in 1992, a decision that has hamstrung subsequent meetings by effectively awarding veto power to every nation. Other tactics include delaying talks by raising objections and points of order during meetings and flooding the official agenda with additional discussion areas.

Read more

The secret weapon that could finally force climate action

What was new at COP31 was seeing a group like the EU ditching a deal rather than finding a weak compromise in the name of progress, says Joanna Depledge at the University of Cambridge, a seasoned COP observer. “The usual political dynamics were completely upended,” she says of COP31’s endgame. “Usually the EU always backs down at the end. It doesn’t want to be seen as a blocker, but this time it played hardball.”

Many in the climate world are cheering the EU for standing its ground. Bill Hare, the CEO of the influential Climate Analytics think tank, said the deal was “clearly unacceptable”. “The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process, but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels,” he said in a statement.

But the “no deal” outcome of COP31 is far from good news for those concerned about the world’s direction of travel on climate issues. The global consensus on action is fragmenting, even as climate impacts escalate and the world economy accelerates its embrace of renewable energy and electric technologies. Where does all this leave the COP process?

The debacle underscores the growing scepticism of so-called cover decisions at COPs. With nations at an impasse over even mentioning fossil fuels in any final text, it leaves many wondering what the point of a cover text is at all if it can’t ramp up the ambition signal sent to the rest of the world. Next year’s summit will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the hosts are highly unlikely to want to risk pushing for a cover decision.

With nations unlikely to agree on bold steps unanimously, the next-best thing is for large groups of countries to forge ahead with real-world change regardless. That means COPs will become more focused on the so-called action agenda, where groups of countries voluntarily band together to make pledges and set out roadmaps for adopting cleaner technologies. Yet whether that can be as powerful as all nations standing together under a singular message of ambition is doubtful.

Read more

The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come

But despite the disarray of the last fortnight, there are still reasons for hope. Meyer points out that progress was made in other areas of the COP, with 70 countries agreeing to accelerate the electrification of their economies, and countries including Brazil, Denmark and Spain presenting their roadmaps for removing fossil fuels from their economies. “In the real world, there’s a lot of progress,” he says.

The collapse of the negotiations might force better planning and strategy from nations going forward, he suggests. “I think, in a strange kind of way, the breakdown in the negotiations may serve as a wake-up call to the vast majority of countries that want to see progress on climate change,” he says.

There is also a clear signal from the wider economy that change is already under way. Renewables continue to grow faster than analyst predictions at every turn, while electric vehicles are hitting adoption tipping points in growing numbers of countries. The Iran conflict has underscored to many governments the security benefits of home-grown power over fossil fuel imports, with solar and nuclear energy the biggest beneficiaries, the International Energy Agency reported last week. Decarbonisation isn’t happening anywhere near fast enough, but the direction of travel is unmistakable.

UN climate summits have been teetering for many years, with the appearance of consensus maintained thanks to delicately constructed phrases and back-room horse trading. COP31 has brought the disputes and distrust out into the open in a spectacular fashion. Perhaps, out of the flames of this summit, a more honest and realistic approach to climate diplomacy can emerge.

articles.title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
articles.summary: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk, once prized in Europe as the horn of a mythical unicorn, conceals an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. Using advanced X-ray technology, an international team of scientists discovered that the tusk contains two intertwined microscopic spirals that twist in opposite directions.

articles.title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
articles.summary: Virginia Tech scientists have discovered how to transform one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into a valuable ingredient for high-performance engine oil. Their innovative process converts discarded PVC into a useful lubricant material in just three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource while making lubricant production more sustainable.

articles.title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time
articles.summary: Scientists have identified two potentially critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory: infancy and the start of formal schooling. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.

articles.title: Scientists discover signs of a hidden extinction crisis deep beneath the ocean
articles.summary: The deep sea has long been considered a safe haven for marine life, but new genetic research suggests a hidden biodiversity crisis may be unfolding far beneath the waves. Scientists analyzing more than a decade of genetic data from five species of deep-sea fish and shrimp in the Gulf discovered troubling signs of extinction risk in every species examined.

articles.title: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years
articles.summary: Giant horned mammals that emerged shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs may have had far fewer physical differences between males and females than scientists once believed. The discovery challenges a classic example of sexual dimorphism and raises questions about how historical biases have shaped our understanding of extinct animals.

articles.title: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work
articles.summary: A major new study challenges a long-standing assumption about how the brain works, revealing that most neurons are versatile multitaskers rather than highly specialized workers. By analyzing recordings from 43 regions of the mouse brain, researchers discovered that although some neurons are dedicated to specific functions, most respond to a wide variety of information in remarkably distinct ways.

articles.title: Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease
articles.summary: A combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin produced results comparable to antibiotics when used alongside standard treatment for severe gum disease, with benefits persisting long after supplementation ended. The surprising discovery could offer an alternative for some patients while reducing reliance on antibiotics.

articles.title: The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men
articles.summary: Men and women appear to be similarly capable of multitasking, but men are more than twice as likely to ignore conversation while juggling multiple activities. Researchers believe this unexpected difference may help explain why women are widely perceived as better multitaskers.

articles.title: Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds
articles.summary: Scientists have solved the mystery of strange trenches scattered across Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain, revealing an extensive hidden world beneath the surface. These subtle landscape features are created as deeply buried cave systems slowly collapse upward over millions of years. The discovery could help researchers locate unexplored caves containing ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.

articles.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
articles.summary: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.

articles.title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
articles.summary: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

articles.title: Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars
articles.summary: A mysterious object named Phoebe, detected when it briefly magnified a distant star, could be a primordial black hole formed just after the Big Bang. With an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon, it may be a 13-billion-year-old cosmic relic that offers new clues to the mystery of dark matter.

articles.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
articles.summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

articles.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
articles.summary: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

articles.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
articles.summary: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

articles.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
articles.summary: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

articles.title: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang
articles.summary: A surprising discovery by MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists reveals that Einstein’s famous theory of particle motion misses something important when particles travel near the speed of light. Their new calculations show that heavy quarks moving through an ultra-hot plasma experience rare but unusually powerful jolts that Einstein’s traditional model cannot fully explain.

articles.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
articles.summary: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

articles.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
articles.summary: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

articles.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
articles.summary: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

articles.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
articles.summary: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

articles.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

articles.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
articles.summary: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

articles.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
articles.summary: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

articles.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
articles.summary: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

articles.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

articles.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

articles.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

articles.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
articles.summary: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

articles.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
articles.summary: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

articles.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
articles.summary: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.

articles.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
articles.summary: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

articles.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel: at extreme speeds, the light propelling futuristic solar sails could actually begin slowing them down. Once a spacecraft reaches 75% of the speed of light, some scattered light starts producing drag, potentially complicating humanity’s plans to reach distant stars.

articles.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
articles.summary: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

articles.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

articles.title: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
articles.summary: Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as the U.S. tightens its push to keep AI chips out of China.

articles.title: Is Alice Huang a spy or not?
articles.summary: The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed exec with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair, is a Chinese spy.

articles.title: X finally gets parental controls after 20 years
articles.summary: Elon Musk's social network X has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see on the platform.

articles.title: A month with the iPhone Duo has changed how I use my phone
articles.summary: From reading more books to breaking mindless scrolling habits, Apple's foldable has changed my daily routines in ways I didn't anticipate.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
articles.summary: On the same day that Anthropic entered the public market, a painstakingly human video game became one of most successful entertainment launches of all time.

articles.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
articles.summary: The credit rating agency may lower Nvidia's credit rating to AA-, the fourth-highest rating.

articles.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
articles.summary: The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

articles.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
articles.summary: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.

articles.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
articles.summary: Most codes of conduct serve as a reflection of corporate culture. In Nvidia's case, that could have consequences.

articles.title: The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America
articles.summary: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck last month, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared to 65.5 days for trucks overall.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
articles.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model development.

articles.title: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
articles.summary: The password manager maker said an attacker gained access to an employee's corporate account and took some information about customers.

articles.title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
articles.summary: New York has banned AI chatbot toys for five years as new research from Common Sense Media reveals troubling safety failures, including exposure to inappropriate content and risks to emotional development.

articles.title: DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers
articles.summary: U.S. prosecutors accused the former executive of defrauding victims of ransomware by paying the hackers, charging victims more, and pocketing the difference.

articles.title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
articles.summary: The proposed Character.ai bankruptcy sale includes sensitive personal data from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including 2.1 million registered to minors, the state AGs said.

articles.title: X’s latest update for creators focuses on vertical video
articles.summary: As short-form video ramps up in popularity, X's new creation tools are part of its effort to compete with YouTube and Instagram.

articles.title: WhatsApp now lets you schedule messages in group and individual chats
articles.summary: Users can schedule messages from 10 minutes later to after 14 days.

articles.title: AI data centers are becoming harder to build, and neoclouds are feeling it
articles.summary: ⁠Nvidia has made clear⁠ it won’t backstop an AI data center until it’s nearly ready to run, and that’s landing just as neoclouds report construction delays and more expensive debt. articles.title: The M5 MacBook Air just got its biggest discount since Apple raised the price
articles.summary:
The M5-powered MacBook Air is $300 off in both size configurations for Black Friday. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June, you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike. If you want a larger display, Amazon and Best Buy are also taking $300 off the otherwise identical 15-inch model with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, dropping it to $1,199.

Apple MacBook Air 13 (M5)

Where to Buy:

$1299 $999 at Amazon (512GB)

$1299 $999 at Best Buy (512GB)

$1599 $1199 at Amazon (1TB)

Apple MacBook Air 15 (M5)

Where to Buy:

$1299 $1199 at Amazon (512GB)

$1299 $1199 at Best Buy (512GB)

$1799 $1499 at Amazon (1TB)

The M5-equipped MacBook Air is a good middle ground if you need more power than the MacBook Neo — which, thanks to a $100 discount, is $599 — but don’t want to splurge on a MacBook Pro. Its faster chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage make it better suited for multitasking and creative work in apps like Photoshop and Premiere. You also get a higher-resolution display, better speakers, a backlit keyboard that makes typing in the dark easier, and faster ports. Plus, its sharper webcam supports Apple’s Center Stage feature, which automatically adjusts the framing to keep you in view during video calls.

Of course, the Air can’t match the performance or higher-end displays you can get with a MacBook Pro, whether you opt for an M5 model, the newer M5 Pro model with a PROLED XDR Display, or one of the M6-powered machines. A Pro may be worth the extra money if you regularly edit video or work on more demanding creative projects. But if you mostly need a laptop for work, browsing, and occasional photo or video editing, the M5 Air is more than capable.

Read our M5-powered MacBook Air review.

articles.title: The absolute best Black Friday deals you can still get
articles.summary:
Black Friday is nearly over, but many of this year’s best deals are still available. You can still find some of the lowest prices we’ve seen in-store and online for video games, wireless earbuds, TVs, robot vacuums, and so much more. We can’t guarantee a deal you’ve had your eye on will last through Cyber Monday; however, if prior years are any indication, most will stick around through the long weekend.

As usual, we sorted through thousands of deals to find the ones truly worth sharing, with an eye for the products and services we’ve tested here at The Verge. With prices up across multiple categories due to RAMageddon, some deals may not seem as big as in prior years. For example, Apple’s latest MacBook Air recently fell to its pre-price-hike level for the first time since July. articles.title: We found 60-odd Black Friday deals we love for $100 or less
articles.summary:
The translucent Beats Studio Buds Plus are down to $89.95, matching their lowest price to date. | Photo: Chris Welch / The Verge

Between holiday travel, gifts, and the rising cost of just about everything, expenses can quickly add up during this time of year. Thankfully, you don’t have to dip too far into your savings to take advantage of some of the better Black Friday deals we’ve seen.

Below, we’ve rounded up a range of great stuff currently on sale for $100 or less, from noise-canceling earbuds and portable Bluetooth speakers to pocket-sized e-readers, photo printers, games, and more. You’ll also find deals on Ember’s temperature-controlled mug, Kodak’s tiny keychain camera, and a variety of Lego sets, all of which would make great holiday gifts or simply a nice treat for yourself.

Disney Plus, Hulu Bundle

You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.

Where to Buy:

$12.99 $4.99 at Hulu (ad-supported, monthly)

$21.99 $14.99 at Hulu (ad-free, monthly)

Amazon Echo Time

Although it’s not Amazon’s first bedside alarm clock, the Echo Time is focused on helping you sleep better. The camera-less Alexa speaker can detect your sleep stage via ultrasound and use smart alarms to ease you into the day, but only if you want it to.

$199.99 $99.99 at Best Buy

$199.99 $99.99 at Target

articles.title: This purple electric Chinese minivan can go up to 559 miles on a charge
articles.summary:
Electric minivans could be the ultimate in utility, with room for passengers, gear, and huge batteries. While VW's ID Buzz only gave us 200 miles of real-world driving on a charge in 2023, China's BYD has just announced a flagship purple peoplemover that can go an estimated 559 miles (900 km) on electricity.

It's called the BYD Whale, and some back-of-the-napkin math suggests it lives up to the name. The van would be bigger than a Honda Odyssey, bigger than a Chrysler Pacifica, and bigger than a Toyota Sienna, at 17.3 feet (5,270mm) long, 6.5 feet (1,996mm) wide, 6 feet (1,815mm) tall, and with a 123-inch (3,130mm) wheelbase.

articles.title: The best Black Friday deals you can still get on AirPods, Macs, and other Apple gear
articles.summary:
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR has hit a new low price just a few months after release. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Black Friday is entering the evening, which means one of the best times of the year to save some cash on a new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch is coming to a close. After all, the holiday savings can help offset the unfortunate price hikes from earlier this year, when Apple raised the cost of some of its most popular gear. Some discounts still apply to recent releases like the Apple Watch Series 12 and touchscreen MacBook Pro, too, which are available at their lowest prices to date.

In addition to a variety of discounts across retailers, Apple is offering up to $300 in gift cards with select purchases between November 27th and November 30th. How much you get back is determined by how much you spend, with up to $100 available for some iPhone and Apple Watch purchases, and up to $300 for the 16-inch MacBook Pro. That said, in some cases you may be able to save more by buying from other retailers.

Earbud and headphone deals

AirPods Pro 3

The latest AirPods Pro offer improved noise cancellation and richer bass, along with built-in heart sensors that work with Apple’s Fitness app to monitor calories burned across more than 50 workouts. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$249 $149 at Amazon

$249 $149 at Walmart

$249 $149.99 at Best Buy

Beats Powerbeats Pro 2

Beats’ fitness-focused earbuds feature ear hooks designed to stay put during even the most intense workouts as well as built-in heart rate monitoring. They also deliver relatively bass-rich sound for their design, along with solid noise cancellation, wireless charging, and AirPods features like adaptive audio thanks to Apple’s H2 chip. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$249 $179.95 at Amazon

$249 $179.95 at Walmart

$249.99 $179.99 at Best Buy

You can buy the AirPods 4 on sale at Walmart for around $89 ($40 off), which is $20 shy of their best price. Apple’s last-gen earbuds lack active noise cancellation, but they still deliver good, relatively bass-rich sound, even if they don’t quite match the newer AirPods 5. They also offer voice call quality on par with the latest AirPods Pro. Read our review.

The second-gen AirPods Max are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, which is $19 shy of their best price to date (Target also has them for about $10 more). Like the original, Apple’s latest over-ear headphones feature a luxurious build consisting of aluminum, steel, and a mesh fabric, but they offer better sound and noise cancellation. The new H2 chip also enables features like adaptive audio and live translation. Read our review.

Beats Studio Pro

The latest Beats Studio Pro feature improved noise cancellation, sound quality, and comfort. They also support lossless audio over USB-C and offer native support for a range of iOS and Android features like other Beats headphones. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$349.99 $139.95 at Amazon (select colors)

$349.99 $99 at Walmart (select colors)

$349.99 $139.95 at Best Buy (select colors)

Beats 360 headphones

The Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym. They’re Beats’ first IP-rated cans, with ear cushions that you can easily remove for cleaning (or style points). They also stay in place during most exercises, while still delivering solid bass. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$349.99 $249 at Amazon

$349.99 $249.99 at Best Buy

If you want over-ears and are comfortable going without active noise cancellation, the Beats Solo 4 are on sale starting at $79.99 ($120 off) at Amazon and Target — a new low price. The headphones are a noticeable improvement over their predecessor, delivering more detailed sound and support for lossless audio. They also last up to 50 hours on a single charge, while their memory foam ear cushions make them comfortable enough for long listening sessions. Read our review.

The Beats Studio Buds Plus are down to around $89.95 ($80 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Target, nearly matching their lowest price to date. The wireless earbuds feature a slick, eye-catching transparent option and solid noise cancellation, especially at this price. They’re also exceptionally comfortable, with four ear tip sizes to help you find a secure fit. Sure, you don’t get wireless charging, but they offer IPX4 water resistance and up to nine hours of battery life on a single charge. Read our review.

MacBook deals

MacBook Neo

Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$799 $699.99 at Amazon (512GB, Touch ID)

$699 $649 at Best Buy (256GB)

$699 $599 at Amazon (256GB)

Apple MacBook Air 13 (M5)

Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$1299 $999 at Amazon (512GB)

$1299 $999 at Best Buy (512GB)

$1599 $1199 at Amazon (1TB)

The recently released 16.3-inch MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage is on sale starting at $3,099 ($300 off) — a new low price — at Amazon. The redesigned laptop is Apple’s first with an OLED touchscreen, which allows for rich colors and deep blacks. It’s also noticeably thinner and lighter than the non-touchscreen 16-inch MacBook Pro, and features a new Dynamic Island that replaces the notch and provides quick access to controls and notifications. Read our review.

The 14-inch M6-powered MacBook Pro is on sale starting at $1,749 ($250 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, which is a new low price. The Pro builds on its predecessor with a faster chip and support for Wi-Fi 7. In our testing, it handled multitasking, photo editing, and occasional video editing with ease while still delivering exceptional battery life. It lacks the newer MacBook Pro’s gorgeous OLED display, but its Mini LED screen still looks great, especially given its smooth 120Hz refresh rate. It also offers excellent speakers and a good selection of ports, including three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an SD card slot. Read our review.
