The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review.

$399 $329 at Best Buy (GPS, 42mm)

$449 $349 at Amazon (GPS, 46mm)

The Apple Watch SE 3 is on sale in the 40mm / GPS configuration starting at $179 ($50 off) at Amazon and Walmart, matching its best price to date, while Best Buy is currently $20 higher. Apple’s newest entry-level smartwatch remains our top recommendation for anyone who wants a basic fitness tracker, as it offers all the essentials alongside an always-on display and Apple’s S10 chip, which enables on-device Siri requests. Read our review.

The fan-favorite folding design returns with the comfortable, slightly improved XM4C headphones. | Photo: John Higgins / The Verge

Instead of purely looking forward with its headphone designs, Sony went back to its popular WH-1000XM4 design and made some improvements to make it even better. The 2026 version, called the WH-1000XM4C, sounds nearly as good as the pricier XM6 model (currently $348), but is down to $198 during Black Friday at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart. $299.99 $198 at Walmart

There’s a reason why Sony went back to refine the XM4. Our former reviewer Chris Welch praised them for being super comfortable and for having close to perfect features for the price, especially compared to its successor, the XM3 (still my daily driver, for what it’s worth). The XM4s had better sound quality and noise cancellation, plus improved mics, multipoint connectivity, and a sensor that can detect when you remove them to automatically pause audio. Now, with the XM4C, there are further improvements, most notably a 10-band equalizer in the app (compared to the original XM4’s five-band) that my colleague John Higgins says really helped the headphones’ midrange frequencies open up.

These are a great buy, but they aren’t your only Sony headphones deal to consider right now. Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are available during Black Friday at Best Buy for $169, their lowest price yet from a major retailer. There are upsides and downsides to this model: They feature improved noise cancellation thanks to more mics, despite using the same ANC chip as the XM4C, but they can’t fold up as compactly, making them a little bigger to pack in your bag. Either one you choose, you’ll have some great headphones to listen to going into 2027.

I’m not saying you should read on an iPad next to fountain. I’m just saying you can. | Photo: David Pierce / The Verge

We were big fans of Apple’s new iPad Mini when we reviewed it in early November, but its steep starting price of $699 was hard to swallow. Thankfully, the small tablet is already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. Right now, Amazon and Walmart are both selling the 2026 iPad Mini with Wi-Fi and 128GB of storage starting at $599 ($100 off), its lowest price to date.

Where to Buy:

$699 $599 at Walmart (Wi-Fi, 128GB)

$799 $749 at Amazon (Wi-Fi, 256GB)

The new Mini is a notable upgrade over its predecessor, with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display that delivers deeper blacks and better contrast than the previous model’s 8.3-inch LCD. Despite the bigger screen, the tablet itself is smaller and lighter, making it easier to carry. Apple also added IP67 dust and water resistance, so you have less reason to worry about where you use it. As my colleague David Pierce noted in his review, that made a big difference in his day-to-day use; he felt more comfortable handing the Mini to his spill-prone toddler or keeping it nearby in the kitchen to follow recipes. He even took it into the shower to keep watching a football game.

The upgraded A20 Pro chip also made apps load faster and demanding games run better in Pierce’s testing, while battery life held steady at around nine hours of screentime. At $599, though, the new Mini is still relatively expensive if you mainly want a tablet for browsing the web or streaming shows. The last-gen iPad Mini, which runs on Apple’s A17 Pro chip, is available for under $500 if you’d rather save another $100 and can live without the OLED screen and water resistance. But if you’ve been waiting for a more worthwhile upgrade to Apple’s smallest tablet, the current Black Friday discount makes the new model easier to justify.

articles.title: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
articles.summary:
Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.

A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

articles.title: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment

Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory.

Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid's 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.

But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.

He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics.

LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online.

The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI.

Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this "smoke taint" adversely affected not only local wine production, but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant.

That's why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists.

As previously reported, the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018, OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper—identified the growing popularity of "dry hopping" (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon.

articles.title: Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans

Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China's Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that's vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world.

The chemical makeup of the teeth's enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we'd previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans.

A handful of teeth with a lot to say

Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.

My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional but don't meet your daily driving needs. It's tucked out of view, living out its life in a drawer until being erased and donated after someone asks why you're holding onto outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren't hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use.

The PhoneBox home screen displays useful stats and what's currently playing in your browser.
Credit:
Nick Indge

I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible big-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I quickly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life in "the drawer."

Launch applications on your PC from the connected Android device.
Credit:
Nick Indge

Installation is a doddle

Getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn't have been simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as easy as plugging the tablet in to my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service, so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you'd like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device.

articles.title: Ukraine sinks Russian warship, strikes cargo ships from Mediterranean to Baltic
articles.summary:
Ukrainian explosive naval drones sank a Russian warship docked in the port city of Benghazi in Libya while also striking a Russian cargo ship that it was escorting. The incident demonstrates the expanding scope of Ukrainian military strikes on Russian ships from the coast of North Africa to the Gulf of Finland.

The Russian Navy’s missile corvette Merkury sank at port after being struck by at least two Ukrainian naval drones on November 22, according to The Associated Press. Ukraine’s Security Service described using seven naval drones launched from a mother ship to target the Merkury, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video footage showing the drone boats approaching and exploding against both the burning Russian warship and a Russian dry cargo ship, MV Angara.

Zelenskyy noted that a Ka-27 combat helicopter onboard the Merkury was also destroyed. He described the cargo ship MV Angara as transporting weapons—Russia provides material support to the Libyan National Army that currently controls Benghazi and is battling the internationally recognized Libyan government based in Tripoli.

articles.title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
articles.summary:
On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.

SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).

Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked. Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first, Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.

articles.title: Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more
articles.summary:
“It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want.

But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age.

Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history, smart devices, and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price.

articles.title: Amazon fights Delivery Protection Act by putting stickers on its packages
articles.summary:
Amazon is placing a sticker on some of its delivery boxes to urge customers to oppose a New York City bill.

This weekend, some Amazon shoppers reported getting a delivery from Amazon with a sticker on it that reads: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The sticker reportedly includes a QR code that leads to a link for contacting NYC Councilmembers. The sticker encourages the package’s recipient to “Scan to tell your council member: no increases for New Yorkers.”

Amazon is looking to stoke opposition to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. The proposed law would require Amazon and other companies with last-mile delivery facilities in the city, such as FedEx, to directly employ third-party contractors Amazon uses for making deliveries.

articles.title: “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science
articles.summary:
At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).

These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.

These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.

articles.title: Buklod: Songs of an unfinished struggle
articles.summary:
To be an activist in the years immediately after the 1986 EDSA Revolution meant sailing against the optimistic tide that swept the nation following the ouster of the Marcos dictatorship. Democracy had been restored, Cory Aquino was president, and the mood was blazing yellow. Everyone, it seemed, wanted to move on and celebrate.

And to be a protest musician at a time when vacuous pop, delivered by singers and bands with gelled hair and shoulder pads, ruled the airwaves meant strumming an acoustic guitar in the middle of Euphoria: nobody could hear you, and those who did wished you weren’t there.

They played on anyway. 

Protest musicians of the post-EDSA years did not come out of nowhere. They followed a tradition of protest artists from the ’70s and early ’80s whose songs were in the form and vernacular of folk and folk-rock: Jess Santiago, Paul Galang, Susan Fernandez, Pancho Lara, Gary Granada; folk groups like Pahayagan and Sinaglahi. Asin and Heber Bartolome’s Banyuhay carried it into the mainstream, proving that a song about the environment, or the daily struggles of working people could sell records. 

The folk group Buklod was that period’s best-kept secret. 

Noel Cabangon, Romeo Dongeto, and Rene Boncocan sang at political gatherings long before anyone thought of them as recording artists. Their first album, Bukid at Buhay, came out in 1988 as a trio; Boncocan left the following year, and Cabangon and Dongeto carried on as a duo in “Tatsulok” (1991) and “Sa Kandungan ng Kalikasan” (1992).

Buklod’s songs found a home in mainstream compilation albums such as Karapatang Pantao and Dear Cory, masterminded by maverick producer Ed Formoso, known for the psychedelic-folk group Dinosaur, a trio with Boy Camara and Jett Montelibano, and for birthing the supergroup Lokal Brown.

It wasn’t until “Kanlungan” was used in a burger commercial, and “Tatsulok” was covered by Bamboo many years later, that the secret was out. 

“Kanlungan” became the song everyone requested from Cabangon, by then an established solo recording artist. It didn’t matter, of course, that a song about longing and the passing of time performed by activists became a jingle for an American fast food chain. Or that “Tatsulok,” an indictment of oppressive class structures, became a rock anthem for a generation largely spared from a policeman’s truncheon. By then, Buklod had long disbanded.

Buklod would jam occasionally, but there was never a full reunion or a new album. Not until 2018, 30 years after their first record, when the three went back to the studio for 3 Dekada: Ang Muling Pag-awit.

The comeback, the urge to make their voices, now older, heard again, was triggered by the brazen extra-judicial killings and rights violations under the then two-year old regime of now detained former president Rodrigo Duterte. Three decades on, the old songs still resonated and it was the trio’s way of joining the outrage. 

A few nights ago, they reunited again, this time for a fund-raiser for ailing painter Federico “Boy” Dominguez, known in activist and art circles as BoyD. In the crowd were battle-hardened activists, finding comfort in familiar songs.

Forty years after EDSA, Buklod’s songs still carry the same weight as the day they were first sung. The promise of the EDSA Revolution has since soured: old and new elites, despots who use the rhetoric of democracy to undermine its values, disenchantment with its failure to lift people from chronic hunger and poverty, activists who dared to protest treated with the same iron fist as Marcos the father. And Marcos the son is back in Malacañang.

Buklod and the other post-EDSA protest artists were right all along: The revolution left too much undone. In the face of public indifference, they still said it and sang about it, even if it meant preaching to the converted, dodging bullets at rallies, raising families on a folk singer’s income, or enduring years of separation over ideological and political disagreements.

In the end, it is the songs that outlast the quarrels. Songs that bring old friends and comrades together and remind them, and the rest of us, that the fight they sang about was never finished. – Rappler.com

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Rodrigo Duterte on trial at the ICC
articles.summary:
The historic trial of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte at the International Criminal Court (ICC) begins on Monday, November 30, as he faces charges of crimes against humanity.

The charges against Duterte stem from killings linked to his so-called war on drugs during his time as mayor of Davao City and his presidency. He is the first former Asian leader to be tried at the court in The Hague, going on trial more than a year since his pivotal arrest in March 2025.

On this page, we bring you the latest news, analyses, videos, and photos of Duterte’s trial at the ICC. For more updates and to share your own views, you can also join the Justice and Crime chat room in Rappler’s Muni app.

articles.title: Will Sara Duterte finally attend her impeachment trial?
articles.summary:
Will Vice President Sara Duterte ever show up at her impeachment trial? 

That question has persisted since Day 1 of the trial on July 6, amid mounting calls for the Vice President to appear in court and personally respond to the allegations against her. 

Duterte has visited the Senate on at least two occasions outside her trial. The first was on July 7, when she met with her defense team and delivered a one-sentence statement to the media, “In this bloodbath and bludgeoning, I will be bloodied but unbowed.” 

She left the Senate before the trial could resume. 

On November 26, Duterte returned to the chamber while the trial was suspended to attend plenary deliberations on her office’s proposed P785.2 million budget for 2027. 

She exchanged pleasantries with some of the senators serving as judges in her trial. But when the media asked questions, including whether she will attend her trial, she only responded with “Merry Christmas.” 

Duterte’s defense team has repeatedly said her attendance would depend on how the trial unfolds, stressing that her physical appearance is not required because she is fully represented by counsel. 

Duterte herself said in August that the participation of her lawyers was “sufficient” and tantamount to her attending the impeachment proceedings. 

But in a rare, nearly hour-long press conference at the Office of the Vice President central office in Mandaluyong City on Friday, November 27, Duterte claimed that she had long wanted to attend her trial. It could be recalled that the Vice President herself had repeatedly questioned the impeachment proceeding itself, describing it as “political theater” in the guise of accountability.

On Friday, Duterte said that her defense lawyer and former spokesperson, Michael Poa, ignored her whenever she raised the possibility of her appearance at her trial.

“Ilang beses na ako nagsabi sa kanya: ‘Michael Poa, allow me to enter my appearance for myself. Allow me to lawyer for myself and stand there as a lawyer.’ Hindi niya talaga ako pinapansin at all. Somehow, nililihis niya ‘yung usapan,” Duterte said at her latest press conference. 

(I’ve told him several times, “Michael Poa, allow me to enter my appearance for myself. Allow me to represent myself and stand there as a lawyer.” He really didn’t pay attention to me at all. Somehow, he keeps steering the conversation away from the subject.)

Poa, defense spokesperson, has yet to respond to requests for comment. 

Asked whether she could still be presented as a witness at this point, with the defense nearing the end of its presentation, Duterte said she had yet to discuss the matter with her lawyers. “We are not there yet but sabi kasi nila tapos na sila this week e. So hindi pa namin napag-uusapan kung a-attend ako as witness o hindi,” Duterte said. 

(We are not there yet but they said they will be done this week. So we have not discussed yet if I will attend as a witness or not.)

The defense team is set to present two witnesses when the trial resumes next week. Both are expected to testify in relation to Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company at the center of allegations of unexplained wealth against Duterte.

Will Duterte at least be present when the impeachment court hands down its decision? The court targets a ruling by December 18. The Vice President indicated that this event, which her political fate hinges on, is not a priority.

“If I’m in Davao, then no. Because we have a series of activities for Davao thanksgiving for December,” she said in response.

Duterte also said her office is “preparing for the worst” and that she would accept the court’s decision. However, she cautioned that removing an elected vice president would have “consequences,” pointing to possible negative public reaction.

Play Video

Meanwhile, the Vice President said she would not fly to The Hague for the trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte for a crimes against humanity case before the International Criminal Court beginning November 30.  She said it would be a “waste of money” as visits to her father would not be allowed during the trial.

She shared that she owed friends at least P5 million which helped cover for her trip to The Hague last year, as well as legal expenses for her impeachment trial and her father’s case. She said she planned to sell properties to repay her debt.

Duterte is facing one remaining allegation in her impeachment case: unexplained wealth. The House prosecution panel dropped the three other articles of impeachment, which involved grave threats, misuse of confidential funds, and bribery. – Rappler.com

articles.title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?
articles.summary:
The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, the central role of Nvidia in the U.S.-China AI competition, and the U.S. economy’s reliance on the AI boom might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?

The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: central processing units, or CPUs.

GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering.

As a researcher of high-performance computing and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier: software that made GPUs useful beyond graphics, a research breakthrough that showed what they could do for AI, and a global commercial and political race to build ever-larger AI models.

GPUs vs. CPUs

The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.

A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion, or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.

From pretty pictures to AI data centers

Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.

In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.

The second major shift occurred when AlexNet, a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.

Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.

Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.

AI takes off

In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer, a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.

The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including U.S.-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centers composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.

These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.

Nvidia’s GPUs dominate the AI market, but rival companies developing other chips are trying to knock Nvidia off its throne.

AI ‘arms race’

Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.

The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.

Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry. – Rappler.com

This article first appeared on The Conversation.

Jeffrey Young, Principal Research Scientist, Partnership for an Advanced Computing Environment, Georgia Institute of Technology

articles.title: Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
articles.summary:
WASHINGTON DC, US – Hackers have breached the US Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters, in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.

The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.

In a statement to Reuters, the Air Force said it “does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities.”

A one-stop shop

Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve as a one-stop shop for the Air Force’s IT needs, combining the resources of four operators — Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet — to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.

Among them are the Air Force’s Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defense radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 US Air Force locations around the world.

SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One until 2026, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to a request seeking comment. Leidos referred questions to the Air Force.

Cloud One is among the US military’s biggest cloud platforms, according to two of the sources.

“A breach here is a big deal,” one of the sources said.

Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the US military’s cyber force, to assess the damage, one of the sources said.

Cyber Command did not respond to requests for comment.

A range of disruption

The discovery of the hack led to a range of disruption. Two of the sources, along with a fourth person familiar with the matter, said that efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, have been paused.

Updates to applications already running on Cloud One were blocked, leaving Air Force personnel unable to apply fixes just as a new batch of serious software vulnerabilities has been disclosed across the technology industry. A fifth source said that some users had their administrator rights revoked.

All five sources spoke on condition of anonymity.

One source said that the cyber intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control plane. That person likened the control plane to a universal remote, as intruders in theory could leverage their access to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts, though it was unclear whether the hackers did so in this case.

Reuters could not identify the specific vulnerability exploited by the hackers.

String of hacks

News of the breach comes amid heightened anxiety over AI-powered intrusions, a particularly serious problem for cloud-based networks because of the ability of AI models to swiftly detect weaknesses across wide surface areas.

The US government already has been dealing with the fallout from at least six other recently disclosed cyber incidents, including two at the FBI, a previous hack of Pentagon data, a recent leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel information, a breach affecting at least two spy agencies and a hack at the Treasury Department.

Cloud One has long been in the crosshairs of hackers.

In a 2023 commentary carried by the online publication FedScoop, Cloud One’s leadership touted what they called a “100% success rate” in beating back what they said was a “staggering” number of attempts to penetrate the platform.

“There is no room for error when it comes to security,” Cloud One’s leadership wrote. – Rappler.com

articles.title: In ‘Shux,’ Bicol band Kilyab calls out ‘ayuda’ politics, climate neglect
articles.summary:
ALBAY, Philippines – Bicol pop band Kilyab isn’t just singing about change — they’re marching for it in the streets, too. With their new single, “Shux,” the band pushes back against the idea that climate suffering is unavoidable, blaming decades of systemic neglect for the ongoing struggles in their community.

“Drawing inspiration from Camarines Sur, we saw how even delivering ayuda (relief aid) is being used to mind-condition voters instead of really solving the issues that worsen climate change,” songwriter and lead vocalist Karl Ramirez  said.

“If we don’t talk and do something about it, most of our fellow citizens will continue to fall prey to the same system,” he added.

PROTEST. Kilyab’s lead vocalist Karl Ramirez speaks on the importance of socially relevant songs during a rally against Pax Silica in Naga on November 17, 2026. Photo by Jascyl Jee Hugo Sayson 

The band emphasized that voters are often left with almost no real alternatives when choosing their leaders, trapping them in a recurring cycle: enduring calamities while politicians exploit those same disasters for self-promotion.

“These politicians don’t even hide it anymore — they even post videos on their social media accounts showing them handing out money disguised as prizes during their relief operations,” Ramirez said.

For Ramirez, “Shux” reflects the band’s firm belief in using socially relevant music to awaken their fellow citizens — and help end the cycles of neglect in their province and the wider Bicol region.

“Now and any time is the right time to sing songs that reflect the hardship and condition of our nation, and inspire all of us to continue taking a stand against corruption and imperialism,” he noted.

Verna Velasco, Kilyab’s keyboardist and a Bicol Pop mentor who coined the song’s title, said the word comes from a Gen Z expression. 

“Shux” is a shortened version of “shucks,” used to convey disdain or disappointment.

“Using the ‘shux’ expression feels like a call for the youth and their communities to be more vigilant, starting with reflecting on why we vote for the people we put into power,” Velasco said.

“Like what the lyrics ask, ‘Ba’t ba kasi sila ang binoto niyo?’ (Why did you vote for them in the first place?), the song explains to us that we also have a shared responsibility for the neglect happening now amid the sufferings and issues we face,” she added.

CIVIC ADVOCACY. Bicol Pop band Kilyab performs its original hits in Naga City at major gatherings advocating for youth empowerment and anti-corruption accountability.

In a world quick to move past pressing issues, Velasco hopes the song will help people remember — especially when selecting new leaders.

That call for electoral reflection lands in a province long shaped by entrenched political power. Camarines Sur has been dominated by the Villafuerte dynasty for nearly 40 years.

In the 2025 midterm elections, the family maintained its grip on the province as Luis Raymund “LRay” Villafuerte reclaimed the gubernatorial seat, while his sons, Migz and Luigi, also secured seats in Congress. (READ:  Iriga City bet decries harassment, vote buying in Camarines Sur).

Water crisis

Ramirez told Rappler that the song’s lyrics were written in one sitting during a songwriting class with Bicol Pop students back in April. 

Set against soaring oil prices and looming warnings of a Super El Niño, the track was sparked by growing frustration over the government’s failure to step up.

“Our government can do major things regarding the climate crisis, or at least to ease the suffering of those affected. But instead of helping, we still allow some of our local watersheds — like Mount Isarog in Camarines Sur — to be destroyed,” Ramirez said.

That environmental vulnerability is already playing out on the ground. In 2025, San Jose Mayor Jerold Peña pointed out that rampant quarrying near the Rangas River had accelerated erosion within the Mount Isarog watershed and worsened flooding.

“What we are witnessing is not only the force of nature, but also the consequence of human actions — rampant quarrying and a widespread lack of understanding of the natural dynamics of the Rangas River,” Peña said at the time.

SOCIAL RELEVANCE. Kilyab recorded its new single, ‘Shux,’ to reflect issues surrounding El Niño and inflation caused by bad governance.

A year later, in preparation for El Niño, the mayor assured residents that the local government had formed a task force to monitor the watershed and secure community water supplies, though he acknowledged that meeting agricultural demands during the dry season would remain a steep challenge.

For Kilyab, the strain on Mount Isarog and Bicol’s watersheds highlights a stark disconnect between what local leaders prioritize and what communities actually need to survive worsening climate impacts.

Rather than treating floods and dry spells as mere acts of nature, the band argues that years of unchecked quarrying, weak environmental enforcement, and band-aid relief operations are the real drivers of the region’s recurring crises — the exact cycle of neglect that “Shux” wants to expose.

Rooted in their environmental protection advocacy, Kilyab cuts straight to the heart of political accountability with the song’s biting line: “Bakit ba kasi sila ang binoto niyo? Oh ayan, naghihirap tayo (Why did you vote for them in the first place? Look now, we’re suffering).” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Food for feed: The price paid beyond the plate
articles.summary:
In May 2025, a regional office of the Philippines’ fisheries agency in Visayas announced an initiative that would invite fishers to government meetings held to expand fish farming in the region. 

Officials would introduce the fishers to ongoing fish breeding, processing, and distribution projects as part of a push to transform the local economy “from fish hunting to fish farming.” They emphasized that this transformation would ease stress on the ecosystem. 

“Instead of constantly taking from the sea, let’s try to cultivate fish and give the ocean a chance to recover,” said community development officer Joel Lutao.

But critics worldwide have questioned whether the practice of catching and reducing whole, fresh fish to grow more seafood can ever be considered sustainable. The most popular types of farmed seafood — milkfish, tilapia, salmon, shrimp, and trout — are fed the kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, not slowing it. 

Two-thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fishmeal and fish oil. Before it reaches market, a farmed salmon, for instance, eats at some farms more than six times its weight in wild-caught fish.

The concerns about aquaculture extend far beyond the fate of the oceans. The feed that powers most of this industry comes with a huge variety of other hidden costs, according to a wide-reaching investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization based in Washington, DC. 

These costs include the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, violent protests typically spurred by the horrid smell from fishmeal factories, and escalating geopolitical tensions as countries compete for scarce sources of protein. 

‘There’s no fish left here’

What economists often call “externalities,” these social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury seafood is eaten.

In The Gambia and Mauritania, the investigation documented how the industry drives food insecurity, as fish that once sustained local communities are increasingly being diverted into fishmeal factories for export. 

In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labor on ships, at farms, and in factories. 

In other countries, including India and Peru, this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some of them violent, usually in the form of labor strikes and community protests sparked by the water pollution or stench from factories cooking thousands of tons of decomposing fish, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries. 

WORK. Workers offload catch at a fishmeal plant in Ullal. Photo courtesy of Changing Markets Foundation

In Senegal, fishmeal has put local fishers out of work, so increasingly they are selling — or repurposing — their boats to flee to Europe, typically taking the roughly 930-mile sea journey to Spain’s Canary Islands, a route that claimed more than 3,000 lives in 2025.

“We’re fishermen, but there’s no fish left here, so we left,” said Cheikhou Omar, a 21-year-old fisher, in September 2024 as he sat on a beach in Senegal, rescued after the fishing boat he took trying to get to Spain capsized, killing two dozen.

The five-year investigation mapped roughly the entire global fishmeal industry, including more than 1,400 fishmeal factories across 64 countries, tracing supply chains from fishing vessels to processing plants, feed mills, fish farms, and seafood retailers. The reporting effort involved dozens of journalists from as many countries, visiting factories and farms and boarding fishmeal ships at sea. 

Unsustainable fishing

The oceans bear an especially heavy and largely invisible burden of the fishmeal and fish oil industry. More than a fifth of wild-caught fish around the world is used for non-human consumption, especially as feed for fish, but also chickens and pigs. 

The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fishmeal production, operating in the waters of at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by leading ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets. 

For example, less than 30% of the fleet had publicly available location information, and under 25% had a unique vessel identification number, or ship license plate. Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.

Scientific studies classified at least half of the species landed by the assessed fishmeal vessels as “overexploited” or worse. Most of the ships in this fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish. Both gear types are associated with high levels of waste, routinely hauling in large volumes of bycatch and non-target species. 

At least 165 of the ships in the global fishmeal fleet were bottom trawlers, conducting a particularly destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their paths. 

The problem of unsustainable fishing is compounded by heavy government subsidies that keep too many vessels operating, accelerating pressure on already stressed fisheries.

“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at University of British Columbia. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”

The problem with fishmeal

As commodities, fishmeal and fish oil promise to grow in international importance. 

Starting in 2022, more than half of the seafood eaten globally came from fish farms rather than wild catch. Aquaculture is a $313-billion industry and the fastest-growing segment of global food production. Most of these fish farms are powered by fishmeal and fish oil. 

Fishmeal processing in the Philippines is concentrated in three cities. The first is the port city of Navotas, known as the country’s “fishing capital.” Located in Metro Manila on the island of Luzon, it has at least one fishmeal plant. 

The second is Zamboanga, a city on the island of Mindanao regarded as the Philippines’ “sardine capital,” home to half a dozen fishmeal plants. The third is General Santos. The national “tuna capital,” it lies in Mindanao and hosts four fishmeal plants.

Many of these plants focus primarily on processing seafood for human consumption, but they also redirect inedible offcuts into fishmeal. This practice is widely cited as sustainable and socially beneficial, since it uses materials that would otherwise be thrown away. 

Therefore, fishmeal production in the Philippines is less of a driver of food insecurity than it is in other countries that use whole edible fish. However, the Philippines suffers from severe food insecurity because of general overfishing and the export of most catch, be it small anchovies or larger species like tuna. 

The far greater burden of food insecurity, social unrest, and air and water pollution is borne by the poorer countries that produce the fishmeal or fishmeal-fed seafood the Philippines imports. The country imported more seafood than it produced as of 2023. 

Half of all seafood globally is farmed, and most of that is fed fishmeal. The fish farms in several of the countries that export the most seafood to the Philippines — including China, Vietnam, Papua New Guinea, Chile, and Japan — have ties to severe problems caused by fishmeal production, according to the investigation. 

Hidden costs

The investigation revealed a surprising diversity of hidden costs in the global feed industry. 

In Senegal, fishmeal production accelerated overfishing, eroding traditional fishing grounds and contributing to thousands of young men attempting deadly and desperate voyages at sea to Europe. 

In Russia, fishmeal workers were held captive in secluded company towns in remote parts of the country, or stuck on ships far from shore. 

“People have nowhere to go, no money,” one worker said in a plea to Russian President Vladimir Putin, who participated in an episode of a call-in television show about the fishmeal plant. “Please, help us,” a second worker said. 

In Chile, several hundred protesters burned tires and blocked coastal highways and railway tracks, demonstrating against the early closure of the fishing season, a move partly driven by overfishing tied to fishmeal.

The investigation also unveiled the hidden role of forced labor and land appropriation in China’s growing aquaculture industry. (To be continued) – Rappler.com

The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project.

articles.title: The week in photos: November 21-27, 2026
articles.summary:
MANILA, Philippines — On November 24, the Supreme Court of the Philippines dismissed petitions questioning the arrest of former president Rodrigo Duterte, stating they were moot since he is in the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC).

Duterte has been detained in The Hague, the Netherlands, since March 2025 after he was arrested due to crimes against humanity. His case stemmed from his drug war and the killings allegedly committed by the Davao Death Squad.

On November 30, the former president will be the first Asian head of state to face a trial due to crimes against humanity before the ICC. 

Meanwhile, the Senate began plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 on November 23, with lawmakers proposing P204.634 billion in amendments that prioritize “basic needs,” including health care and education, while cutting billions of pesos in infrastructure projects.

articles.summary: A Brazilian couple visiting Korea for the first time found themselves in a state of panic almost as soon as they arrived at Seoul Station after taking the Airport Railroad Express (AREX) from Incheon International Airport. Maria Diatrix, 61, and her husband stood in front of a transfer passageway with three large suitcases, unable to get through the ticket gates because the QR code on their express train tickets was not being recognized. As crowds streamed through three separate passageways leading to Seoul Metro Lines 1 and 4 and the Airport Railroad, the couple stood helplessly in front of the gates. They pressed the assistance button, only to receive an announcement over the speaker advising them to exit via the second basement level or purchase new single-journey transit cards. Confronted with a complicated maze at what was supposed to be their first gateway to Korea, the couple did not know what to do. articles.title: Foreign workers demand right to switch workplaces without letter of release
articles.summary: Many foreign workers in Korea are stuck in their current jobs without the freedom to seek better employment, due to a regulation that a union of foreign language teachers wants abolished. For many foreign workers living in Korea on an E-series visa, their continued stay in the country is tied directly to their jobs. In the eventuality that they have to change jobs in the middle of a contract, they must seek consent from their employer through a document known as a letter of release. Korean employers effectively sponsor visas for foreign employees by guaranteeing their status in the country. This leaves foreign employees vulnerable to exploitation by employers, who wield disproportionate control over their working conditions, wages and even housing. By withholding a letter of release, employers can effectively trap workers in unfair or abusive workplaces, denying them the freedom to seek better employment and leaving them with little power to challenge mistreatment. Three years later, he told The Korea Times his dream was to become an Air Force pilot. A decade on, the 29-year-old is living that dream. As a captain with the 19th Fighter Wing, Lee leads a flight of four F-16 fighter jets and helps defend Korea’s airspace every day. “I take pride in every mission because this is a job that not just anyone can do or is trusted with, and because I longed to be in this position,” Lee said in an interview with The Korea Times. Born to a Korean father and a Japanese mother, Lee grew up navigating two cultures — and it was that dual heritage that planted the seed of his ambition. “Flying to see my maternal grandparents in Japan was always thrilling, so I grew even more interested in airplanes. articles.title: Internet Post Office hacking leaks personal data of at least 113,000 customers
articles.summary: A hacking attack on the Internet Post Office has exposed the personal information of at least 113,855 customers, with the full scope of the breach still under investigation, the postal service said Saturday. The Korea Post, under the Ministry of Science and ICT, said it has confirmed that hackers had accessed mailing records containing customers' personal information and is working to determine the full scope of the breach. The attackers accessed the mobile Internet Post Office's delivery location change service and viewed the names, addresses and phone numbers of recipients of registered mail being delivered between Nov. 17 and 24. An analysis of data from a single day alone found that 113,855 people had their information exposed. Korea Post said it became aware of signs of the breach on Wednesday and requested a police investigation. articles.title: PM Shehbaz, CDF Munir speak on phone with Pakistani astronaut aboard China’s Tiangong space station
articles.summary:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir held a phone call on Saturday with Pakistani astronaut Zeeshan Ali, who is aboard the Shenzhou-24 mission.

The premier and the military chief spoke with Zeeshan from the headquarters of the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (Suparco).

On Wednesday, Wing Comm­ander Muhammad Zeeshan Ali became the first foreign astronaut to board China’s Tiangong space station, marking a historic milestone in Pakistan’s space ambitions and Beijing’s efforts to expand its space diplomacy.

The 40-year-old pilot, who is the first Pakistani in orbit, is working as a payload specialist and is set to stay at the station for 5 to 10 days. He also learnt Chinese songs and poetry, practised calligraphy and played table tennis.

The Shenzhou-24 crew, comprising Chinese commander Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi and Wing Commander Ali, was greeted with hugs by the three astronauts of the Shenzhou-23 mission already aboard the station. They had also prepared a cake to welcome the newcomers.

“As the first foreign crew member to board the China Space Station, I am incredibly excited. China Space Station here I come!” said Wing Commander Ali in Chinese, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.

The spacecraft had docked with Tiangong three hours and 38 minutes after liftoff.

A Long March-2F rocket carrying the spacecraft lifted off at 8:18am Beijing time (5:18am

Pakistan time), under a pink sky, in a cloud of flames and smoke, footage aired by CCTV showed.

According to Pakistan’s Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (Suparco), docking took place at 11:56am Beijing time (8:56am Pakistan time). The spacecraft separated from the carrier rocket about 10 minutes after liftoff and entered orbit, the CMSA said.

“The spacecraft is functioning well. I declare the Shenzhou-24 launch mission a complete success,” an official at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre announced.

Scientific experiments

During the mission, Pakistani scientific payloads will be deployed in the Wentian and Mengtian laboratories aboard the Tiangong station, according to Suparco.

The experiments include cultivating microalgae as a potential source of food and oxygen for future space missions and studying the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds.

The CMSA said the crew would conduct around 90 experiments during the mission. Its objectives also include an orbital rotation with the Shenzhou-23 crew, routine operations and maintenance of the station, and further space science research involving various payloads.

‘Carrying hopes of 250m Pakistanis’

In April, Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud were chosen from Pakistan to start training in China. Pakistan’s space agency Suparco and CMSA signed a cooperation agreement in February 2025, under which two Pakistanis were to train in China, with one joining a mission on the Tiangong space station operated by Beijing.

Eventually, Ali was chosen to join the Chinese mission.

Speaking at a press briefing in Jiayuguan on Tuesday, Ali said he was “deeply grateful” to the Chinese government for helping “us realise our dream of going into space”.

He said he arrived at the Astronaut Centre of China a few months ago, carrying with him the hopes of 250 million Pakistani people.

Ali said he believed that “what comes after this flight matters more than the flight itself”.

“This mission is not a finish line; it is a launch pad. And I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut, one flight to multiple joint flights, to the Moon, Mars and beyond.”

On Wednesday, PM Shehbaz congratulated the nation on Ali’s departure for the Tiangong space station, saying Pakistan had begun its journey “beyond the stars”.

He described the mission as a journey not just for one astronaut but for 240 million Pakistanis, particularly the younger generation and scientists.

The military leadership, including CDF Munir, also congratulated Suparco and the scientific community on the launch, according to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).

articles.title: PTA says submarine cable fault fixed, internet services return to normal
articles.summary:
The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) on Saturday announced the restoration of the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5) international submarine cable system following the repair of a fault, saying internet services across the country had returned to normal.

On November 18, PTA said that a fault had been reported in the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5) international submarine cable system, approximately 11 kilometres from Pakistan’s coast.

In a statement today, the regulator said the cable was now fully operational and the fault had been rectified through coordination between Transworld Associates (TWA) and the international SMW5 consortium.

It said technical teams had worked round the clock to repair the fault and restore connectivity. Meanwhile, temporary rerouting of internet traffic through alternative international links had helped minimise disruptions during the outage.

The PTA confirmed that internet services had returned to normal operating capacity following the restoration of the cable.

Submarine cables are a critical part of international telecommunications infrastructure, carrying data between countries and continents. Faults in these systems can affect internet speeds and connectivity, particularly when traffic has to be redirected through alternative routes.

Currently, seven submarine cables provide internet connectivity to Pakistan: Asia-Africa-Europe 1 (AAE-1), South East Asia-Middle East-West Europe 4 (SMW4) and India-Middle East-Western Europe (IMEWE), operated by PTCL; and South-East Asia-Middle East-Western Europe 6 (SEA-ME-WE 6), South East Asia-Middle East-West Europe 5 (SMW5) and Transworld Associates 1 (TWA-1), operated by Transworld Associates.

Cyber Internet Services operates the seventh cable named Pak­istan and East Africa Connecting Europe (PEACE).

In July this year, a fault in the same SMW5 cable system had caused widespread connectivity issues in Pakistan. The PTA subsequently announced that the fault had been repaired on July 3, following its detection on July 1.

articles.title: Building tragedy
articles.summary:
FOLLOWING Wednesday’s building collapse in Karachi’s Baloch Colony, the removal or suspension of over a dozen officials has been ordered.

Speaking to journalists, Sindh CM Murad Ali Shah said categorically that such disasters cannot occur without the involvement of government officials.

Investigations and accountability are as necessary as pinning responsibility and punishing the errant. But it is clearly not enough. While other officials easily replace those removed, very little is done to address the lack of oversight.

As a result, unauthorised buildings are proliferating in Karachi. Much of the material used to raise them is substandard. Technical planning is flawed while owners recklessly add extra floors without assessing the strength of the foundations.

Those responsible for monitoring construction are indifferent, induced to look the other way as regulations are flouted, or restricted by stay orders that bar action. In the most recent incident — where such a stay order had been acquired — workers added four floors to the reportedly ground-plus-one mandated structure.

The CM has promised a “reset” at the Sindh Building Control Authority. There is reason to be sceptical: such vows have followed construction disasters in the past too — but have remained mere words. For instance, more than one building collapse was witnessed after the announcement of comprehensive SBCA reform in February this year. This shows official apathy and the lack of political will to take action.

Governance is interconnected, and the rot in one department is invariably linked to the overall failure of public administration. The Sindh government will have to look within to find answers to why laws are flouted with impunity, why corruption prevails, and why there is reluctance to ensure accountability for those who play with people’s lives.

As the search for survivors and dead bodies continues, the administration should remember that a system built on broken promises usually proves to be the cause of its own undoing.

Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026

articles.title: CDA seals Fazl’s Islamabad residence after 'foreign' owner's CNIC cancelled
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: The Capital Development Authority (CDA) on Saturday sealed the Islamabad residence of Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman after the identity card of the property’s legal owner was cancelled.

The move comes amid continuing tensions between the JUI-F and the federal government.

A notice affixed on the property gate on Thursday said the building has been sealed by CDA’s Building & Housing Control “on account of cancellation of ownership”.

A CDA notice affixed on a gate of JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s residence in Islamabad on Nov 28, 2026. — via Kashif Abbasi

CDA’s Building & Housing Control swung into action a day after the deputy director for CDA’s Estate Management-I ordered sealing of the property due to the change of title being cancelled.

In an order dated Nov 27, the deputy director for CDA’s Estate Management-I noted that the owner, Amanullah, son of Muhammad Younus, had been “identified as a foreign national and his Pakistani Computerised National Identity Card (CNIC) had accordingly been cancelled”.

“In exercise of the powers delegated by the Authority to the member (Estate) and after consideration of the available record and observance of the prescribed process, the change of title granted in favour of Mr Aman Ullah s/o Muhammad Younas, […] has been CANCELLED with immediate effect,” read the order, available with Dawn.

It directed the director general of the CDA’s Building & Housing Control Department to seal the property, adding that he could seek assistance from CDA formations and the Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) administration, if required.

“Consequential legal action shall be taken by Directorate of Estate Management-1,” it added.

The CDA order noted that the focal person for Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) Illegal Foreigners’ Repatriation Plan (IFRP), in a letter dated Nov 25, also confirmed the cancellation of Amanullah’s Pakistani CNIC “following verification by Nadra and requested initiation of appropriate legal proceedings in respect of immovable properties reportedly acquired by him in Islamabad”.

CDA highlighted that Amanullah had been given an opportunity of hearing as a show-cause notice was issued to him on Nov 25 to appear personally before the CDA member for Estate on Nov 26 and explain why the change of title in his favour should not be cancelled.

The CDA said Amanullah could not be found at the “subject property for personal service of the notice, whereupon the notice was duly pasted at the premises of the subject property” to communicate the proceedings to him.

However, Amanullah allegedly failed to appear before the CDA Estate member on Nov 26, nor “did he avail himself of the opportunity of hearing to rebut the allegations or produce any valid identity document or prior written permission of the competent government” for acquiring the property.

CDA had also issued notice against the same property on Oct 30 for placing a generator outside and for alleged illegal/unauthorised construction.

‘Violation of prescribed transfer requirements’

According to the CDA order, the matter regarding Amanullah’s nationality and identity credentials was brought to its notice through “official communications received from various government agencies”, including the Office of the District Magistrate, the focal person for IFRP, ICT and the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra).

It noted that as per a Nadra letter, Amanullah had originally obtained his CNIC on the basis of his parents’ CNIC, whereas “discrepancies had been observed in the family record, including the existence of two CNICs of his late father, Muhammad Younas”.

The order said that subsequent verification by Nadra established that the identity document furnished by Amanullah “for the purpose of obtaining change of title in respect of the subject property was not a valid Pakistani CNIC and had been cancelled by the competent authority, thereby rendering the mandatory identity requirement for processing the change of title unfulfilled”.

It stated that under Chapter 6 of the CDA Property Manual, which requires producing a valid CNIC, furnishing an invalid identity document constituted a “material violation of the prescribed transfer requirements and vitiates the administrative process through which the change of title was obtained”.

The CDA also cited Section 3 of the Foreigners Act 1946, which empowers the government to regulate the acquisition of property by foreigners, stating that a 1984 order under it provided that no foreigner shall “acquire land or any interest in land or landed property in Pakistan except with the previous permission in writing of the federal government or of the provincial government”.

“No such permission has been produced or placed on the record of the Authority in respect of the subject property,” the order maintained.

Consequently, the CDA’s Estate Wing initiated proceedings to cancel the change of title granted in Amanullah’s favour, the document added.

Fazl-govt rift

Fazl had criticised the Centre for imposing governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and making the then-PTI provincial government non-functional. The JUI-F chief also accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments despite his efforts to mediate between the PML-N and PTI governments.

Tensions escalated when Fazl accused the Centre of depriving the provinces of their rights, resulting in the veteran politician and key federal ministers exchanging harsh remarks.

In recent weeks, PPP Chairman Bilawal-Bhutto Zardari — a key ally of the ruling PML-N — has voiced his support for Fazl and condemned the “government’s actions” against him.

Last week, police and Federal Constabulary (FC) personnel deployed to protect Fazl and other members of his family were withdrawn from the residences they guarded in Islamabad and Dera Ismail Khan.

A JUI-F spokesman had confirmed the withdrawal, alleging that Fazl’s Islamabad residence had been cordoned off by capital police and that security personnel had harassed visitors. He also claimed that the party’s Central Secretariat in Islamabad had been besieged by police.

An Islamabad police official, however, said only one police guard had been withdrawn.

The JUI-F chief’s son has also come under scrutiny from the anti-graft watchdog, with the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) summoning former federal communications minister Asad Mahmood over alleged irregularities in 4,252 appointments at Pakistan Post during his 2022-23 tenure. Mahmood skipped two consecutive summonses issued for Nov 10 and 14, according to a NAB source.

The JUI-F staged protests in parts of Sindh and Balochistan on Nov 7 against a “coordinated character assassination campaign” targeting Fazl.

Party leaders and workers condemned the alleged drone surveillance of his residence and the circulation of footage on social media, demanding an impartial investigation and action against those responsible.

On Tuesday, Fazl claimed he had been put under an hours-long “state siege” to prevent him from attending a multiparty conference hosted by the Lahore High Court Bar Association.

On Thursday, authorities barred the JUI-F chief and eight other leaders of his party from entering, residing or remaining in Sargodha — where the JUI-F planned to hold a rally that day — for 30 days. Despite the restriction, Fazl said in a video message that he was setting out for Sargodha.

The next day, hours after Fazl claimed that he was under arrest, Lahore Capital City Police Officer Bilal Siddique Kamyana denied that the politician had been taken into custody.

The JUI-F also claimed that several party activists and workers had been arrested and booked across Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as the party staged protests at various locations on Thursday and Friday.

Additional input by Kashif Abbasi

articles.title: Lahore ranked world's most polluted major city; Sargodha, Peshawar also record hazardous air
articles.summary:
LAHORE: Lahore was ranked the world’s most polluted “major city” on Saturday morning as its air quality index (AQI) reached 400, while Peshawar and Sargodha also recorded AQIs above 400, according to monitoring firm IQAir.

The Swiss air quality monitoring organisation placed Lahore at the top of its ranking for global major cities for the 9am to 10am period on Nov 28, with Kabul second at an AQI of 304 and Delhi third at 238.

The ranking at that time showed other cities in the region reporting high pollution levels, with Dubai at an AQI of 168, Kathmandu 166, Kolkata 161 and Karachi 160. Cairo, Chengdu and Kampala also featured among the 10 most polluted major cities.

Screengrab from IQAir.

Lahore’s AQI of 400 fell in the hazardous category, according to IQAir’s scale, which ranks AQI above 300 as such. Exposure to such pollution can pose serious risks, particularly to children, older people and those with respiratory or cardiovascular conditions.

The deteriorated air quality comes as smog continues to affect several parts of Punjab, with pollution levels remaining elevated across major urban centres.

By 1pm, Lahore’s AQI had declined to 293, falling in the “very unhealthy” category.

The concentration of PM2.5 — particulate matter so small they can be absorbed into the bloodstream upon inhalation — was “43.6 times the World Health Organisation annual PM2.5 guideline value”, IQAir noted.

Screengrab from IQAir.

Within Lahore, pollution levels varied considerably between localities, with several monitoring stations recording readings substantially higher than the citywide level.

For 9-10am, Allama Iqbal Town recorded an AQI of 680, the highest among the listed monitoring stations, followed by ARM at 557 and ARC at 461. Bedia Thethar Road recorded 416, while A Block, Model Town, reported 392.

Barki Road, among the relatively less polluted locations in the city, still recorded an AQI of 208, indicating “very unhealthy” air quality.

The pollution crisis extended beyond Lahore, with several cities across Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa reporting very unhealthy to hazardous air quality.

Screengrab from IQAir.

An IQAir ranking of Pakistani cities, for 9-10am, placed Peshawar at the top with an AQI of 414, followed by Sargodha at 404, Gujranwala at 388 and Faisalabad at 384. Lahore ranked fifth nationally with an AQI of 363, followed by Multan at 347, Rahim Yar Khan at 328, Sialkot at 301, Bahawalpur at 280 and Muzaffargarh at 259.

By 1pm, Sargodha had overtaken Peshawar — which now had 327 AQI — with an AQI of 412, and Lahore had declined to 293.

Residents were advised to limit outdoor exposure, remain indoors where possible and use N95 masks if outdoor activities cannot be avoided.

Vehicular emissions, industrial pollution and crop residue burning are among the major sources contributing to smog, while winter weather conditions can restrict dispersal of pollutants and allow them to accumulate near the ground.

With winter setting in, the recurring smog crisis has raised concerns over public health and the effectiveness of measures aimed at reducing pollution across Punjab.

articles.title: Death toll in Baloch Colony building collapse rises to 11 as rescuers recover three more bodies
articles.summary:
KARACHI: Rescue workers recovered three more bodies from the rubble of a six-storey building that collapsed near Karachi’s Baloch Colony area on Saturday, taking the death toll to 11.

On Wednesday, three people were killed and 14 others injured when the under-construction building — reportedly being constructed illegally on a residential plot — collapsed. Another body was recovered on Thursday, taking the death toll to four. On Friday, four more bodies were recovered, taking the toll to eight.

Videos shared by Rescue 1122 from the site showed members of the Urban Search and Rescue team using heavy-duty bolt cutters to cut through rebar and recover bodies, while clearing rubble with various tools.

At least eight more people are still missing, according to reports submitted by their relatives at the information desk set up at the site of the collapsed building.

Commissioner’s office submits report to CM

The Karachi Commissioner’s Office has submitted a report to the chief minister on action taken against illegal and unauthorised buildings in the city, stating that 516 buildings have been sealed so far as part of an ongoing crackdown, as of November 27.

According to the report, action was taken against 262 buildings under construction in various districts. Of these, 158 were sealed, while notices were issued to 12 buildings. Construction work was found to have been halted at one site during an inspection.

In Korangi district, 41 of the 48 buildings were sealed, while notices were issued to seven. In Keamari, 12 of the 19 buildings were sealed and notices were issued to five, while construction work was found to have stopped at one site. The report also recorded 12 buildings in West, 21 in Malir, 64 in Central, 61 in South and 37 in East. Of these, eight buildings in Malir, five in Central, 55 in South and all 37 in East were sealed.

Karachi Commissioner Syed Hassan Naqvi has directed deputy commissioners to continue action against illegal and unauthorised constructions and ensure that those violating building regulations are dealt with in accordance with the law.

Man rescued alive after 54 hours

A day earlier, emergency services rescued a man alive from beneath the rubble, two days after the building collapsed.

Rescue 1122 said that 28-year-old Muhammad Adil was rescued alive from the rubble. It said that the search operation for any other individuals feared trapped was underway.

Its spokesperson, Hassaanul Haseeb Khan, termed the rescue a “breakthrough”. He added that rescue operations were ongoing to search for other survivors from the debris.
