articles.title: Hungary lifts entry ban on Robert "Magyar" Brovdi
articles.summary:
A three-year entry ban on Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, a Ukrainian military commander of Hungarian descent, has been removed from the Hungarian immigration authorities' register.

Source: Hungarian newspaper Magyar Hang, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Hungary has lifted its entry and residence ban on Robert Brovdi, a Ukrainian drone commander. According to the newspaper's report, the National Directorate-General for Aliens Policing (NDGAP) has removed the ban from its system.

Brovdi is the highest-ranking military officer of Hungarian descent serving in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. A Russian court has sentenced him to life imprisonment in absentia.

Background:

The ban was announced in August 2025 by the then Hungarian foreign minister Péter Szijjártó following attacks on the Druzhba oil pipeline. Szijjártó said at the time that the commander of the military unit responsible for the attacks would be banned from entering Hungary and the entire Schengen Area.

In response, Magyar told the then Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán and his team to shove the sanctions "up their arses".

articles.title: Russia kills four people and injures eight in Donetsk Oblast
articles.summary:
Four people have been killed and eight injured in Russian attacks on Donetsk Oblast on 27 November.

Source: Donetsk Oblast Military Administration

Details: The Russians killed three people and injured three in Sloviansk.

One person was killed and another injured in Malotaranivka.

Four people were injured in Russian attacks on Kramatorsk.

A total of 4,500 civilians have been killed and 11,062 injured in Donetsk Oblast since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion. These figures do not include casualties in Mariupol or Volnovakha.

Background: Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 162 drones (74 jet-powered) on the night of 27-28 November. Hits were recorded at 13 locations and debris from downed UAVs fell at another seven.

articles.title: Austrian far-right leader proposes deporting Syrians and Afghans to Ukraine in return for aid
articles.summary:
Herbert Kickl, leader of the opposition far-right Freedom Party of Austria (FPÖ), has proposed that Ukraine be required to accept refugees whom the EU cannot return to their countries of origin in return for the financial aid it has received.

Source: Kickl's statement posted on the Freedom Party's website on 27 November, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Kickl said that the EU and Austria have "pumped hundreds of billions in Ukraine" and in return, he proposed that Syrians and Afghans are sent to Ukraine, arguing that "they could also help with the rebuilding there after the war".

"Once the guns fall silent there, it will be high time to demand something in return. Ukraine owes us something! It would be an absolute win-win situation if Kyiv were to take in those Syrians and Afghans whom we cannot return to their countries of origin. They could immediately start helping with the reconstruction there. Anyone who doesn't like that is free to leave at any time – just not to come here," he stated.

According to Kickl, the current governing coalition is nothing more than a vote of no confidence in the will of the electorate and is further fuelling illegal immigration.

"Anyone who does not live by our values, our culture and our traditions has no right to an Austrian passport. For years, the supposedly conservative People's Party has taken no action to put an end to this and has failed to support our legislative initiatives," he added.

Background: Kickl has previously sharply criticised the EU's policy on Ukraine and claimed that the European Union was putting the Austrian population at risk.

articles.title: Russia attacks Ukraine with 162 drones, hits recorded at 13 locations
articles.summary:
Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 162 drones (74 jet-powered) on the night of 27-28 November. Hits have been recorded at 13 locations and debris from downed UAVs have fallen at another seven.

Source: Ukraine's Air Force

Details: The Russians launched Shahed and Gerbera attack drones and Parodiya decoy UAVs from the Russian cities of Oryol, Millerovo and Kursk as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea.

Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack.

As of 08:00, Ukrainian air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 141 Russian drones (54 jet-powered).

Hits by drones have been recorded at 13 locations and the fall of downed UAVs (debris) at seven locations.

The attack is ongoing, with several Russian drones still in Ukrainian airspace.

articles.title: Number of people injured in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast rises, child among them

Source: Oleksandr Hanzha, Head of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration, on Telegram

Details: Hanzha said five people had been injured, including a child.

Quote: "Transport infrastructure facilities have been damaged in Dnipro. A 26-year-old woman has been taken to hospital in a serious condition and a 47-year-old man in a moderate condition."

Details: Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration also said that the Russians had targeted the city of Nikopol and the Marhanets and Pokrovske
hromadas
A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories
in the Nikopol district. A 29-year-old man and a 15-year-old boy have been taken to hospital in a moderate condition.

The Russians damaged premises belonging to a business and infrastructure facilities in the Synelnykove district.

A business was damaged and one person was injured in the Ternivka hromada in the Pavlohrad district.

Background: One person is known to have been injured in a Russian attack on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on the evening of 27 November.

articles.title: One person killed and five injured in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia Oblast

The Russians also conducted 18 airstrikes and attacked settlements in Zaporizhzhia Oblast with 539 drones of various types.

articles.title: Russia claims over 460 drones attacked Moscow and surrounding area
articles.summary:
Russian authorities have claimed that more than 460 drones attacked Moscow and the surrounding area. Some Moscow airports have suspended operations and passengers have been made to disembark from one aircraft.

Source: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin; Russian media outlet Astra

Details: Sobyanin claimed that 48 drones had already been destroyed.

Meanwhile, restrictions were imposed at Vnukovo and Domodedovo airports.

No restrictions were announced at Sheremetyevo Airport, but Russian media outlets and Telegram channels reported that a flight from Moscow to Vladivostok had not taken off.

The aircraft was due to depart for Vladivostok on the evening of 27 November. After passengers had spent almost three hours waiting on board, the captain announced that the departure had been delayed indefinitely. Airline staff were unable to explain the reasons for the delay to passengers. At around midnight, passengers were made to disembark and told that they would fly to Vladivostok on another aircraft. They were later informed that their departure had been postponed until 10:00.

Passengers received a text message informing them that the flight would include an additional stop. However, a blank space was left in the message instead of the name of the city where the aircraft was due to land.

Update: Sobyanin later claimed that another 21 drones that were "heading towards Moscow" had been shot down.

Sobyanin said in the morning that 462 drones had flown towards Moscow and the surrounding area since the previous evening and throughout the night.

He claimed that 123 drones had been destroyed on their approach to Moscow.

"Most of the drones have been downed by the Ministry of Defence's air defences far from the capital," Sobyanin added.

articles.title: Russian oil refinery in Novoshakhtinsk and Samara oil pumping station come under attack – videos
articles.summary:
An oil refinery in the Russian city of Novoshakhtinsk has come under attack for the second time in a week, causing a large-scale fire. Telegram channels have also reported a strike on Russia's Samara oil pipeline control station.

Source: Russian media outlet Astra, citing local Telegram channels and media outlets; Exilenova+; other Telegram channels

Details: Local residents have captured footage of a glow in the sky near the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery. A series of explosions had previously been heard in Novoshakhtinsk in Russia's Rostov Oblast.

"Heavy drones have attacked Novoshakhtinsk! The situation is difficult, a fire has broken out," local media outlets reported.

The Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery began operating in 2009 and has a design capacity of 5.6-7.5 million tonnes of oil per year. The refinery is considered one of the largest suppliers of petroleum products in southern Russia.

The Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery produces petrol, diesel, aviation kerosene, fuel oil and bitumen. The refinery is connected to Transneft's main oil pipeline network.

Exilenova+ also reported another strike on the Samara oil pipeline control station near Prosvet in Russia's Samara Oblast.

Update: Astra later reported that fuel storage tanks are likely on fire at the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery.

Background:

On the night of 9-10 October, Ukraine's defence forces struck the Samara oil pipeline control station in Russia's Samara Oblast again and attacked several Russian military assets in the occupied territories and Bryansk Oblast.

It was reported that Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in Russia's Rostov Oblast was hit once again on the night of 22-23 November, although the fire reported in the area may have broken out at the privately owned company Tata-Gaz instead.

It later emerged that Russia's Novoshakhtinsk Petroleum Products Plant had suspended operations following a large-scale missile and drone attack.

articles.title: Putin's envoy says AI is being used to prepare for talks and draft diplomatic agreements
articles.summary:
Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund and Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin's special envoy, has said that he uses AI to prepare for negotiations and draft diplomatic agreements.

Source: Dmitriev speaking at the AI Journey 2026 conference, as quoted by Radio Liberty; Kremlin-aligned Russian news agency TASS; Russian media outlet Astra

Details: Dmitriev claimed that AI can be used to find ways to make an agreement better reflect Russia's position and address its concerns.

Quote: "AI certainly helps prepare for negotiations. What's more, you can even enter data and ask what an agreement, a diplomatic one, for example, might look like, and AI will offer its suggestions.

You can ask a question like: 'How can we make this agreement better reflect Russia's position, present Russia's concerns in an even more convincing way and address them?' It really is a very important tool."

Details: Dmitriev did not specify which AI models he uses but praised Russian developments in this field. He also stressed that Russian AI models can be used not only to solve practical problems but also to prepare for "geopolitical breakthroughs".

Background: Putin said that Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to present their position on ending the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian military flotilla en route to Libya turns back after Ukrainian attack on ships – Reuters
articles.summary:
A Russian military flotilla in the Mediterranean Sea that had been transporting military equipment to Libya has turned around since Ukrainian naval drones sank a Russian corvette in the port of Benghazi on 22 November.

Source: Reuters, citing military and security sources, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Reuters notes that the previously unreported change of course by the convoy illustrates how Russia is attempting to protect its naval forces following the Ukrainian naval drone attack that sank a Russian warship in Libya, roughly 2,000 km (1,240 miles) away from the theatre of war in Ukraine.

Another convoy that was being escorted by a Russian naval frigate, the Golovko, turned back near the Strait of Sicily on the day the attack in Benghazi took place, according to a European military official who had been tracking the convoy's movements. The strait is a key chokepoint off the coast of North Africa.

A representative of Ukrainian military intelligence and a separate Middle Eastern security official familiar with the convoy's situation confirmed that the second flotilla has changed course, diverting from its route to Libya, and is currently off the coast of Algeria.

Russia's Ministry of Defence has yet to respond to Reuters' request for comment.

Background:

On 23 November, Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukrainian naval drones had sunk the Russian corvette Merkury, which had a Ka-27 helicopter on board, and also struck the dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Russia was using to transport weapons, near the Libyan port of Benghazi.

Italy later said that Ukraine did not coordinate its actions in Libya with its allies or inform them about its attack on a Russian ship. This was confirmed by Zelenskyy during a phone call with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

articles.title: Zelenskyy confirms that attack on Russian ship in Libya was not coordinated with Ukraine’s partners
articles.summary:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has held a telephone conversation with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, during which the two leaders discussed the recent attack on Russian ships in Libya.

Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda

Details: Zelenskyy noted that the operation in Libya was not coordinated with Ukraine's European partners.

Quote: "We discussed the issues we are dealing with right now, and it's important that we understand each other. I confirmed that the recent operation in Libya was conducted without prior coordination with our European partners."

Details: Zelenskyy also told Meloni that Ukraine is committed to "making sure our respective authorities share all necessary information and maintain direct, regular and effective communication".

Background:

Zelenskyy had previously said that Ukraine always coordinates its attacks on Russian ships with the countries in whose waters or near whose infrastructure the Ukrainian forces are operating.

However, the Italian side subsequently said that Ukraine did not coordinate its actions in Libya with its partners or inform them about its attack on a Russian ship.

On 23 November, Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukrainian naval drones had sunk the Russian corvette Merkury, which had a Ka-27 helicopter on board, and also struck the dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Russia was using to transport weapons, near the Libyan port of Benghazi.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni later commented on the Ukrainian strikes on Russian ships in the port of Benghazi, stressing that the war must not spread to the Mediterranean.

articles.title: EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance may triple its number of participants
articles.summary:
The industrial cooperation initiative between the EU and Ukraine in the field of unmanned aerial vehicles is preparing for a significant expansion of its participating companies.

Source: Rapporteur, citing its own sources, as reported by European Pravda

Details: The EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance has held only two meetings since its launch in the summer, yet it has already generated so much interest that it could soon more than triple in size. According to officials, a decision has been made to expand the alliance from its current 18 members to 80. The European Commission has also confirmed this plan to the publication.

At its inaugural meeting, European Commissioner Andrius Kubilius outlined the alliance's objectives: to facilitate the creation of joint ventures, develop readiness to scale up production, and contribute to European Defence Projects of Common Interest, namely the Drone and Counter-Drone European Resolve (DECODER).

A total of 18 founding drone manufacturers – nine each from the EU and Ukraine – only recently finalised their governance structure, selecting the German company Quantum Systems and Ukraine's UFORCE as co-chairs for the next six months.

In the first round, more than 400 companies applied to join. Plans are underway to announce a second call for applications in the near future to increase membership. According to the Rapporteur's sources, this could happen as early as December, as no additional approval from the steering board is required. The founding companies will retain their exclusive status within the leadership, while interested industry players will be able to apply to join as regular members of the expanding alliance.

Currently, existing members have formed four working groups focusing on supply chains, secure industry cooperation, scaling up production, and operational training. Many of them have expressed interest in establishing a joint drone market between the EU and Ukraine.

Background:

As European Pravda previously reported, the inaugural meeting of the EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance comprising nine Ukrainian and nine European companies took place in Brussels on 11 September.

In July 2026, the EU and Ukraine agreed on the Drone Deal, which aims to provide a single, coherent framework for cooperation between the EU and Ukraine to facilitate, coordinate, and support the full implementation of bilateral drone agreements that Kyiv has signed with several EU capitals.

articles.title: Poundland: the collapse of a high street chain can mean major economic fallout
articles.summary:
TTL Deez/Shutterstock

With so many households struggling with the cost of living, Poundland should have been thriving. But the discount retailer has just gone into administration, putting around 11,000 jobs at risk.

So why did the chain collapse? After all, there is evidence that when budgets get tighter, consumers tend to substitute expensive products for cheaper alternatives.

But the same inflationary pressures that encourage consumers to seek cheaper products also make discount retailers more expensive to operate. Poundland’s original business model of selling products for £1 illustrates this tension perfectly.

For if the cost of supplies, transport and wages all go up, profit margins get really squeezed. Increasing prices risks losing customers.

Discount retailers may therefore attract more customers while earning less on each product sold, relying on much higher sales volumes to remain profitable.

In June 2025, when an American investment firm bought Poundland for a nominal £1, the symbolic price reflected a business burdened by substantial debts and other financial commitments. The objective of such acquisitions is usually to increase business value by restoring profitability and restructuring those financial obligations.

And there were signs that the strategy was working. According to unaudited management figures, Poundland’s earnings improved, and sales were growing.

But it wasn’t enough.

And the reason may be the difference between profitability and liquidity.

Popularity and profit

Imagine a restaurant which is fully booked for the next month – but does not have enough cash available today to buy ingredients or pay staff. Despite having customers and the potential to generate profits, it may be forced to close.

Something similar appears to have happened to Poundland, where management reported restrictions on access to cash and borrowing facilities in late October 2026. By November 19, there were reports of stock shortages leaving daily sales way below expectations.

This creates a vicious circle. Without finance, the company cannot replenish stock. Without stock, it loses sales. Without sales, its financial position deteriorates further.

The American economist Hyman Minsky explored this relationship through the concept of what he called “financial fragility”. He argued that business survival depends not simply on generating income, but also on being able to meet financial commitments.

Research I carried out with colleagues also examined how financial conditions, alongside productivity, influence which businesses survive. In the case of Poundland, its owner maintained that it provided £85 million in financing and that the company remained financially vulnerable.

But improving operating earnings does not guarantee long-term viability.

Tight margins.
Lenscap Photography/Shutterstock

Poundland now looks like it will be broken up, with competing retailers expressing interest in taking over individual stores.

Although these acquisitions may preserve some jobs, the economic consequences of dismantling the business extend well beyond its workforce.

When workers lose their jobs, they spend less money, reducing the income of other local businesses, which may in turn be forced to cut back on staff. Economists call this the “multiplier effect”, and recent research highlights its economic and social importance.

The economic harm also includes former Poundland suppliers receiving fewer orders.

And poorer households may lose access to affordable products, while unemployment puts pressure on public finances through higher welfare expenditure and lower tax revenues.

Further economic loss stems from the fact that a company is often much more than the sum of its assets. Its “organisational capital” – the accumulated knowledge, employee experience and supplier relationships – can take decades to develop.

Poundland’s owners have said: “Our thoughts are with Poundland colleagues. We recognise how difficult the continued uncertainty is for them.

"Efforts to preserve as many jobs and stores as possible will continue, led by the administrators.”

But questions will persist about whether Poundland could have continued to operate under more sustainable financing arrangements. For the wider economic and social costs of losing a potentially viable business may end up exceeding the financial losses that come with its collapse.

Danilo Spinola does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Plant-based ‘tuna’ or pea crisps? Focus groups suggest new recipes for local, sustainable protein alternatives
articles.summary:
New Africa/Shutterstock

People prefer plant-based products to be local and sustainable, minimally processed and familiar, according to our latest research. This is alongside typical consumer expectations for food products such as taste and value.

Understanding consumer needs for plant-based food is vital for their success, and
that’s an essential part of building a more sustainable food system that moves away from carbon-intensive meat products.

Introducing new and exciting plant-based alternatives might encourage meat and dairy lovers to substitute some of their animal-based intake. However, many of those alternatives are ultraprocessed, so there are still potential health concerns surrounding such products.

Our project involved working with consumers to create ideas for plant-based food and drink products. As part of Protein-I, a project investigating how to diversify plant protein production and consumption around Ireland and Northern Ireland, we ran five workshops with consumers.

These workshops focused on plant proteins that could be grown for human consumption locally (such as barley, oats, peas, rye and wheat), rather than ones that are typically imported such as soy. Crop trials across research sites and farms had found that varieties of these crops can be grown in sufficient quantities in countries such as Ireland at a quality suitable for human consumption (rather than animal feed).

Following guided group discussions, interesting ideas from our 38 participants included a plant-based tuna alternative called “toona”, made from wheat and pea protein, pea and onion crisps plus wheat and barley pasta.

Many ideas focused on peas. However, some of the industry and academic experts we interviewed had reservations about peas, as they have a strong taste and colour, which can be off-putting to some people. To make them appealing as an ingredient in products, processing would be needed to refine the taste and colour, which may lead to products classed as ultraprocessed and concerns associated with this.

After the 38 participants voted for their favourite products and following input from experts, a vegetarian bolognese and flavoured protein oat milk came out as favourites.

A follow-on project from our work (Protein-I-2), which has just started, will explore the development of minimally processed products, using local and sustainable crops.

Highlighting the source or origin of plant-based products on labelling may encourage consumer uptake.
VH-studio/Shutterstock

Research shows that familiarity is an important factor in helping uptake of alternative proteins. Unsurprisingly, many of the food product ideas that originated during our research had similarities to existing products. Our participants weren’t given limits on the ideas that they could come up with, yet many of them suggested products based on existing foods such as porridge and pasta.

In our research, when asked what sustainability meant to them, participants often
mentioned where a product comes from and locality. One said: “How it’s like made …what it is or where it comes from, ye know?” Another commented: “If I’m shopping and I see something that’s been flown in from Kenya; beans or something, no I wouldn’t buy. I always go for something that’s local.”

Plant-based provenance

Highlighting the source or origin of plant-based products on labelling may encourage consumer uptake. As part of the Protein-I project, a digital track and trace platform was developed to improve food supply chain transparency. This enables consumers to access information on a product’s origin, production journey and environmental footprint through a QR code on the product label.

To explore the connection with local familiar foods, Protein-I ran a hands-on bread-making workshop using Irish-grown cereals. Feedback from participants was positive. Many reported feeling a stronger appreciation of Irish-grown cereals and left with an intention to purchase Irish cereal products in the future.

The workshop helped strengthen participants’ connection with where their food comes from and raised awareness of the role Irish-grown cereals can play in a more sustainable food system. By tailoring new product launches to consumers’ wants, there is a greater chance of acceptance, which should ultimately be better for sustainability and our environment.

Tony Benson receives funding from Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Northern Ireland) and Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (Republic of Ireland).

Many of us have been here. New Africa/Shutterstock

Rachel Bernasconi is the Editor’s Choice award winner in Vitae’s 2026 Three Minute Thesis competition sponsored by The Conversation UK.

It’s something we’re all familiar with – the frustration of a bad night’s sleep. But what is a bad night’s sleep, exactly? For some, it might look like lying awake, being unable to fall asleep. For others, sleep may come quickly, only to be interrupted by unwanted early morning wake ups.

Others may find that even with a solid eight hours a night, the struggle to get out of bed in the morning makes the thought of “five more minutes” an irresistible prospect. If only we could start our days with the same vigour we use when hitting the snooze button.

Bad nights are more than just inconvenient. Poor sleep is associated with a suite of negative health outcomes, ranging from cardiovascular disease and diabetes to poor mental health and dementia. And with clinically significant insomnia affecting over 15% of the general adult population, it is unsurprising that insufficient sleep has been branded a public health epidemic.

There is no shortage of opinions on how to get a better night’s sleep. We are also spoilt for choice by the healthtech industry, where a booming gadget market vies for our attention with promises of making sleepless nights a thing of the past. Yet the guidance we receive from these sources tends to be quite generic. And because we each sleep a bit differently, one-size-fits-all advice just doesn’t cut it.

We need advice that is tailored to our specific sleep needs and problems. Personalised tools that give personalised predictions are essential.

Mathematical modelling

Sleep researchers have long used mathematical tools, or mathematical models, to understand sleep. For instance, the seminal two-process model of sleep regulation, developed in the early 1980s, shaped our understanding of sleep timing; our bed and rise times are regulated by the interaction of our body’s circadian “clock” and a homeostatic variable that accumulates sleep “pressure” as we continue to stay awake. Similarly, pioneering work by McCarley-Hobson in the 1970s used mathematical models to rationalise how distinct groups of neurons coordinate the transitions between the two main sleep stages: rapid eye movement (REM) and non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep.

The two-process and McCarley-Hobson models have both spawned numerous adaptations that have themselves been applied broadly, from predicting alertness in resident physicians to debating whether moving school start times will combat adolescent fatigue. The usefulness of these models comes from the fact that their variables can be related to measurable features of sleep. For example, the variables of the two-process model tell us about the onset and duration of sleep. In this way, models act as a mathematical playground in which we can simulate different sleep patterns and predict what sort of things might make sleep better or worse.

Of course, predictions are only helpful if they are tailored to that individual. And while available models are good at simulating the “average” person’s sleep, there are clinically important features of sleep that models haven’t yet fully considered. For example, preferred sleep timing varies a lot from person to person, with some people preferring to stay up late and others preferring to go to bed and wake up early.

Another feature of sleep is the cycling that occurs between NREM and REM sleep states across the night. In healthy young adults, NREM sleep predominates at the start of the night, and REM sleep predominates at the end of the night. This pattern is disrupted in sleep disorders and changes as we age.

In my PhD, I was curious as to whether existing models were able to simulate these two features of sleep. So I selected two models: one model – grounded in the two-process model – described sleep timing; the other model – built on the McCarley-Hobson model – described the cycling pattern between NREM and REM sleep. Next, I used theories from applied maths – coupled oscillator and geometric singular perturbation theories, to be precise – to uncover the geometric building blocks of each of the models. In doing so, I was able to discern what sort of sleep patterns could be constructed in model simulations.

When I looked at the first model, I saw that it had all the necessary mathematical building blocks to predict sleep timing in lots of different people. I could simulate sleep timing not just in the “average” person, but also in people with extreme “night owl” or “early bird” tendencies.

When it came to the second model, things were a bit more complicated. Its building blocks were put together in a way that meant that the model couldn’t simulate the predominance of NREM at the start of the night, and REM at the end of the night. However, I figured out a way to rearrange the model’s building blocks. The result? The model became more flexible, allowing me to simulate a progressive increase in REM duration across the night. All in all, my research showed that it is possible to make models that predict some of the key, finer details of sleep – the kind of details that vary from person to person.

Simulate your sleep

At the University of Surrey, we are developing digital tools, for both clinical and personal use, to help people calibrate models of their own sleep patterns. With a personalised model, it’s possible to simulate different lifestyle changes and predict which ones will be most effective at helping you get better sleep.

And the results might be surprisingly achievable – getting a good night’s sleep might be a matter of spending a short period out in the Sun each morning. You can see the impact light has on sleep with our online Visualisation Tools, available here.

Simulate your own sleep patterns.
University of Surrey

Disturbed sleep will still trouble many of us, but now with the help of mathematical models we can take a glimpse into a future where each one of us can say goodnight to those bad nights – and hello to better sleep in nights to come.

Rachel Bernasconi has received funding from the UKRI Higher Education Innovation Funding scheme, the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre and the University of Surrey.

articles.title: Should you correct a friend’s health myth? Ask yourself this question first
articles.summary:
Kaspars Grinvalds/Shutterstock.com

“You must drink eight glasses of water a day” is the kind of advice a friend might offer. But what the advice leaves out is that our daily fluid intake comes from a variety of sources, including other drinks and food.

Some health advice gets repeated so often that few people think to question where it came from. Some of these claims are harmless, even if they simplify what the science actually says.

So before correcting a family member or friend, ask yourself: could this belief change a decision about their medical care? If not, correcting it may achieve very little.

The water example is a good one. A review of the evidence has found limited support for the idea that everyone needs a fixed number of glasses each day. Our requirement varies with age, activity and environment. Even so, the simplified version may still encourage people to stay hydrated.

The same goes for other familiar beliefs: that wet hair causes colds, that chicken soup makes you better when you are ill, or that you should be aiming for 10,000 steps a day.

All are half-truths. The science is more complicated than the slogan, but the beliefs may still encourage healthy behaviour.

However, some claims are harder to overlook. What counts is whether the belief could affect a decision about medical care and increase the risk of illness.

Cancer specialists have warned about juice diets and coffee enemas being promoted as alternatives to treatments that have been shown to work. Unlike misconceptions about hydration or wet hair, these claims can influence whether someone accepts, delays or rejects medical care.

Someone who believes an alternative therapy can cure cancer may turn down treatment that could save their life.

Vaccination is another example. A parent who comes across misleading information online may decide to avoid or delay childhood vaccinations.

Across Europe and parts of central Asia, measles cases doubled in 2024 to their highest level since 1997. More than 40% of cases were in children under the age of five.

Measles is returning because of health misinformation.
Habanero Pixel / Shutterstock.com

The same applies when people choose supplements or alternative remedies instead of prescribed treatments. The trouble starts when someone believes that herbal remedies such as turmeric, or dietary changes, can replace treatments that have been shown to work.

People do not have to accept every recommendation a doctor makes, and they are entitled to decline treatment or seek a second opinion. Problems arise when decisions rest on misinformation about medical care. Informed choice depends on understanding the options, and misinformation distorts the information that choice is built on.

Facts alone won’t cut it

Even then, correcting someone is rarely straightforward. Being told you are wrong can feel judgmental, embarrassing and dismissive, particularly when a belief is tied to family traditions, personal experience or hope during a difficult time, such as a cancer diagnosis.

Research on misinformation consistently shows that people do not always abandon a belief when they are given the facts. Beliefs are often tied to identity, experience and values, rather than being a simple misunderstanding of the evidence.

As a nurse whose research examines how healthcare professionals respond to health misinformation, I have seen how rarely facts alone correct these claims.

How a conversation begins makes a difference. Telling a friend or relative outright that they are wrong may encourage resistance. An approach based on questioning is often more productive.

Asking where they heard the claim, what makes the source trustworthy, or whether they have discussed it with a healthcare professional can open a more constructive conversation. Pharmacists, doctors and other healthcare professionals remain an important source of clarification when there is uncertainty.

Health advice is often less tidy than the slogan. Sometimes the missing details make little difference, as with the water. Other times they change a decision about someone’s medical care.

Knowing which is which helps us decide which claims to let pass, and which are worth challenging.

Josh Sharman does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Once logging stops, recovery of Vietnam’s tropical forests isn’t guaranteed
articles.summary:
Parilov/Shutterstock

Deep in the jungle of central Vietnam, the heat is heavy, the mosquitoes are relentless and the terrain offers no easy paths. My colleagues and I don’t hike on clear trails, we wade up riverbeds, stepping carefully over slippery rocks to access the thousands of trees we have been measuring for the last decade.

In 2024, I spent nearly two months camping in the forests of Động Châu–Khe Nước Trong, a nature reserve in central Vietnam. I worked with a field team of 12 people, in the gruelling conditions required to gather long-term ecological data.

Logging was particularly intense in the tropical forests of Vietnam between 1982 and 2007. As a result, the forest cover and the quality of those forest ecosystems has declined substantially. While forest cover in Vietnam has increased since the 1990s due to plantations and natural regeneration, the quality of forest recovery is less clear.

We visited every tree in our 24 study plots to measure them by hand in a meticulous, physically exhausting process that has been carried out four times since 2016. By identifying the species of each tree, measuring their diameter with a tape measure and noting any trees that have died, we tracked how these once-logged forests were recovering. Our findings challenge a key assumption about tropical forest regrowth.

Both governments and global carbon markets (a trading system that incentivises cuts in greenhouse gas emissions) invest in natural climate solutions. This often involves investing in schemes to plant new trees that absorb atmospheric carbon during photosynthesis in order to offset other carbon emissions. But these schemes rely heavily on an assumption: that once logging stops, tropical forests will naturally bounce back and recover, rapidly taking up carbon dioxide and storing it in growing trees.

In our latest study, published in the journal Environmental Research Letters, we show that rapid and predictable recovery may be overly optimistic.

Field researchers walk a measuring tape through dense trees to mark out a permanent forest plot in central Vietnam.
Amy Bennett, CC BY-ND

Since 2007, when selective logging in the region ended, these forests have not recovered as expected. Between 2016 and 2024, the forests showed no net increase in the carbon stored in their trunks and branches. The trees are still growing, but carbon gains from growth were almost entirely offset by tree deaths. Recovery rates were far below what the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates for the region and rates reported for comparable logged forests in Southeast Asia.

Heat restricts growth

Part of the explanation lies in the very conditions that made our fieldwork so challenging – rising temperatures. Since we have been monitoring these forests, temperatures have risen sharply, and we linked rising maximum temperatures to lower carbon gains. In 2024, the region where our forest plots are located endured severe, prolonged heatwaves in April and four in a row in August. Heat is already limiting tree growth here.

A field team member carries a ladder across a shallow, rocky river in Động Châu–Khe Nước Trong Nature Reserve, central Vietnam.
Amy Bennett, CC BY-NC-ND

These ecological constraints have financial and policy implications. Southeast Asia is central to carbon markets and the ecosystem restoration industry, hosting the majority of profitable forest restoration projects. Protecting young, regrowing forests from being cleared again helps limit greenhouse gas emissions by keeping the carbon already stored in the trees safe, as recovering forests are particularly vulnerable to repeated logging and clearing.

Yet, when calculating the value of protecting or restoring these forests, projects tend to assume steady, rapid tree growth, rather than measuring true forest function under the stress of extreme heat. Without long-term ground monitoring, schemes risk both underfunding necessary protection and overestimating carbon removal that may not be happening.

Despite harsh conditions and past disturbance, the forests managed to keep almost all the carbon stored in their trunks and branches intact. Long-term monitoring by our team and partners provided the evidence base that helped designate Động Châu–Khe Nước Trong as a nature reserve in 2020. Protection as a nature reserve has helped prevent further degradation through logging, securing these forests and the carbon they store.

Easy to overestimate

However, mechanisms allowing countries to work together toward their climate pledges under Article 6 of the Paris climate agreement tend to rely on generalised estimates of recovery. Those mechanisms also risk overestimating how much carbon recovering tropical forests can actually absorb.

To achieve realistic climate solutions in a warming world, policies must remain grounded in committed, local field surveys, no matter how hard those data are to collect.

Sleeping in hammocks in humid jungles, enduring insect swarms and battling steep terrain isn’t just about collecting data; this research offers a true insight into how forests are functioning in a changing world.

Amy Bennett has received funding from the Natural Environment Research Council, the European Research Council, the European Space Agency, the British Council, the Royal Society and the European Union.

articles.title: England and Wales are in a winter drought – which could make next summer even drier
articles.summary:
Water levels in reservoirs in England are still low this winter. AndyGriffin/Shutterstock

Historically, Great Britain’s most severe water crises have been associated with dry winters.

The summer drought of 1976 was made worse by an exceptionally dry preceding winter. More recently, the dry winter of 2021/22 set the stage for the severe summer drought of 2022, especially in chalk aquifers of England.

A dry winter in early 2023, including the driest February in 30 years across England, prevented reservoirs in south-west England from refilling, extending hosepipe bans through an entire year and stressing river ecosystems.

The drought of 2026 in parts of England and Wales is still evolving, but recent data shows that the very dry summer conditions from June to August have continued. There was below average rainfall, and lingering low river and groundwater levels, into early October. Catchment areas where there are dry conditions in the winter have the potential to have more severe summer drought conditions next year. However, rainfall in November has started to hit normal levels for the time of year.

Why dry winters are important

Drought is normally thought of as a summertime phenomenon. Extremely hot weather drives up water demand for crops and public supply, as seen during the widespread hosepipe bans and irrigation water restrictions across England and Wales in the summer of 2026. However, droughts also occur during the cooler winter months when rainfall drops below normal.

What happened during the drought of 1976.

Because British winters are typically wetter than summers, a winter drought rarely feels like a problem, especially as most of us prefer crisp, dry winter days to cold, wet weather.

Yet winter is the critical window when low evaporation and dormant vegetation allow rain to infiltrate through the soil and replenish underground aquifers and reservoirs.

When winter droughts occur, the impact often emerges months later in spring and summer as that deficit moves slowly through the hydrological system. This delay is particularly pronounced in regions reliant on groundwater for public supply and river flow, such as the chalk catchments of east and south-east England and the sandstones of the Midlands. Because water takes months or even years to percolate through soil and porous rock, a winter rainfall shortage can impact river flows and groundwater levels the following summer.

Groundwater levels in England and Wales, summer (left) and October 2026 (right)

The maps show the rank (1 = driest) of the summer (Jun-Aug) and October 2026 groundwater levels.
Graph using data from Jonghun Kam and Seunghui Choi, Pohang University of Science and Technology., CC BY-NC-SA

Low winter rainfall strongly dictates summer groundwater levels as well as river flow levels, substantially increasing the odds of a summer drought.

Seasonal rainfall forecasts for the rest of this winter indicate there will be a recovery from the summer’s drought conditions for much of England and Wales, but a heightened chance for drought to persist in the south, east and northeast. This means that some parts of England could already be banking a hidden water deficit for next summer.

Whether winter droughts are becoming more frequent or severe with climate change remains unclear from the historical record alone. However, future climate projections point to a critical shift in how the seasons interact. By 2070, UK winters are projected to become up to 20% wetter, and summers significantly drier.

Wetter winters will not eliminate winter droughts. Year-to-year atmospheric variability means dry winters will still occur, and hotter, drier summers are likely to leave soils much drier by autumn. Much early winter rain will be absorbed simply re-wetting dry soils and meeting higher demand, shortening the seasonal window to top up groundwater levels and altering the link between winter rain and summer water supplies.

How to deal with winter droughts

Summer droughts in England and Wales are becoming increasingly disruptive, not only through agricultural irrigation restrictions and domestic hosepipe bans like those in 2026, but also by hampering river navigation, damaging freshwater ecosystems, and even curtailing electricity generation from power stations reliant on river cooling water, which can drive up energy prices.

As water demand rises alongside a growing population and a push for national food security, water planners need to track how winter rains top up the water system as well as summer demand.

Society must also shift from responding to summer water shortages to enhancing year-round water storage.

This includes building more reservoirs on farms to help supply agricultural crops, actively pumping excess winter floodwater into underground aquifers (an underground layer that retains water), and restoring wetlands to slow runoff from the land.

These measures could help mitigate the increasing pressure on our water systems as climate change creates warmer and drier weather more frequently.

Justin Sheffield receives funding from UKRI and European Space Agency.

articles.title: How to recognise when video gaming becomes an addiction
articles.summary:
Gaming disorder can develop when someone loses control over their gaming habits and continues to play despite negative effects on their everyday life. Studio Nut/Shutterstock

Most people who play video games can spend hours enjoying them without experiencing any problems. But for a small minority, gaming becomes so important that relationships, education or work begin to suffer. How can we tell when enthusiasm has become a disorder?

In 2019, the World Health Organization (WHO) formally recognised gaming disorder in its International Classification of Diseases. It describes a persistent pattern in which someone loses control over gaming, gives it priority over other activities and continues playing despite harmful consequences. For a diagnosis, the behaviour must seriously affect everyday life, usually for at least 12 months.

The diagnosis has prompted debate. Gaming brings enjoyment and social connection to millions of people, and researchers disagree about where intense involvement ends and a clinical problem begins.

In 2013, the American Psychiatric Association included “internet gaming disorder” in its diagnostic manual. However, it classified it as a condition requiring further study rather than an established diagnosis. The WHO subsequently adopted its own diagnostic criteria for gaming disorder.

I have researched problematic gaming for decades, beginning with work examining similarities between video games and slot machines. Researchers use terms such as “excessive gaming”, “problematic gaming” and “gaming addiction”, sometimes interchangeably. I regard addiction as the extreme end of a spectrum of gaming-related difficulties. The crucial question is whether someone is losing control and experiencing harm.

Why some people are more vulnerable

In a review of research, my colleagues and I examined what may contribute to the development of gaming disorder. We found that no single factor explains it. Personality, motivations for playing, mental health, biological differences and the design of games can all play a part.

Research has repeatedly found an association between gaming disorder and a personality trait known as neuroticism. People with higher levels of neuroticism tend to be more sensitive to stress and more prone to negative emotions.

People who experience more anxiety or distress may find virtual worlds reassuring or easier to control than their everyday circumstances. Gaming can offer temporary relief, but relying on it to escape difficulties may become problematic.

Gaming disorder has been linked to depression and anxiety. Research also suggests that people with ADHD or autism may be more likely to develop problems with gaming. Some studies have found a link between problematic gaming and suicidal thoughts, although this does not mean that gaming causes them.

However, much of this research on mental health examines people’s gaming habits and mental health at a single point in time. We cannot assume that gaming causes these difficulties, or that they necessarily cause gaming disorder. The relationship may work in both directions.

Studies using brain scans have identified differences in the brains of some people with problematic gaming. These differences occur in areas involved in how people respond to rewards, make decisions and control their behaviour.

Similar findings have been reported in research on other addictions. However, we cannot tell from these studies whether the brain differences existed before the gaming problems began or developed alongside them.

The games people choose may also matter. “Massively multiplayer online role-playing games” have frequently been associated with problematic gaming. In these games, large numbers of players share a virtual world that continues to exist even when they log off.

Researchers have also identified links with shooting and strategy games. But games vary considerably, as do the people who play them. A game’s genre alone does not make it addictive.

Game design can encourage repeated play through challenges, achievements and rewards. Some rewards arrive unpredictably, giving players a reason to try again because the next attempt might bring something valuable.

Psychologists call one form of this “variable-ratio reinforcement”. Players receive rewards but cannot predict how many attempts it will take to earn them. Such reward systems can help explain why some players find it difficult to stop, although their effects differ from person to person.

There are also concerns about how some games make money. Some games offer microtransactions, which allow players to spend real money on items or features within the game. These include loot boxes, which provide random virtual rewards without players knowing exactly what they will receive. The resemblance to gambling has attracted particular attention because loot boxes can be available to children.

A systematic review of research found associations between spending on loot boxes and both problematic gambling and gaming. However, this evidence does not establish that buying loot boxes causes either condition. Nor does it establish that buying loot boxes leads people into gambling later.

When should someone seek help?

One warning sign is being unable to cut back on gaming despite repeated attempts. Others include withdrawing from relationships or losing interest in other activities. Some people continue playing even when gaming is seriously affecting their work or education.

Some people become irritable or anxious when they cannot play, or conceal how much time they spend gaming. No single warning sign is enough to diagnose gaming disorder, but ongoing problems deserve attention.

If gaming is taking over someone’s life, they can seek help from a GP or mental health professional. These professionals can help assess the problem and determine whether specialist support is needed.

In England, the NHS also has a National Centre for Gaming Disorders, which provides specialist support for people aged 13 and over.

It is equally important to remember that many people play for long periods without suffering any harm. As I have argued throughout my research, the difference between a healthy enthusiasm and an addiction is that one adds to life while the other takes away from it.

Dr. Mark Griffiths has received research funding from a wide range of organizations including the Economic and Social Research Council, the British Academy, the Responsibility in Gambling Trust, and Norsk Tipping. He has also carried out consultancy for numerous gaming companies in the area of social responsibility and responsible gaming (including Camelot Plc). Views expressed here are his own and not those of these funding bodies.

articles.title: Gene therapy for blindness moves closer to patients
articles.summary:
EduBFoto/Shutterstock.com

Some people who had lost almost all their sight to an inherited eye disease could find objects on a table again after a single gene injection and training with special goggles.

None could read or recognise a face, but before treatment, the best any of them could see was a hand moving in front of the eye.

The results come from a small trial recently published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

A related gene treatment that needs no goggles is under review by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which is due to decide by mid-2027 whether to approve it for patients. It would be the first treatment of its kind to win approval.

Both rely on optogenetics, the technique recognised with this year’s Nobel prize in physiology or medicine. In retinitis pigmentosa, the inherited disease in these trials, the eye’s light-catching cells slowly die. The nerve cells wired to them often survive, but cannot sense light.

Read more:
How pond algae led to a Nobel prize and a new way to study the brain

Optogenetics uses a harmless virus to give the surviving cells a gene for a light-sensitive protein. It is like fixing a camera with a broken sensor by making its wiring sense light.

In the goggle trial, ten blind adults received the gene in one eye and then wore goggles that turn the scene into pulses of amber light. Seven became more sensitive to light. Four of these seven also did consistently better at tasks such as finding objects on a table when wearing the goggles.

The first patient, described in 2021, could touch a notebook almost every time while wearing the goggles, but a box of staples only a third of the time. The patient also reported being able to spot the white stripes of a pedestrian crossing.

The therapy under FDA review, called Mogenry, needs no goggles because its protein responds to everyday light. Its main trial enrolled 27 adults who could not make out from 20 feet (6.1 meters) what most people see from 1,600 feet.

A year later, treated patients could, on average, read about three more lines on a low-vision chart, while those given a dummy injection barely changed. That is a real gain, though far from reading a newspaper or driving.

How the same scene might look with advanced age-related macular degeneration.
Merve Sen, CC BY

What about a far more common form of sight loss?

Retinitis pigmentosa is rare. Age-related macular degeneration is not. An estimated 196 million people had it in 2020, and that number is projected to rise to 288 million by 2040.

Age-related macular degeneration damages the macula, the small central patch of the retina we use to read and recognise faces. The light-sensing cells there depend on supporting cells beneath them. In our lab in Tübingen, we study how a common genetic risk factor affects these cells and the thin layer they sit on.

With age, that layer thickens and fills with deposits. The supporting cells become stressed and dysfunctional, and the light-sensing cells that depend on them die.

In one late form, called geographic atrophy, it leaves a blank patch in the middle of whatever a person looks at. The patch slowly grows and central vision is lost. As a result, people can no longer read, recognise faces or watch TV, although their side vision remains.

Two drugs approved in the US slow its spread but cannot bring back lost sight. Optogenetics might, because nerve cells inside these patches often survive. The company behind Mogenry plans a trial in geographic atrophy, but it has not started yet.

The evidence is still thin. The goggle trial had ten people and no comparison group, and Mogenry’s main trial treated just 18 people. After four years, only about four in ten Mogenry patients could still read three extra lines. For a treatment given only once, we do not yet know how long the benefit lasts.

Read more:
Nobel laureate Karl Deisseroth on how light is changing what we know about the brain

Both treatments are a single injection into the eye rather than an operation, but the goggles are bulky and take training to use well. Side-effects were mostly mild or moderate inflammation and raised eye pressure.

Suitable patients are likely to be adults who have already lost almost all their sight but whose eyes can still send signals to the brain, with no other serious eye damage.

Cost will also decide who gets it.

Luxturna, an earlier gene therapy that replaces one faulty gene through eye surgery, launched in the US at US$425,000 per eye (£326,040).

An independent US institute judged that Mogenry would be fair value at US$67,400 to US$101,300 per eye.

The institute’s experts said most eye doctors would be able to administer Mogenry in their clinics. Approval is expected first in the US and Japan, which has granted priority review. No application for approval in Europe has yet been announced.

Optogenetics is unlikely to restore normal sight any time soon. In the next few years, key developments to watch include the FDA’s decision on Mogenry and its price, longer-term results from larger groups of patients (the current follow-up extends to four years) and findings from the first trial of optogenetics in people with geographic atrophy.

For now, optogenetics returns a sliver of sight to a small group of people, and the coming years will show whether that sliver becomes brighter.

Marius Ueffing receives funding from
Helmut Ecker Foundation, EU, BMFTR, German Research Council, DFG

Merve Sen does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Russia wants to build a new security framework to end the war. This is why it won’t work
articles.summary:
When negotiators from Russia, the United States and Ukraine met in Abu Dhabi recently for peace talks on ending the Ukraine war, the Russians pushed a long-held demand for a new security architecture for Europe. Washington has appeared open to this, with US President Donald Trump touting a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”.

While little was revealed about what such a framework would look like specifically, a recent speech by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov provides some clues.

Sergei Lavrov’s speech at the Minsk International Conference on Eurasian Security.

At a security conference in Minsk, Belarus, earlier this month, Lavrov proposed a new security architecture for the entire Eurasian continent.

Reiterating the claim Russia has long made to justify its war in Ukraine, Lavrov said NATO had repeatedly pledged not to expand eastward to contain Russia, but did so anyway. And, he said, the West is now pursuing a new “NATO-style military-political bloc in Asia”.

In response, Lavrov said Russia wanted to build a new security framework that would encompass all of Europe and Asia – echoing the Soviet Union’s communist alliances during the Cold War.

A new arrangement like this would be “committed to the principles of indivisible security, openness and equality”, Lavrov said, adding European nations were welcome to join. Russia does not “desire nor plan any war whatsoever with Europe”, he stressed. But he added:

If Europe, as it threatens, is itself preparing for war and initiates one, we are ready.

A security proposal based on “sovereignty” and “equality” may sound appealing to some states across the region. However, there are several reasons to be sceptical.

What Europe wants

The prevailing view in Europe is that Russia is the continent’s principal security threat. So, the idea of European states joining Russia in a new arrangement of any sort is unlikely to gain broad acceptance.

And despite Russian President Vladimir Putin’s claims he is not against “having a dialogue with Europe, Moscow has made clear it does not want European representatives in the Ukraine peace talks. So it stands to reason Europe wouldn’t have a voice in a future security agreement either.

That said, the political view towards Russia in Europe is evolving. As economic pressures continue to mount, support for right-wing, populist parties is growing, including one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters, Germany.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party opposes financial and military support for Ukraine, arguing the war is not in Germany’s national interests.

In fact, its platform in one recent eastern state election where it finished first called for a revival of Russian language teaching, an end to sanctions and closer energy ties with Russia.

This highlights the diversity of views in some countries on both the war and Europe’s broader strategic priorities.

Some have raised the possibility of a more robust Organization for Security and Co-operation (the only European security group that Russia belongs to), or a revived NATO-Russia Council. However, this seems far-fetched in the absence of trust between the two sides.

Many in Europe believe Russia’s true aims for a new security framework are to carve up the continent into Cold War-era spheres of influence and expand its influence beyond its borders.

Read more:
Russia wanted a new world order. This wasn’t the one it had in mind

What China wants

Second, it remains unclear how China, the region’s other major power, and its own security ambitions fit within Russia’s vision.

Chinese foreign policy has long emphasised a principle of not interfering in the domestic affairs of other states. This has proven attractive to many authoritarian countries. At the same time, China has successfully advanced major global economic initiatives, notably the Belt and Road Initiative. And Beijing often promotes its own vision of the international order.

As such, Russia’s proposed security framework would need to accommodate another major power with its own interests and priorities.

Despite their growing cooperation in recent years, China and Russia are also competing for influence in a pivotal Eurasian region – Central Asia. While Russia has traditionally been the dominant power in the region, China has quietly advanced to the point where it can now compete with, if not surpass, Russia’s influence.

What the rest of Asia wants

Lastly, Eurasia is already home to a complex landscape of international organisations, blocs and multilateral security agreements. Beyond the European Union, these include the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, the BRICS (the group originally comprised of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), and the Gulf Cooperation Council, among others.

Each of these groupings has its own distinct strategic interests and priorities. So, it remains unclear how a new Russia-led security framework would interact with these groups, or potentially compete with them.

Indeed, there seems to be a growing preference, especially in Asia, for smaller alliances between countries with similar ideological world views, such as the new security pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey.

At the same time, other nations, particularly those in Southeast Asia, have held fast to their non-aligned status, preferring to seek partnerships with an array of countries that suit a variety of interests.

Read more:
What Australia could learn from its Southeast Asian neighbours about power and the changing global order

What comes next?

We may be witnessing the gradual erosion of the post-second world war international order. Now, the big question is what comes next.

While Russia’s aims seem reminiscent of Soviet influence during the Cold War, this is a new world, and there are too many hurdles for its vision of a new security framework to become a reality.

New international orders do not emerge overnight. Rather, they evolve through the cumulative decisions of states pursuing their own interests, forming new alignments, alliances and partnerships along the way.

Dilnoza Ubaydullaeva receives funding from the Japan Foundation Program.

articles.title: Elon Musk has approval to launch 1 million satellites. An astronomer explains how this would impact the sky
articles.summary:
A long-exposure image of the Orion Nebula with a total exposure time of 208 minutes showing satellite trails in mid-December 2019. A. H. Abolfath/Wikimedia

This week, on the eve the Thanksgiving holiday, the United States Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s plan to launch one million “Starmind” artificial intelligence (AI) data centre satellites. This decision reflects the convergence of a satellite boom, an AI bubble and the Trump administration’s disregard for environmental regulation.

If Starmind proceeds in full, the number of operational satellites will be multiplied by a factor of 50. Space and our night skies will become vastly busier places.

SpaceX’s pitch is to take the impact of data centres away from Earth, using a million solar-powered satellites to do AI data crunching in space and beam the results to Earth.

But what is the impact of one million satellites, both in space and on Earth? Why has the Federal Communications Commission made this decision? And will a million satellites actually end up in orbit?

Ups and downs

We are currently in a satellite boom, and constellations of hundreds or thousands of satellites are a key feature.

The Starlink internet satellites (another SpaceX project) is the best known example of such a constellation. Orbital rocket launches have increased to almost one per day, while the number of operational satellites is creeping towards 20,000.

But Starmind represents something else. A million satellites.

To get so many satellites into orbit would be a vast undertaking. If the satellites have a lifetime of five years (similar to Starlink satellites), then roughly 500 satellites would need to be launched every day.

This also implies that roughly 500 satellites would eventually need to be disposed of every day. For satellites less than 2,000 kilometres above Earth, disposal usually means reentry and burning up in the atmosphere. And this has consequences.

When satellites burn up in the atmosphere, their materials react with and are deposited into the upper atmosphere. We now have satellites depositing far more aluminium, titanium, copper and lead into the atmosphere than the natural quantities from meteors.

Aluminium is of particular concern, as alumina can lead to the destruction of ozone in the upper atmosphere. This could increase ultraviolet light on Earth and the risk of skin cancers.

It’s getting busy

Increasing the number of satellites by a factor of 50 is going to change our view of the sky.

If you look up during the early evening, you will see the stars your ancestors saw. But within a minute or two you will see a satellite. A point of light silently moving from horizon to horizon.

Satellites are already common enough, and Starmind would make matters worse.

Our view of the night skies could fundamentally change.

Each satellite would be 75 metres wide and in the early evening they will be brighter than any star. And with a million satellites in orbit, there will be hundreds of Starmind satellites above the horizon irrespective of where you are.

The orbital clutter comes with real risks.

Satellites travel at speeds of roughly seven kilometres per second, and collisions produce clouds of debris that can produce further collisions. A nightmare scenario is the Kessler Syndrome – a runaway cascade of debris producing collisions that render low Earth orbit unusable.

Of course, SpaceX is aware of the risks of orbital collisions, and it already mitigates this risk with Starlink by manoeuvring satellites away from potential collisions. However, such manoeuvres require operational satellites and it is inevitable some satellites will fail.

Those uncontrolled satellites will pose a real danger.

Regulator or promoter?

The Federal Communications Commission has been a key regulator for American satellites. This has included regulating the radio frequencies that satellites use for communications to and from Earth, the disposal of satellites at the end of their useful lives and environmental impacts.

However, under the Trump administration, the commission is taking a looser approach to regulating satellites. This includes no consideration of environmental impacts, which is reflected in the commission’s decision on Starmind. It says the commission “will not require further environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act […] for SpaceX’s Starmind system”.

There are also some statements from the commission on Starmind that are, quite frankly, bizarre. For example, it claims Starmind “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”.

This is sci-fi silliness. A Kardashev II civilisation would need many trillions of square kilometres of technology in orbit around the Sun. Starmind is not a stepping stone to a vast “Dyson sphere” – a hypothetical megastrucutre that would surround the Sun and capture its energy.

But can it work?

One reason data centres are so unpopular on Earth is their use of precious resources, including water for cooling hot computer processors. But cooling in space is harder still. When stuck in a vacuum, one can only radiate heat away. And if you are familiar with vacuum flasks, you will know this can be a slow process.

Of course, it is possible to regulate heat in space, and satellites do it all the time. But they typically aren’t pouring out heat like data centres do.

Google recently launched an AI demonstrator satellite into orbit and tasked it with undertaking AI calculations. But it had to have downtime between calculations to dispose of excess heat.

And apart from the physics there’s the finance.

Right now we are in an AI boom, with the inflow of investment being vastly higher than revenues. And the cost of deploying AI in orbit will be vastly higher than equivalent AI on Earth.

If the AI boom is a bubble, then the burst can bring Starmind back to Earth.

Michael J. I. Brown does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Got a frozen shoulder? It could be down to your blood sugar and genes
articles.summary:
Frozen shoulder can make everyday movements difficult – and it’s more common in people with diabetes. PeopleImages/Shutterstock

Frozen shoulder can develop seemingly out of nowhere. One day your shoulder feels uncomfortable. A few months later, even putting on a coat or reaching into a cupboard can be difficult. Research on blood sugar offers a clue to why some people are more likely to develop it, particularly those living with diabetes.

Pain is often the first symptom, particularly at night. Over time, the shoulder grows stiffer. The flexible tissue that wraps around the joint, called the shoulder capsule, thickens and tightens, making it harder to move the arm.

That stiffness is a clue when a doctor or physiotherapist examines the shoulder. Even when someone else tries to move your arm for you, the movement is restricted. This is often most noticeable when they turn the arm outwards. The condition often improves, although recovery can take months or years.

Frozen shoulder is estimated to affect 2% to 5% of people and is most common between the ages of 40 and 60. It’s more common in women and people with diabetes are at higher risk. It can also develop after an injury or operation that stops you moving the arm as usual. Often there’s no clear trigger.

In type 1 diabetes, the body makes little or no insulin, the hormone that helps control blood sugar. In type 2 diabetes, the body makes too little insulin or has trouble using it. In a 2014 study, nearly a third of participants reported a history of frozen shoulder. They had lived with type 1 diabetes for an average of 31 years. A 2021 study using genetic data also found evidence that type 1 diabetes increases the risk of frozen shoulder.

High blood sugar

A 2024 study using data from nearly 380,000 UK Biobank participants investigated whether raised blood sugar might help explain that link. Some inherited differences in DNA are linked to higher blood sugar. Because those differences are present from birth, they give researchers a kind of natural experiment. They can use them to estimate the effects of having higher blood sugar over many years, something a single blood test can’t capture. The study found evidence that persistently higher blood sugar makes frozen shoulder more likely.

One possible explanation is that sugar gradually changes the structure of the tissue around the joint. Sugars can react with collagen, a protein that gives the tissue much of its strength. The substances formed in that reaction can join collagen fibres together, making the tissue less flexible. In one small study of tissue taken during shoulder surgery, researchers found stronger signs of these compounds in samples from people with frozen shoulder than in samples from people with other shoulder problems. It’s a clue to how the tissue might stiffen. To find out whether these substances help cause frozen shoulder, researchers would need to know whether they build up before the shoulder stiffens.

Long-term high blood sugar has been linked to both frozen shoulder and Dupuytren’s disease, a hand condition that can make it difficult to straighten the fingers.
gdragan/Shutterstock

A 2021 study found five stretches of DNA linked to frozen shoulder. The strongest link was near a gene called WNT7B, which helps cells send signals to one another. Intriguingly, the same stretch of DNA has also been linked to Dupuytren’s disease, a condition in which tissue in the palm thickens and can pull the fingers inwards, making them hard to straighten. This suggests the two conditions may share some of the processes that cause tissue to thicken and tighten. The blood-sugar study found another link. Years of higher blood sugar appeared to make Dupuytren’s disease more likely, too.

For people with diabetes, persistent shoulder stiffness is worth bringing up at a routine appointment, especially if it’s starting to interfere with sleep or everyday tasks. For clinicians, it deserves attention alongside more familiar problems diabetes can cause in the eyes and kidneys. Whether improving blood sugar control can help prevent frozen shoulder or speed up recovery once it has developed is still an open question.
